How to read the table

Raw score: the number of words the child knows (only some rows are shown).
PR: the percentage of 10-year-olds scoring lower.
T, IQ-style, Sten, Stanine: the normalised standard scores.
95% CI for T: the range in which the child’s score would fall in 95 of 100 testings, given the reliability of the test. With \(r_{xx}\) = .95 it is about ±4.4 T points.

A 10-year-old with 170 words has T = 46, 95% CI [42, 51]: a little below average on the point score, but the interval includes 50, so the test cannot tell this child apart from an average one. Reports that give only the point score suggest a precision the test does not have.
Two refinements are common in manuals. Some centre the interval on the estimated true score, \(50 + r_{xx}(T - 50)\), which is pulled slightly towards the mean. And many use 90% instead of 95% intervals. rawTable() of cNORM produces both kinds of table from a norm model (section 6).
The table has another flaw: the steps are uneven. Raw scores with many children jump, others barely move, and a single child more or less in the norm sample would change the values. Real norms are smoothed, which is one of the things continuous norming does.

title: Test Norms in R: Percentiles, T-Scores, Stens and Age Norms
section: 5. How large must a norm group be, and who must be in it?
text:
5. How large must a norm group be, and who must be in it?
The norm scores of the table are estimates from 411 children; another sample of 10-year-olds would give slightly different ones. How much? We draw many samples of a given size from the 10-year-olds (with replacement, a bootstrap) and see how much the raw score at three points of the scale varies: T = 30 (the 2nd percentile), T = 40 and T = 50 (the median).


Code
set.seed(1)
targets <- c("T = 30 (2nd percentile)" = pnorm(-2), "T = 40 (16th percentile)" = pnorm(-1),
             "T = 50 (median)" = 0.5)
sizes <- c(50, 100, 200, 400)
err <- expand.grid(n = sizes, point = names(targets), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
err$sd_raw <- mapply(function(n, point) {
  sd(replicate(2000, quantile(sample(x, n, replace = TRUE), targets[[point]])))
}, err$n, err$point)
err$point <- factor(err$point, levels = names(targets))
reshape(err, idvar = "point", timevar = "n", direction = "wide")


                     point sd_raw.50 sd_raw.100 sd_raw.200 sd_raw.400
1  T = 30 (2nd percentile) 10.116168   8.050163   6.370151   5.424654
5 T = 40 (16th percentile)  4.481647   3.214380   2.267838   1.689409
9          T = 50 (median)  3.199054   2.466709   1.847321   1.430804




Code
ggplot(err, aes(n, sd_raw, colour = point)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sem_raw, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 400, y = sem_raw, label = "SEM of the test", vjust = -0.6, hjust = 1, size = 3.2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sizes) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E74C3C", "#f39c12", "#0082c8")) +
  labs(title = "Sampling error of the norms: how much the raw score at each point varies",
       x = "children in the norm group", y = "SD of the estimate (raw points)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










The error shrinks with the size of the norm group, roughly as \(1 / \sqrt{n}\).
It is much larger in the tails. With 100 children, the raw score that marks T = 30 varies by about 8.1 points, against 2.5 at the median. Yet the tails are where decisions are made (a learning difficulty, a giftedness programme).
In the tails the error of the norms is larger than the measurement error of the test (the dashed line) even with 400 children, and the two add up.

A few hundred people per norm group is a common minimum for separate tables, and the extremes need more. Continuous norming (section 6) needs fewer, because every age group helps to estimate the others.
Size is not enough: the sample must also be representative. Here 64% of the children come from the south, far more than the south’s share of the country’s children. If children from different regions score differently, the norms are biased, and a larger sample would not fix that. Norm samples are therefore stratified: drawn to match the population on age, sex, region, education and similar variables. When the sample does not match, cases can be weighted to the known population shares; computeWeights() of cNORM does this (raking), and the weights can be passed to cnorm().

title: Test Norms in R: Percentiles, T-Scores, Stens and Age Norms
text:
6. Age norms

Separate tables per age group, and their problem
The traditional solution is a table like the one in section 4 for every age group, say every year of age. Take a child with 150 words and look up their T-score in each year’s table:


Code
t_in_band <- function(score, scores) {                  # normalised T of a score within a group
  pr <- 100 * (mean(scores < score) + 0.5 * mean(scores == score))
  50 + 10 * qnorm(pr / 100)
}
bands <- 7:15
band_T <- sapply(bands, function(a) t_in_band(150, ppvt$raw[floor(ppvt$age) == a]))
data.frame(age_group = paste0(bands, ".00-", bands, ".99"), n = as.numeric(table(floor(ppvt$age))[as.character(bands)]),
           T_for_150_words = round(band_T, 1))


    age_group   n T_for_150_words
1   7.00-7.99 333            54.0
2   8.00-8.99 429            47.9
3   9.00-9.99 412            41.9
4 10.00-10.99 411            36.9
5 11.00-11.99 552            36.0
6 12.00-12.99 505            36.4
7 13.00-13.99 449            34.2
8 14.00-14.99 363            31.2
9 15.00-15.99 235            29.3


The T-score for the same 150 words drops in steps, from one year’s table to the next. A child with 150 words gets T = 42 on the day before their 10th birthday and T = 37 on the day after: a drop of 5 T points overnight, more than the ±4.4 points of the test’s 95% confidence interval. In between, every child of 9.0 and 9.9 years is compared with the same table, although vocabulary grows within the year. And each table uses only the children of its own year, a few hundred at most.


Continuous norming
Continuous (regression-based) norming fits one model for all ages together (Lenhard et al., 2018). The idea, in three steps:

Within each age group, give every child their normalised score, as in section 3. cNORM calls it the location \(L\) (on the T scale here).
Fit a regression of the raw score on powers of \(L\), powers of age \(A\), and their products: \[\text{raw} = \sum_{s=0}^{k}\sum_{t=0}^{k} c_{st}\, L^s A^t\] This is a smooth surface: for every age and every norm score it gives the raw score.
Keep only the terms that matter, chosen by how much they add to \(R^2\).

The surface can then be read in both directions: the raw score for a given norm score and age (the percentile curves), or the norm score for a given raw score and age (the norm table). cnorm() does all three steps; ppvt$group holds the mean age of each child’s age group:


Code
model_all <- cnorm(raw = ppvt$raw, group = ppvt$group, plot = FALSE)   # all candidate models
adj_r2 <- model_all$model$subsets$adjr2
ggplot(data.frame(terms = seq_along(adj_r2), adj_r2), aes(terms, adj_r2)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(terms = 5, adj_r2 = adj_r2[5]), colour = "#E74C3C", size = 4) +
  labs(title = "How well models with more terms describe the data", x = "number of terms",
       y = expression("adjusted " * R^2))









By default cnorm() picks the largest model without inconsistencies (22 terms here). But adjusted \(R^2\) hardly grows after about 5 terms (0.9899 with 5, 0.9916 at most), and simpler models are smoother and less likely to bend strangely at the edges. We keep 5:


Code
model <- cnorm(raw = ppvt$raw, group = ppvt$group, terms = 5, plot = FALSE)
cat(model$model$report[1:3], sep = "\n")


User specified solution: 5 terms
R-Square Adj. = 0.989925
Final regression model: raw ~ L3 + L1A1 + L2A1 + L1A2 + L3A3



User specified solution: the number of terms, chosen by us with terms = 5 (without it, cNORM reports its own choice here).
R-Square Adj.: the share of the variance of the raw scores the surface explains, given the age and the location of each child. Above .99 is typical for a good norm model.
Final regression model: the terms. L1A1 is \(L \times A\), L2A1 is \(L^2 \times A\), and so on. The individual coefficients mean nothing by themselves; only the whole surface does.

Always check that the percentile curves do not cross (a higher norm score must always need a higher raw score):


Code
crossing <- checkConsistency(model, minAge = 3.2, maxAge = 16.4, minNorm = 25, maxNorm = 75)


No relevant violations of model consistency found.


The check covers ages 3.2 to 16.4 (the mean ages of the youngest and oldest groups) and T-scores 25 to 75. It returns TRUE if it finds curves that cross; here it returned FALSE. Outside the ages of the norm sample, the model extrapolates and should not be used.


Percentile curves
For each T-score, the model gives the raw score needed at every age:


Code
ages <- seq(3.2, 16.4, by = 0.1)
norms <- c(30, 40, 50, 60, 70)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(norms, function(nt) data.frame(
  age = ages, raw = sapply(ages, function(a) predictRaw(nt, a, model$model$coefficients)),
  T = paste0("T = ", nt, " (PR ", sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pnorm((nt - 50) / 10)), ")"))))
curves$T <- factor(curves$T, levels = unique(curves$T))
ggplot(ppvt, aes(age, raw)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.7, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(colour = T), linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E74C3C", "#f39c12", "black", "#0082c8", "#8E44AD")) +
  labs(title = "Percentile curves from the continuous norm model", x = "age (years)",
       y = "raw score", colour = NULL)









Each curve is a smooth line through all ages: the black one is the average child (T = 50), the red one the lowest 2%. The curves fan out in the middle years and come together at the top, where the test runs out of hard words.


The birthday problem, solved


Code
fine_ages <- seq(7, 15.99, by = 0.02)
cont_T <- predictNorm(rep(150, length(fine_ages)), fine_ages, model)
comp <- rbind(data.frame(age = fine_ages, T = band_T[match(floor(fine_ages), bands)], method = "separate table for each year"),
              data.frame(age = fine_ages, T = cont_T, method = "continuous norm model"))
ggplot(comp, aes(age, T, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0082c8", "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "T-score of a child who knows 150 words, by age", x = "age (years)", y = "T-score",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
round(c(day_before_10th_birthday = predictNorm(150, 9.99, model), day_after = predictNorm(150, 10.01, model)), 1)


day_before_10th_birthday                day_after 
                    40.3                     40.3 


The continuous model gives a T-score that falls smoothly with age: the same child gets the same score on either side of their birthday. The separate tables do not even fall steadily: from the 11-year-olds’ table to the 12-year-olds’ the T-score goes up, a fluke of two samples of a few hundred children each.


The norm table from the model
rawTable() gives the smoothed table for any exact age, here 10.5 years, with the 95% confidence intervals of section 4 computed for us. The model’s T-scores follow the empirical ones of section 4, without their jumps:


Code
model_tab <- rawTable(10.5, model, step = 1, CI = 0.95, reliability = reliability)
scores <- c(140, 150, 165, 180, 195)
comparison <- data.frame(raw = scores,
                         T_one_year_table = tab$T_norm[match(scores, tab$raw)],
                         T_continuous_10.5 = model_tab$norm[match(scores, model_tab$raw)])
round(comparison, 1)


  raw T_one_year_table T_continuous_10.5
1 140             33.3              35.4
2 150             36.9              38.6
3 165             43.9              44.4
4 180             51.4              51.9
5 195             64.6              63.5

title: Test Norms in R: Percentiles, T-Scores, Stens and Age Norms
text:
7. Reporting norms
A test manual or a report of norms (AERA et al., 2014) should describe the norm sample (size, when and where it was collected, how it was drawn, how well it matches the population), the norm scores and how they were derived (linear or normalised, separate tables or continuous norming, smoothing), the reliability and the SEM behind the confidence intervals, and the limits of the norms (ages covered, groups not represented). We collect the numbers from the R objects:


Code
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
r2 <- model$model$subsets$adjr2[5]


Method (norms):

Norms were derived from 4,542 children and adolescents aged 2.5 to 17.0 years (48.7% female; 27.7% with a migration background). Raw scores were converted into normalised T-scores (M = 50, SD = 10) with continuous norming (Lenhard et al., 2018): within 15 age groups, raw scores were ranked and transformed to normal scores, and the raw scores were then modelled as a polynomial function of the normal score and age. A model with 5 terms explained 99.0% of the variance (adjusted R² = .990), and its percentile curves did not intersect between 3.2 and 16.4 years. Confidence intervals are based on a reliability of .95 (SEM = 2.24 T points). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the cNORM package.

title: Test Norms in R: Percentiles, T-Scores, Stens and Age Norms
text:
8. Summary







Why norms
A raw score means something only compared with a reference group of similar people


Percentile rank
\(\text{PR} = 100\,(B + F/2) / N\), the mid-point convention; easy to explain, unequal steps


Standard scores
z; T = 50 + 10z; IQ-style = 100 + 15z; sten = 5.5 + 2z (1 to 10); stanine = 5 + 2z (1 to 9)


Linear or normalised
Linear: \((x - \bar x) / s\), keeps the skew. Normalised: qnorm(PR / 100), the same meaning everywhere


Confidence intervals
\(\text{SEM} = SD\sqrt{1 - r_{xx}}\); on the T scale \(T \pm 1.96 \times 10\sqrt{1 - r_{xx}}\)


Norm sample
Large (most error is in the tails) and representative (stratified, or weighted)


Age norms
Separate tables jump at the edges of the age groups; continuous norming gives smooth norms for every age


R
qnorm(), pnorm(); cNORM::cnorm(), predictNorm(), predictRaw(), rawTable(), checkConsistency(); snp::plot_normal() for the scales

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
text:
Countries that spend more on health have longer-living people. But how much longer, for each extra dollar? To answer, we draw a line through about 190 countries and read its slope.
Some countries do not follow the pattern. The Central African Republic spends little and its people live much shorter than even that low spending predicts. A few small island states spend a lot and do not live longer. Ordinary least squares (OLS) gives every country the same say, and lets such countries drag the line towards them.
This page asks: how much does one tenfold step in health spending buy in life expectancy, when we do not let a handful of odd countries decide? The answer is robust regression: estimation that resists outliers.










Resists outliers in \(y\)
Resists bad leverage points
Efficient when data are clean




OLS (lm())
no
no
the best


M-estimation (rlm())
yes
no
high (about 95%)


MM-estimation (lmrob())
yes
yes
high (about 95%)


LTS (lqs())
yes
yes
low



The columns are explained in section 3. This page does not re-teach ordinary regression: see hierarchical regression for that.


Code
library(MASS)       # rlm() and lqs(): robust regression (comes with R)
library(robustbase) # lmrob(): MM-estimation (a CRAN package, not part of R)
library(sandwich)   # vcovHC(): heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors
library(lmtest)     # coeftest(), bptest()
library(jsonlite)   # fromJSON(): reads the World Bank API
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)    # labels that do not overlap

# one colour per method, the same in every chart
method_colours <- c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "Huber" = "#eb6834", "Bisquare" = "#1baf7a",
                    "MM" = "#eda100", "LTS" = "#e87ba4")

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

# the sensitivity analysis of section 5: alter the spending of k_bad of the n_poor lowest spenders
k_bad  <- 12
n_poor <- 30

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
text:
1. The data
The World Bank publishes the World Development Indicators through an open API: free, no key and no login. We take two indicators for the year 2021 and the list of countries:

SH.XPD.CHEX.PC.CD: current health expenditure per capita, in current US dollars. The World Bank gets it from the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database. “Current” means money spent in that year on health goods and services (not on buildings); “per capita” means per person.
SP.DYN.LE00.IN: life expectancy at birth, in years: how long a newborn would live if the death rates of that year stayed the same for life. It comes from the United Nations World Population Prospects and national statistical offices.
The country list, with region and income group, which tells countries from aggregates such as “World” or “Sub-Saharan Africa”. The indicators contain both.



Code
base <- "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/"
urls <- c(spend     = paste0(base, "country/all/indicator/SH.XPD.CHEX.PC.CD?format=json&date=2021&per_page=400"),
          life      = paste0(base, "country/all/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN?format=json&date=2021&per_page=400"),
          countries = paste0(base, "country?format=json&per_page=400"))

started <- Sys.time()
files   <- sapply(urls, function(u) { f <- tempfile(fileext = ".json"); download.file(u, f, quiet = TRUE); f })
seconds <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), started, units = "secs"))
kilobytes <- sum(file.size(files)) / 1024

api <- lapply(files, fromJSON)
sapply(api, function(a) a[[1]]$pages)   # 1 each: everything arrived on the first page


    spend      life countries 
        1         1         1 


The three downloads took 0.2 seconds and 235 kB together. Each answer has the number of pages in its first element and the records in its second, so [[2]] holds the data. We join the three, drop the aggregates and the countries with a missing value:


Code
countries <- data.frame(iso3 = api$countries[[2]]$id, name = api$countries[[2]]$name,
                        region = api$countries[[2]]$region$value, income = api$countries[[2]]$incomeLevel$value)
health <- data.frame(iso3 = api$spend[[2]]$countryiso3code, spend = api$spend[[2]]$value)
life   <- data.frame(iso3 = api$life[[2]]$countryiso3code,  life  = api$life[[2]]$value)

d <- merge(merge(health, life, by = "iso3"), countries, by = "iso3")
n_all <- nrow(d)
d <- d[d$region != "Aggregates" & complete.cases(d), ]
d$logspend <- log10(d$spend)          # explained in section 2
rownames(d) <- d$name
n <- nrow(d)
head(d[order(d$spend), c("spend", "life", "region")], 4)


                      spend   life              region
Somalia, Fed. Rep. 15.01880 55.703 Sub-Saharan Africa 
Madagascar         17.17939 62.516 Sub-Saharan Africa 
Congo, Dem. Rep.   21.58849 60.044 Sub-Saharan Africa 
Sudan              21.69141 64.460 Sub-Saharan Africa 


That leaves 192 countries and territories (the join had 261 rows, aggregates included). The terms of use: the World Bank licenses its own datasets under CC BY 4.0 by default (World Bank, n.d.), with attribution; the API does not say the licence of each single indicator, and the two used here come from the WHO and the United Nations, so check the terms of an indicator on its World Bank page before reusing it beyond a tutorial like this one. Names are as the World Bank writes them: “Naoero” is Nauru.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
long <- rbind(data.frame(life = d$life, x = d$spend,        scale = "Spending in dollars"),
              data.frame(life = d$life, x = log10(d$spend), scale = "Log10 of spending"))
long$scale <- factor(long$scale, levels = c("Spending in dollars", "Log10 of spending"))
ggplot(long, aes(x, life)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(v) num(v), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.1))) +
  labs(title = "Life expectancy against health spending, 2021",
       x = "health spending per person", y = "life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_bw()









The right panel shows the same points with the logarithm of spending on the axis. Look at the left panel first. Most countries crowd on the left, and a straight line through them would not describe the curve: the first dollars buy a lot of life, the ten-thousandth dollar very little. Taking the logarithm of spending, base 10, turns equal ratios into equal steps, and the cloud becomes straight. So we model
\[\text{life}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log_{10}(\text{spend}_i) + \varepsilon_i\]
and \(\beta_1\) is the gain in life expectancy for each tenfold increase in spending. Doubling is a smaller step: \(\beta_1 \times \log_{10} 2\).


Code
ols <- lm(life ~ logspend, data = d)

ggplot(d, aes(spend, life)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(ols)[[1]], slope = coef(ols)[[2]], colour = method_colours[["OLS"]]) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = function(v) num(v), breaks = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000)) +
  labs(title = "On a log scale the cloud is straight",
       x = "health spending per person (US$, log scale)", y = "life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_bw()









The OLS line is 47.9 + 8.84 \(\times \log_{10}\)(spend): each tenfold increase goes with 8.8 more years of life, and a doubling with 2.7. Some points lie far from the line, mostly below it.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: why least squares is fragile
OLS chooses the line that makes the sum of squared residuals \(\sum_i e_i^2\) as small as possible, where \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_i\). Squaring is the problem: a country that is 20 years off the line costs \(400\), a hundred times as much as one that is 2 years off. To save that cost, the line moves towards it. One bad point can move the OLS line as far as it likes. To see this, we take one country with a high spending, Switzerland, and slide its life expectancy from 0 to 120 years. At each value we refit the line:


Code
slide <- seq(0, 120, by = 4)
slope_when <- function(value) {
  z <- d
  z["Switzerland", "life"] <- value
  c(OLS = coef(lm(life ~ logspend, z))[[2]],
    Huber = coef(rlm(life ~ logspend, z))[[2]],
    Bisquare = coef(rlm(life ~ logspend, z, psi = psi.bisquare))[[2]])
}
slides <- t(sapply(slide, slope_when))
slides <- data.frame(value = rep(slide, 3), slope = c(slides), method = rep(colnames(slides), each = length(slide)))
slides$method <- factor(slides$method, levels = c("OLS", "Huber", "Bisquare"))
swiss <- d["Switzerland", ]
range_by <- tapply(slides$slope, slides$method, function(s) diff(range(s)))




Code
ggplot(slides, aes(value, slope, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = swiss$life, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = swiss$life - 1.5, y = max(slides$slope), label = "actual value",
           hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 3.3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = method_colours) +
  labs(title = "Moving one country's life expectancy",
       x = "life expectancy given to Switzerland (years)", y = "estimated slope (years per tenfold)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The OLS slope follows the value we gave Switzerland in a straight line: it moves by 1.7 years per tenfold across the range, and nothing stops it. The robust slopes move by 0.2 (Huber) and 0.2 (bisquare): the further away the point is, the less it matters, and that is what we want to build.


Step 2: three kinds of unusual point
“Outlier” is used for three different things, with three different checks. All three come from the OLS fit, with \(p = 2\) parameters and \(n\) points:








Kind
What it is
Measure




Outlier in \(y\)
far from the line, up or down, at a usual \(x\)
studentized residual \(t_i\): the residual divided by its standard error, with the point left out of the fit. Beyond \(\pm 2\) or \(\pm 3\) is unusual


High-leverage point
far from the other points in \(x\), wherever its \(y\) is
hat value \(h_i\), the diagonal of \(H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\). The average is \(p/n\); above \(2p/n\) is high


Influential point
removing it changes the fit a lot
Cook’s distance \(D_i = \dfrac{e_i^2}{p\,s^2}\dfrac{h_i}{(1 - h_i)^2}\): large when both the residual and the leverage are large. A common flag is \(4/n\)



A high-leverage point that sits on the trend is a good leverage point: it makes the line more precise. One that sits off the trend is a bad leverage point, and is the most dangerous kind: it has the leverage to pull the line, and the residual to pull it the wrong way. Because the line bends towards it, its own residual in OLS is small, and the point hides itself.


Code
d$hat     <- hatvalues(ols)
d$student <- rstudent(ols)
d$cook    <- cooks.distance(ols)
flag_cook <- 4 / n
flag_hat  <- 2 * 2 / n
d$flagged <- d$cook > flag_cook | d$hat > flag_hat | abs(d$student) > 2.5
top_cook  <- d[order(-d$cook), ][1:6, c("spend", "life", "hat", "student", "cook")]
round(top_cook, 3)


                             spend   life   hat student  cook
Central African Republic    46.250 40.279 0.014  -5.451 0.188
Naoero                    1636.458 61.331 0.009  -3.494 0.051
United States            12080.073 76.329 0.027  -1.757 0.042
Nigeria                     81.873 53.455 0.010  -2.612 0.034
Chad                        37.592 53.136 0.016  -1.987 0.032
Lesotho                    115.814 54.209 0.008  -2.748 0.031




Code
labelled <- d$cook > flag_cook | abs(d$student) > 2.5 | d$hat > 0.025
ggplot(d, aes(hat, student)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-2.5, 2.5), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = flag_hat, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(size = cook), colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_text_repel(data = d[labelled, ], aes(label = name), size = 3, min.segment.length = 0, max.overlaps = Inf) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 9, name = "Cook's distance") +
  labs(title = "Leverage, residual and influence of each country",
       x = "hat value (leverage)", y = "studentized residual") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Dashed lines mark the flags: hat values above .021, residuals beyond ±2.5. In these data:

The biggest outlier in \(y\) is Central African Republic (studentized residual -5.5) and also the most influential point, with Cook’s distance 0.19, 9.0 times the flag. 5 countries lie beyond ±2.5.
The points of highest leverage are the biggest and smallest spenders: United States is the highest (hat value .027, against an average of .010). On a log scale, spending is not extreme in any country, so no point has enormous leverage, and United States’s studentized residual is only -1.8. Real data seldom come with a bad leverage point on demand: section 5 makes one.



Step 3: M-estimation, the idea
Instead of squares, M-estimation (the “M” is for maximum likelihood type; Huber, 1964) minimises a loss function \(\rho\) of the scaled residuals:
\[\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \sum_{i=1}^{n} \rho\!\left(\frac{e_i}{s}\right), \qquad e_i = y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta\]
\(s\) is a robust scale: an estimate of the typical size of a residual that outliers do not inflate, usually the median absolute residual divided by 0.6745 (so that it equals the standard deviation for normal errors). With \(\rho(u) = u^2/2\) this is OLS. Robust methods replace \(\rho\) by a function that grows more slowly. The derivative \(\psi = \rho'\) is the influence function: how hard a residual of size \(u\) pulls on the line. The weight is \(w(u) = \psi(u)/u\).










\(\rho(u)\)
\(\psi(u)\)
\(w(u)\)




Least squares
\(u^2/2\)
\(u\)
\(1\)


Huber, \(k = 1.345\)
\(u^2/2\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le k\), else \(k\lvert u\rvert - k^2/2\)
\(u\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le k\), else \(k\,\mathrm{sign}(u)\)
\(1\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le k\), else \(k/\lvert u\rvert\)


Tukey’s bisquare, \(c = 4.685\)
\(\dfrac{c^2}{6}\left[1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{u^2}{c^2}\right)^3\right]\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le c\), else \(\dfrac{c^2}{6}\)
\(u\left(1 - \dfrac{u^2}{c^2}\right)^2\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le c\), else \(0\)
\(\left(1 - \dfrac{u^2}{c^2}\right)^2\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le c\), else \(0\)



The constants \(k = 1.345\) and \(c = 4.685\) are chosen so that, when the errors really are normal, the estimator is 95% as efficient as OLS: its standard errors are only about 2.5% larger. They are the defaults of rlm() and lmrob().


Code
huber_rho <- function(u, k = 1.345) ifelse(abs(u) <= k, u^2 / 2, k * abs(u) - k^2 / 2)
huber_psi <- function(u, k = 1.345) pmax(-k, pmin(k, u))
huber_w   <- function(u, k = 1.345) ifelse(abs(u) <= k, 1, k / abs(u))
bisq_rho  <- function(u, c = 4.685) ifelse(abs(u) <= c, c^2 / 6 * (1 - (1 - (u / c)^2)^3), c^2 / 6)
bisq_psi  <- function(u, c = 4.685) ifelse(abs(u) <= c, u * (1 - (u / c)^2)^2, 0)
bisq_w    <- function(u, c = 4.685) ifelse(abs(u) <= c, (1 - (u / c)^2)^2, 0)

# the formulas above agree with the ones inside MASS
u <- seq(-8, 8, by = 0.1)
c(huber = max(abs(huber_w(u) - psi.huber(u))), bisquare = max(abs(bisq_w(u) - psi.bisquare(u))))


   huber bisquare 
       0        0 




Code
curve_names <- c("Least squares", "Huber", "Bisquare")
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(u, value = u^2 / 2,     fn = "Loss, ρ(u)",         method = "Least squares"),
  data.frame(u, value = huber_rho(u), fn = "Loss, ρ(u)",        method = "Huber"),
  data.frame(u, value = bisq_rho(u),  fn = "Loss, ρ(u)",        method = "Bisquare"),
  data.frame(u, value = u,            fn = "Influence, ψ(u)",   method = "Least squares"),
  data.frame(u, value = huber_psi(u), fn = "Influence, ψ(u)",   method = "Huber"),
  data.frame(u, value = bisq_psi(u),  fn = "Influence, ψ(u)",   method = "Bisquare"),
  data.frame(u, value = 1,            fn = "Weight, w(u)",      method = "Least squares"),
  data.frame(u, value = huber_w(u),   fn = "Weight, w(u)",      method = "Huber"),
  data.frame(u, value = bisq_w(u),    fn = "Weight, w(u)",      method = "Bisquare"))
curves$method <- factor(curves$method, levels = curve_names)
curves$fn     <- factor(curves$fn, levels = c("Loss, ρ(u)", "Influence, ψ(u)", "Weight, w(u)"))
curves <- subset(curves, !(fn == "Loss, ρ(u)" & abs(value) > 12))   # keep the loss panel readable

ggplot(curves, aes(u, value, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ fn, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Least squares" = method_colours[["OLS"]],
                                 Huber = method_colours[["Huber"]], Bisquare = method_colours[["Bisquare"]])) +
  labs(title = "Loss, influence and weight of a residual",
       x = "scaled residual u = e / s", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Read the three panels from top to bottom:

Loss. OLS (blue) squares the residual, so the loss climbs steeply. Huber’s loss turns into a straight line after \(k\): big residuals cost much less. The bisquare loss stops growing altogether after \(c\): beyond that, it does not matter how far away a point is.
Influence. OLS influence grows with the residual forever. Huber’s is bounded: no residual pulls harder than \(k\). Bisquare’s redescends: it rises, falls back, and is exactly zero beyond \(c\). Such a point has no say at all.
Weight. Every OLS residual has weight 1. Huber gives weight \(k/\lvert u\rvert\) beyond \(k\): smaller, but never zero. Bisquare gives zero weight to residuals beyond \(c = 4.685\) scaled units.



Step 4: how R finds the numbers, by iteratively reweighted least squares
No formula gives the minimum of \(\sum\rho(e_i/s)\) directly, but the weights turn it into a series of ordinary regressions (iteratively reweighted least squares, IRLS):

Fit OLS and compute the residuals \(e_i\).
Estimate the scale \(s\) from the residuals, and the scaled residuals \(u_i = e_i/s\).
Give every point the weight \(w_i = w(u_i)\).
Fit a weighted least squares line with those weights: minimise \(\sum w_i e_i^2\). (For weighted least squares, see the page on it.)
Go back to step 2, until the coefficients stop changing.

A country that the line fits badly gets a small weight, so next time the line follows it less, its residual stays large and its weight small. The final weights show who was ignored. We will do the loop by hand in section 4.


Step 5: the limit of M-estimators, and the breakdown point
M-estimators bound the influence of a large residual, but do nothing about leverage: a point far out in \(x\) drags the line so that its own residual is small, and so it keeps a large weight. Worse, IRLS starts from OLS, which the bad point has already ruined.
The breakdown point measures this in plain words: the share of the data that can be replaced by anything, however absurd, before the estimate can be taken anywhere you like.

OLS: one point, so a breakdown point of \(1/n\), almost 0%.
Huber M-estimator: it resists bad \(y\) values but a bad \(x\) value can break it, so with leverage points it too has a breakdown point of about \(1/n\).
Estimators with the highest possible breakdown point, 50%: the least trimmed squares (LTS, Rousseeuw, 1984), which minimises the sum of the smallest half of the squared residuals, and S-estimators. They resist up to nearly half of the data being bad. They are far less efficient when the data are clean.
MM-estimators (Yohai, 1987) combine the two: an S-estimate gives a first fit and a robust scale \(s\) (that is the 50% breakdown part), then a bisquare M-step starting from it, tuned for 95% efficiency. This is why lmrob() is the usual first choice today (Maronna et al., 2019).

The same numbers by hand: IRLS in six lines


Code
X <- model.matrix(~ logspend, d)
y <- d$life
b <- coef(ols)                                     # step 1: start from OLS
for (i in 1:50) {
  e  <- y - X %*% b
  s  <- median(abs(e)) / 0.6745                    # step 2: robust scale
  w  <- huber_w(e / s)                             # step 3: Huber weights
  b_new <- solve(t(X) %*% (c(w) * X), t(X) %*% (c(w) * y))   # step 4: weighted least squares
  if (max(abs(b_new - b)) < 1e-8) break
  b <- b_new
}
rbind(by_hand = c(b), rlm = coef(huber))

Code

coef(lts)

lqs(method = "lts") has the 50% breakdown point, but gives no standard errors, so we use it as a check on the others rather than as the final fit.


The comparison


Code
slope_row <- function(method, est, se, scale) {
  data.frame(method = method, intercept = est[1], slope = est[2], se = se, scale = scale,
             lower = est[2] - qnorm(.975) * se, upper = est[2] + qnorm(.975) * se)
}
robust_fits <- function(z) {
  fits <- list(OLS      = lm(life ~ logspend, z),
               Huber    = rlm(life ~ logspend, z),
               Bisquare = rlm(life ~ logspend, z, psi = psi.bisquare),
               MM       = lmrob(life ~ logspend, z))
  rows <- lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
    f <- fits[[m]]
    sm <- summary(f)$coefficients
    sc <- if (m == "OLS") summary(f)$sigma else if (m == "MM") f$scale else f$s
    slope_row(m, sm[, 1], sm[2, 2], sc)
  })
  list(fits = fits, table = do.call(rbind, rows))
}
clean <- robust_fits(d)
comparison <- clean$table
comparison$method <- factor(comparison$method, levels = names(method_colours)[1:4])

The slopes are close: from 8.74 to 8.84. In these real data the line is more or less right under every method, which is what we hope to see: nobody can claim the result depends on the estimator. OLS is 0.10 years lower than MM.
The intercepts are 47.85 for OLS and 48.64 for MM, because the down-weighted countries all sit below the line: the robust line rides higher through the bulk of the countries.
The residual scale is what changes most: 4.42 years for OLS and 3.61 for MM. The OLS figure is inflated by a few countries; the robust one describes the typical country. The standard errors are also smaller for the robust fits (0.35 against 0.44), as the outliers no longer inflate the noise. Robust regression can be more efficient than OLS when the errors have heavy tails.
The “scale” of Huber and bisquare comes from rlm() and the MM one from lmrob(), so they are comparable only roughly.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
section: 5. Where M-estimation is not enough: bad leverage points
text:
5. Where M-estimation is not enough: bad leverage points
The real data have outliers but no bad leverage points, so every method gives much the same line. To see what happens when there is one, we damage the data on purpose. Suppose a data-entry error made the spending of the 12 countries with the shortest-lived people, among the 30 lowest spenders, a thousand times too large (a unit slip: that is 3 steps of \(\log_{10}\)). Those are the countries that pull the OLS line flat:


Code
make_bad <- function(k, shift = 3) {
  poorest <- d[order(d$spend), ][seq_len(min(n, max(n_poor, round(2.5 * k)))), ]   # the lowest spenders
  bad     <- rownames(poorest)[order(poorest$life)][seq_len(k)]   # the k with the lowest life expectancy
  z <- d
  z[bad, "logspend"] <- z[bad, "logspend"] + shift
  z$altered <- rownames(z) %in% bad
  z
}
d_bad <- make_bad(k_bad)
bad   <- robust_fits(d_bad)
bd    <- bad$table
rownames(bd) <- bd$method
set.seed(1)
lts_bad <- lqs(life ~ logspend, data = d_bad, method = "lts")
lts_clean <- lqs(life ~ logspend, data = d, method = "lts")
data.frame(method = bd$method, slope = round(bd$slope, 2), clean = round(cl$slope, 2))


    method slope clean
1      OLS  3.00  8.84
2    Huber  6.41  8.81
3 Bisquare  8.17  8.74
4       MM  8.17  8.74




Code
d_bad$spend_shown <- 10^d_bad$logspend
lines_bad <- data.frame(method = names(bad$fits), do.call(rbind, lapply(bad$fits, line_of)))
names(lines_bad)[2:3] <- c("intercept", "slope")
lines_bad <- rbind(lines_bad, data.frame(method = "LTS", intercept = coef(lts_bad)[[1]], slope = coef(lts_bad)[[2]]))
lines_bad$method <- factor(lines_bad$method, levels = names(method_colours))
d_bad$status <- factor(ifelse(d_bad$altered, "Spending altered", "As published"),
                       levels = c("As published", "Spending altered"))
ggplot(d_bad, aes(spend_shown, life)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = status, size = status), colour = "grey40", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(data = lines_bad, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = method), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("As published" = 16, "Spending altered" = 17)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c("As published" = 1.7, "Spending altered" = 3)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = method_colours) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(38, 88)) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = function(v) num(v), breaks = c(10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1), shape = guide_legend(order = 2), size = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Twelve countries with a wrong spending value",
       x = "health spending per person (US$, log scale)", y = "life expectancy (years)",
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL, size = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The 12 altered countries (triangles) sit far to the right at a low life expectancy: bad leverage points, 6.2% of the data. Their slopes:



Method
Slope, original data
Slope, 12 altered countries




OLS
8.84
3.00


Huber
8.81
6.41


Bisquare
8.74
8.17


MM
8.74
8.17


LTS
7.76
7.78




OLS drops from 8.84 to 3.00: it loses 66% of its slope. The altered countries have so much leverage that the line bends to them.
Huber is hurt too (6.41), as predicted in section 3: bounding the influence of a residual does not bound the pull of a point far out in \(x\), and the OLS start is already bent.
Bisquare, MM and LTS hold up much better (8.17, 8.17 and 7.78). LTS is lower than the M-estimators on the original data too (7.76): it fits only the best half of the countries, and is noisier. The bisquare weight is exactly zero for a point that is far enough from the line. Here the OLS start was bent but not too much; with more damage it can get stuck, because it is a local search started from a bad place. lmrob() starts from the S-estimator, which does not depend on OLS, so it is the one with the guarantee.

How much damage can the methods take? Alter more and more countries, from the lowest-spending ones, and watch the slope. This is the breakdown point in practice:


Code
ks <- seq(0, 70, by = 5)
set.seed(1)
break_slopes <- t(sapply(ks, function(k) {
  z <- make_bad(k)
  c(OLS      = coef(lm(life ~ logspend, z))[[2]],
    Huber    = coef(rlm(life ~ logspend, z, maxit = 100))[[2]],
    Bisquare = coef(rlm(life ~ logspend, z, psi = psi.bisquare, maxit = 100))[[2]],
    MM       = coef(suppressWarnings(lmrob(life ~ logspend, z)))[[2]],
    LTS      = coef(lqs(life ~ logspend, z, method = "lts"))[[2]])
}))
breakdown <- data.frame(k = rep(ks, 5), slope = c(break_slopes),
                        method = factor(rep(colnames(break_slopes), each = length(ks)), levels = names(method_colours)))




Code
ggplot(breakdown, aes(100 * k / n, slope, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = method_colours) +
  labs(title = "The slope as more spending values are wrong",
       x = "share of countries with an altered value (%)", y = "estimated slope (years per tenfold)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











Code
share <- 100 * ks / n
tol <- 3
first_off <- function(m) {        # the first share where the slope is more than tol years away from its start
  off <- which(abs(break_slopes[, m] - break_slopes[1, m]) > tol)
  if (length(off)) round(share[min(off)], 1) else NA
}


OLS moves at once and keeps moving. By the rule “more than 3 years from its starting value”, Huber gives way at about 7.8% altered countries, the bisquare M-estimator at 13% and MM at 31.2%. LTS never moves by more than 3 years up to 36%, the end of the chart. In theory no estimator survives more than half of the data being bad, because from then on the bad points are the majority, and nothing tells which group is the right one. In practice the limit is lower, and depends on where the bad points are.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
section: 6. Do not just delete the outliers
text:
6. Do not just delete the outliers
When a point looks wrong, deleting it is tempting. It is rarely the best answer:

Find out why it is unusual first. A typing error or a unit slip, like the one we made up, may be corrected. A measurement taken under a different condition may belong to another population. A genuine but rare case, such as a country in a war, is information, not noise.
Deleting by a rule picked after looking is a researcher’s degree of freedom. If you delete the points that hurt your hypothesis, the answer is yours, not the data’s. If you delete, say which, why and by what rule, set before fitting.
A 0/1 decision is blunt. A robust fit makes the decision smoothly: a country gets a weight between 0 and 1 by how far it is, with a rule that is fixed in advance (the tuning constant) and an automatic result.
The outliers are often the interesting part. The countries the robust line cannot explain are the ones to study.

Compare, for these data, the OLS line after deleting the flagged countries with the robust fit:


Code
keep      <- !d$flagged
ols_drop  <- lm(life ~ logspend, data = d[keep, ])
n_dropped <- sum(!keep)
c(ols = coef(ols)[[2]], ols_without_flagged = coef(ols_drop)[[2]], bisquare = coef(bisquare)[[2]], mm = coef(mm)[[2]])


                ols ols_without_flagged            bisquare                  mm 
           8.844089            8.675227            8.737465            8.742125 


Deleting the 19 flagged countries (Cook’s distance above .021, hat value above .021 or studentized residual beyond ±2.5) moves the OLS slope from 8.84 to 8.68, which is close to the robust values 8.74 (bisquare) and 8.74 (MM). The robust methods get there without a human choosing who goes, and keep every country in the sample (with a small weight if need be).

What the robust fit says about the outliers
The residuals of the MM fit are the honest measure of how far each country is from the trend, because the trend was not bent towards them:


Code
d$resid_mm   <- resid(mm)
d$w_mm       <- mm$rweights
outliers <- d[order(d$resid_mm), c("spend", "life", "region", "resid_mm")][1:8, ]
outliers$spend    <- round(outliers$spend)
outliers$resid_mm <- round(outliers$resid_mm, 1)
outliers


                         spend   life              region resid_mm
Central African Republic    46 40.279 Sub-Saharan Africa     -22.9
Naoero                    1636 61.331 East Asia & Pacific    -15.4
Lesotho                    116 54.209 Sub-Saharan Africa     -12.5
Eswatini                   298 58.228 Sub-Saharan Africa     -12.0
Nigeria                     82 53.455 Sub-Saharan Africa     -11.9
Namibia                    450 60.850 Sub-Saharan Africa     -11.0
South Africa               593 62.010 Sub-Saharan Africa     -10.9
Tuvalu                    1122 65.824 East Asia & Pacific     -9.5


Code
n_neg <- sum(d$w_mm < 0.5 & d$resid_mm < 0)
n_pos <- sum(d$w_mm < 0.5 & d$resid_mm > 0)


Of the 9 countries with an MM weight under 0.5, 9 lie below the line and 0 above it. Central African Republic is the extreme one: 22.9 years below what its spending predicts. The data cannot say why. Candidates are things the model leaves out: wars, epidemics such as HIV, and the very different age and disease patterns of small states. The robust fit has done its job when it has made the list. The World Bank’s metadata do not say more about single countries, and no single value was checked against national sources. Part of the explanation may also lie in the data: the life expectancy of a country with poor records is an estimate.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
text:
7. “Robust regression” is not “robust standard errors”
The two names sound alike and do different jobs:









Robust regression
Robust (sandwich) standard errors




Changes the coefficients?
yes, they are estimated differently
no, they are the OLS ones


Changes the standard errors?
yes, as a by-product
yes: that is the whole point


Protects against
outliers and bad leverage points
unequal spread of the residuals (heteroscedasticity)


R
rlm(), lmrob(), lqs()
sandwich::vcovHC(), lmtest::coeftest()



The sandwich estimator of White (1980) keeps the OLS coefficients, and replaces the formula for their covariance \(s^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\) by
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta) = (X^\top X)^{-1}\left(\sum_i e_i^2 \,\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^\top\right)(X^\top X)^{-1}\]
in which each residual counts with its own size: no common variance is assumed. The HC3 version (MacKinnon & White, 1985) also divides by \((1 - h_i)^2\) and works better in small samples (Long & Ervin, 2000).


Code
bp <- bptest(ols)
coeftest(ols)                                    # the usual OLS standard errors



t test of coefficients:

            Estimate Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  47.8502     1.2051  39.706 < 2.2e-16 ***
logspend      8.8441     0.4438  19.928 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC3"))  # the same coefficients, sandwich standard errors



t test of coefficients:

            Estimate Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 47.85016    1.26751  37.751 < 2.2e-16 ***
logspend     8.84409    0.42852  20.639 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
se_hc3 <- sqrt(diag(vcovHC(ols, type = "HC3")))


The Breusch-Pagan test of constant variance gives \(\chi^2\)(1) = 3.72, p = .054. The slope is the same, 8.84, with a standard error of 0.44 in the usual way and 0.43 with HC3. This changes the uncertainty, and the line stays where the outliers left it. Now the damaged data:


Code
ols_bad <- lm(life ~ logspend, data = d_bad)
se_bad  <- sqrt(diag(vcovHC(ols_bad, type = "HC3")))
ci_bad  <- coef(ols_bad)[[2]] + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(.975) * se_bad[[2]]
ci_mm   <- coef(bad$fits$MM)[[2]] + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(.975) * bd["MM", "se"]


OLS now gives a slope of 3.00 with an HC3 standard error of 1.13: a 95% interval of [0.79, 5.21]. The interval is “honest” about the spread, but it is centred on the wrong slope, and it misses the value MM finds, 8.17 [7.49, 8.85]. Sandwich standard errors answer “how uncertain is this estimate?”; they do not ask whether the estimate is any good.
The two can be combined: lmrob() already reports standard errors that are robust to outliers, and a sandwich estimator can be put on top of a weighted fit. For heteroscedasticity with a known pattern, weighted or generalized least squares estimate the variance model directly.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
section: 8. Other things to keep in mind
text:
8. Other things to keep in mind

Median regression is another outlier-resistant method. It minimises \(\sum \lvert e_i\rvert\) (the weight of a residual is \(1/\lvert e_i\rvert\)), so a far residual pulls linearly, not quadratically. It resists outliers in \(y\) but, like Huber, not leverage points, and it can describe other quantiles, not just the centre. See quantile regression.
Heavy tails, not only outliers. If the errors follow a distribution with long tails, such as the t, the best estimator is robust by nature. Robust regression is more than a cleaning tool.
Robust methods do not fix a wrong model. If the relationship is curved, down-weighting does not straighten it. Here the log of spending did that part; see polynomial regression for curves.
Standard errors. rlm() and lmrob() give asymptotic standard errors; with small samples they are optimistic, and a bootstrap is a good check.
Tuning constants trade resistance against efficiency. Smaller \(k\) or \(c\) down-weights more, and costs more efficiency when the data are clean. The defaults are a good place to stay.
A robust fit is not a verdict. It tells which points the model cannot explain. Whether to report, drop or model them is for the researcher, and should be stated.
Compare with OLS, always. If OLS and the robust fit agree, as in section 4, outliers are not an issue. If they disagree, find out why: the difference is itself the finding.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the data, the estimator and its tuning, the diagnostics that led to it, and the OLS results next to the robust ones. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
mm_ci   <- confint(mm)
mm_sum  <- summary(mm)$coefficients
mm_r2   <- summary(mm)$r.squared
ols_ci  <- confint(ols)

est_table <- data.frame(
  Method = c("OLS", "Huber", "Bisquare", "MM"),
  Intercept = f2(cl$intercept),
  Slope = f2(cl$slope),
  SE = f2(cl$se),
  `95% CI` = paste0("[", f2(cl$lower), ", ", f2(cl$upper), "]"),
  `Residual scale` = f2(cl$scale),
  check.names = FALSE)


Method (data analysis):

We analysed 192 countries and territories with data for both indicators in 2021 (World Bank, n.d.): life expectancy at birth in years, and current health expenditure per person in current US dollars. Spending was log-transformed (base 10) because the relationship was curved on the original scale. Ordinary least squares regression was compared with M-estimation with Huber weights (\(k\) = 1.345) and Tukey’s bisquare weights (\(c\) = 4.685; Venables & Ripley, 2002) and with MM-estimation (Yohai, 1987), all with the default tuning for 95% efficiency under normal errors. MM-estimation used the lmrob() function of the robustbase package (Maechler et al., 2024). Outliers were identified with studentized residuals, hat values and Cook’s distance (Cook, 1977) and were not deleted. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

OLS regression gave a slope of 8.84 years per tenfold increase in spending, SE = 0.44, 95% CI [7.97, 9.72]. 5 countries had studentized residuals beyond ±2.5; the largest was Central African Republic (t = -5.5, Cook’s D = 0.19). The robust estimates were close to the OLS estimate (Table 1): the MM slope was 8.74 years, SE = 0.35, 95% CI [8.06, 9.42], p < .001, with a robust residual scale of 3.61 years, against 4.42 for OLS. The bisquare weights were below 0.5 for 7 countries, 7 of them below the regression line, so the conclusion did not depend on the estimator. In a sensitivity analysis in which the spending of 12 countries was altered by a factor of 1,000, the OLS slope fell to 3.00 and the Huber slope to 6.41, while the MM slope stayed at 8.17.

Points to remember:

Say which robust estimator, with its tuning constant and the software. “Robust regression” alone says nothing.
Report OLS next to the robust fit, and the observations that were down-weighted, with a reason when one is known.
Do not call sandwich standard errors “robust regression”, or the reverse.
State the breakdown point or the efficiency of the method if the choice of method matters to the conclusion.
Do not delete points silently.

title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
text:
10. Summary







When
The data have outliers, heavy tails, or points that OLS cannot be trusted with


Idea
Minimise \(\sum\rho(e_i/s)\) with a loss \(\rho\) that grows more slowly than the square; computed by iteratively reweighted least squares


Huber
Bounded influence; weights \(\min(1, k/\lvert u\rvert)\), never zero. Resists outliers in \(y\), not bad leverage


Bisquare
Redescending: weights drop to zero beyond \(c\). Resists large outliers, but needs a good start


MM
An S-estimate (breakdown 50%) as a start, then a bisquare step (95% efficient). The usual first choice


LTS
Fits the best half of the data: breakdown 50%, no standard errors, less efficient


How (R)
MASS::rlm(y ~ x, psi = psi.huber) or psi.bisquare; robustbase::lmrob(y ~ x); MASS::lqs(y ~ x, method = "lts")


Diagnostics
hatvalues(), rstudent(), cooks.distance(); the final weights fit$w (rlm) or fit$rweights (lmrob)


Not the same as
Sandwich standard errors: same coefficients, only the uncertainty changes


Dangers
Deleting points silently; hiding a wrong model behind a robust fit

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
text:
A bike-sharing company in Washington, DC wants to know how many bikes people will rent in the next hour. Too few bikes at the stations and customers walk away; too many and bikes (and staff) sit idle. The company has two years of hourly records: the number of rentals, the hour, the day, the season and the weather.
The pattern is not a straight line. Rentals peak in the morning and in the late afternoon on working days (the commute), and in the middle of the day at the weekend. They rise with temperature, but fall again when it gets too hot. Rain cuts them. The effect of the hour depends on the day type: an interaction. A linear regression needs you to know all of this in advance and write it into the formula.
A random forest (Breiman, 2001) learns such shapes by itself. It is an average of hundreds of regression trees, each grown on a different random sample of the data. This page builds one step by step, and asks four questions:

How well does it predict hours it has never seen, compared with a linear regression and a single tree?
Which predictors does it use, and what does the relation to each look like?
How sure can we be of one prediction?
What can a forest not do?

How a single regression tree grows and is pruned is explained in the decision tree example. The forest is also the main alternative to gradient boosting, the other popular way to combine trees. For a linear model with many predictors, see regularized regression.


Code
library(ranger)    # fast random forests, with permutation importance and quantile regression forests
library(rpart)     # a single regression tree, for comparison
library(ggplot2)

# colours in the order of the site: one per series, the same in every chart
blue <- "#2a78d6"; orange <- "#eb6834"; green <- "#1baf7a"; yellow <- "#eda100"; pink <- "#e87ba4"
palette <- c(blue, orange, green, yellow, pink)

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0)
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

# the three measures of error used throughout
rmse    <- function(o, p) sqrt(mean((o - p)^2))
metrics <- function(o, p) c(RMSE = rmse(o, p), MAE = mean(abs(o - p)), R2 = 1 - sum((o - p)^2) / sum((o - mean(o))^2))
