To read off the sample size for 80% power between the simulated points, fit a logistic curve of “significant” on \(\log n\) to all the simulated studies of a scenario, and solve it for .80:


Code
n_for_80 <- function(sig, n) { fit <- glm(sig ~ log(n), family = binomial); exp((qlogis(0.8) - coef(fit)[1]) / coef(fit)[2]) }
med_n80 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(med, med$scenario), function(s)
  data.frame(scenario = s$scenario[1], joint = ceiling(n_for_80(s$joint, s$n)),
             monte_carlo = ceiling(n_for_80(s$monte_carlo, s$n)))))
med_n80


                                                       scenario joint monte_carlo
a = .14, b = .59 (small, large) a = .14, b = .59 (small, large)   395         394
a = b = .14 (small, small)           a = b = .14 (small, small)   512         521
a = b = .39 (medium, medium)       a = b = .39 (medium, medium)    64          64




Code
med_long <- rbind(data.frame(med_power[, c("scenario", "n")], test = "joint significance", power = med_power$joint),
                  data.frame(med_power[, c("scenario", "n")], test = "Monte Carlo CI", power = med_power$monte_carlo))
ggplot(med_long, aes(n, power, colour = scenario, linetype = test)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E74C3C", "#0082c8", "#f39c12")) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(30, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800)) +              # log scale: the three ranges differ a lot
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Power for the indirect effect a × b (400 simulated studies per point)",
       x = "sample size (log scale)", y = "power", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1), linetype = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










Two medium paths need only about 64 people.
Two small paths need about 521. Fritz and MacKinnon (2007) found the same: with two small paths, even the best tests need more than 500 people for 80% power.
A large \(b\) does not rescue a small \(a\): about 394 people. The weaker path sets the sample size.
The two tests give almost the same power.


Is the bootstrap any different?
We check one design point (two medium paths, \(n = 60\)) on the same 200 data sets with all three tests, and time them:


Code
set.seed(8)
n_b <- 60; a_b <- 0.39; b_b <- 0.39; R_b <- 200; B <- 1000
datasets <- replicate(R_b, {
  x <- rnorm(n_b); m <- a_b * x + rnorm(n_b, sd = sqrt(1 - a_b^2)); y <- b_b * m + rnorm(n_b, sd = sqrt(1 - b_b^2))
  list(data.frame(x, m, y))
})
test_dataset <- function(d, bootstrap) {
  fa <- .lm.fit(cbind(1, d$x), d$m); Xb <- cbind(1, d$m, d$x); fb <- .lm.fit(Xb, d$y)
  a_hat <- fa$coefficients[2]; b_hat <- fb$coefficients[2]
  se_a <- sqrt(sum(fa$residuals^2) / (n_b - 2) / sum((d$x - mean(d$x))^2))
  se_b <- sqrt(sum(fb$residuals^2) / (n_b - 3) * solve(crossprod(Xb))[2, 2])
  if (!bootstrap) {
    ci <- quantile(rnorm(1000, a_hat, se_a) * rnorm(1000, b_hat, se_b), c(0.025, 0.975))
  } else {
    ab <- replicate(B, { i <- sample.int(n_b, n_b, replace = TRUE)
      .lm.fit(cbind(1, d$x[i]), d$m[i])$coefficients[2] * .lm.fit(cbind(1, d$m[i], d$x[i]), d$y[i])$coefficients[2] })
    ci <- quantile(ab, c(0.025, 0.975))
  }
  c(joint = abs(a_hat / se_a) > qt(0.975, n_b - 2) && abs(b_hat / se_b) > qt(0.975, n_b - 3),
    significant = unname(ci[1] > 0 || ci[2] < 0))
}
time_mc   <- system.time(res_mc   <- t(sapply(datasets, test_dataset, bootstrap = FALSE)))["elapsed"]
time_boot <- system.time(res_boot <- t(sapply(datasets, test_dataset, bootstrap = TRUE)))["elapsed"]
round(c(joint_significance = mean(res_mc[, "joint"]), monte_carlo = mean(res_mc[, "significant"]),
        bootstrap = mean(res_boot[, "significant"]), agreement_mc_vs_boot = mean(res_mc[, "significant"] == res_boot[, "significant"]),
        seconds_monte_carlo = unname(time_mc), seconds_bootstrap = unname(time_boot)), 3)


  joint_significance          monte_carlo            bootstrap agreement_mc_vs_boot  seconds_monte_carlo    seconds_bootstrap 
               0.685                0.670                0.715                0.885                0.080                6.470 


The three powers are similar (.685, .670 and .715, each give or take about .06 with 200 data sets; the percentile bootstrap tends to be a little more liberal in small samples). Near the 80% mark many data sets are borderline, so the bootstrap and the Monte Carlo interval disagree on 12% of them, in both directions. But the bootstrap took about 81 times as long. For a whole power curve, use a fast test (and, to be safe, plan a little above 80%); analyse the real data with the bootstrap.

title: Power Analysis by Simulation in R: How Many People Do I Need?
section: 7. Multilevel designs: more groups or more people per group?
text:
7. Multilevel designs: more groups or more people per group?
Many studies sample groups: employees in teams, pupils in classes, patients in clinics. People in the same group are alike (the intraclass correlation, ICC, of the multilevel tutorial), so each extra person in a group adds less new information than the first.
The design effect says how much the clustering inflates the variance of a mean, for \(m\) people per group:
\[\text{design effect} = 1 + (m - 1)\,\text{ICC}, \qquad n_{effective} = \frac{n}{\text{design effect}}\]

A team-level predictor
A well-being programme is given to whole teams: half of the teams take part (a cluster-randomised study). We expect it to raise well-being by \(d = 0.3\) standard deviations, and the ICC of well-being within teams is .15. With \(J\) teams of \(m\) employees, the model is
\[\text{wellbeing}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{programme}_j + u_{0j} + r_{ij}\]
For a balanced design the test of \(\gamma_{01}\) in this random-intercept model is the same as a t-test on the team means, with \(J - 2\) degrees of freedom. Check it on one simulated data set:


Code
icc <- 0.15; d_team <- 0.3
sim_teams <- function(J, m) {
  team <- rep(1:J, each = m)
  programme <- rep(rep(0:1, length.out = J), each = m)           # half of the teams take part
  u <- rnorm(J, sd = sqrt(icc))                                  # team effects: ICC of the total variance 1
  data.frame(wellbeing = d_team * programme + u[team] + rnorm(J * m, sd = sqrt(1 - icc)),
             programme, team = factor(team))
}
set.seed(9)
one_study <- sim_teams(J = 20, m = 20)
fit_team <- lme(wellbeing ~ programme, random = ~ 1 | team, data = one_study)
team_means <- aggregate(wellbeing ~ team + programme, data = one_study, FUN = mean)
round(c(lme_t = summary(fit_team)$tTable["programme", "t-value"], lme_df = summary(fit_team)$tTable["programme", "DF"],
        t_test_on_team_means = unname(t.test(wellbeing ~ factor(programme, levels = 1:0), data = team_means,
                                            var.equal = TRUE)$statistic)), 3)


               lme_t               lme_df t_test_on_team_means 
              -1.016               18.000               -1.016 


That gives a formula. The variance of a team mean is \(\text{ICC} + (1 - \text{ICC})/m\), the two arms have \(J/2\) teams each, so the noncentrality is
\[\delta = \frac{d}{\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{J}\left(\text{ICC} + \dfrac{1 - \text{ICC}}{m}\right)}}, \qquad df = J - 2\]


Code
power_teams <- function(J, m, d = d_team, rho = icc) {
  df <- J - 2; ncp <- d / sqrt(4 / J * (rho + (1 - rho) / m)); crit <- qt(0.975, df)
  1 - pt(crit, df, ncp) + pt(-crit, df, ncp)
}


Now simulate with lme(), 400 studies per design: first four ways of spending the same 400 employees, then 20 teams with more and more employees each:


Code
R_team <- 400
designs <- unique(rbind(data.frame(J = c(10, 20, 40, 80), m = c(40, 20, 10, 5)),   # 400 employees in total
                        data.frame(J = 20, m = c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80))))            # 20 teams, larger and larger
set.seed(10)
designs$simulated <- mapply(function(J, m) mean(replicate(R_team,
  summary(lme(wellbeing ~ programme, random = ~ 1 | team, data = sim_teams(J, m)))$tTable["programme", "p-value"] < 0.05)),
  designs$J, designs$m)
designs$formula <- power_teams(designs$J, designs$m)
designs$design_effect <- 1 + (designs$m - 1) * icc
designs$effective_n <- designs$J * designs$m / designs$design_effect
round(designs[, c("J", "m", "design_effect", "effective_n", "formula", "simulated")], 3)


   J  m design_effect effective_n formula simulated
1 10 40          6.85      58.394   0.173     0.160
2 20 20          3.85     103.896   0.305     0.275
3 40 10          2.35     170.213   0.479     0.485
4 80  5          1.60     250.000   0.649     0.645
5 20  5          1.60      62.500   0.202     0.250
6 20 10          2.35      85.106   0.259     0.268
8 20 40          6.85     116.788   0.336     0.308
9 20 80         12.85     124.514   0.354     0.350




Code
alloc <- subset(designs, J * m == 400)
alloc_curve <- data.frame(J = seq(6, 100, by = 2)); alloc_curve$power <- power_teams(alloc_curve$J, 400 / alloc_curve$J)
more <- subset(designs, J == 20)
more_curve <- data.frame(m = 2:160); more_curve$power <- power_teams(20, more_curve$m)
q1 <- ggplot(alloc_curve, aes(J, power)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = alloc, aes(y = simulated), colour = "#E74C3C", size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Same 400 employees,\nsplit into more or fewer teams", x = "number of teams (J)", y = "power")
q2 <- ggplot(more_curve, aes(m, power)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = power_teams(20, Inf), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = more, aes(y = simulated), colour = "#E74C3C", size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "20 teams, more employees\nin each (dashed: the ceiling)", x = "employees per team (m)", y = "power")
q1 + q2










With the same 400 employees, 80 teams of 5 give a power of 0.65, while 10 teams of 40 give only 0.17.
With 20 teams, adding employees soon stops helping: power can never exceed 0.37 however large the teams, because the team effects \(u_{0j}\) do not average out within a team. Only more teams help.
The simulations (red) agree with the formula (blue) within their Monte Carlo error (about \(\pm\) 0.05 at worst).



A cross-level interaction
Now a question about slopes: employees with a higher workload have lower well-being, and we expect this to be weaker in teams with more support from their manager (a cross-level interaction, as in section 8 of the multilevel tutorial):
\[\text{wellbeing}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{support}_j + \gamma_{10}\,\text{workload}_{ij} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{support}_j \times \text{workload}_{ij} + u_{0j} + u_{1j}\,\text{workload}_{ij} + r_{ij}\]
We assume \(\gamma_{10} = -0.3\), \(\gamma_{11} = 0.15\) (support, in standard deviations, softens the workload slope by 0.15), \(\gamma_{01} = 0.2\), an ICC of .15 and a slope variance \(\tau_{11} = 0.05\). Workload is centred within teams. 200 studies per design, the same two totals of employees split differently:


Code
sim_cross <- function(J, m, g10 = -0.3, g11 = 0.15, g01 = 0.2, tau11 = 0.05) {
  team <- rep(1:J, each = m)
  support <- rnorm(J)                                              # team level, standardised
  workload <- rnorm(J * m); workload <- workload - ave(workload, team)   # centred within teams
  u0 <- rnorm(J, sd = sqrt(icc)); u1 <- rnorm(J, sd = sqrt(tau11))
  data.frame(wellbeing = g01 * support[team] + (g10 + u1[team]) * workload + g11 * support[team] * workload +
               u0[team] + rnorm(J * m, sd = sqrt(1 - icc)),
             workload, support = support[team], team = factor(team))
}
cross_p <- function(J, m) tryCatch(
  summary(lme(wellbeing ~ workload * support, random = ~ workload | team, data = sim_cross(J, m),
              control = lmeControl(opt = "optim")))$tTable["workload:support", "p-value"],
  error = function(e) NA)                                          # a fit that fails counts as missing
cross_designs <- data.frame(J = c(20, 40, 80, 40, 80, 160), m = c(20, 10, 5, 20, 10, 5),
                            total = rep(c(400, 800), each = 3))
set.seed(11)
cross_res <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(cross_designs)), function(i) replicate(200, cross_p(cross_designs$J[i], cross_designs$m[i])))
cross_designs$power  <- sapply(cross_res, function(p) mean(p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
cross_designs$failed <- sapply(cross_res, function(p) sum(is.na(p)))
cross_designs


    J  m total power failed
1  20 20   400 0.540      0
2  40 10   400 0.690      0
3  80  5   400 0.695      0
4  40 20   800 0.845      0
5  80 10   800 0.930      0
6 160  5   800 0.945      0



With 400 employees the power for the interaction is only 0.54 to 0.69; it takes about 800 to pass 80% (0.84 to 0.94). Cross-level interactions need large studies (Arend & Schäfer, 2019).
For the same total, more teams still help, though less and less (0.54, 0.69 and 0.69 for 20, 40 and 80 teams of 400 employees). Unlike for the team-level effect, more people per team help too (40 teams: 0.69 with 10 each, 0.84 with 20), because each team’s slope is estimated from its own employees. The best split depends on the effects, the ICC and \(\tau_{11}\), which is why it is worth simulating.
0 of the 1,200 fits failed to converge here (a failed fit is counted as missing). Count the failures in your own simulations: many of them warn that the planned model is too complex for the data.

title: Power Analysis by Simulation in R: How Many People Do I Need?
section: 8. Sensitivity analysis: what can my sample detect?
text:
8. Sensitivity analysis: what can my sample detect?
Often the sample size is fixed: 120 employees took part, or two classes of 30. Then the useful question is the reverse: what is the smallest effect this sample can detect with 80% power? Leave out the effect size:


Code
pwr.t.test(n = 60, power = 0.8)$d                       # two groups of 60


[1] 0.5157065


Code
f2_min <- pwr.f2.test(u = 1, v = 200 - k_full - 1, power = 0.8)$f2
dr2_min <- f2_min * (1 - r2_controls) / (1 + f2_min)    # ΔR² over controls that explain 10%, n = 200
c(f2 = f2_min, delta_r2 = dr2_min)


        f2   delta_r2 
0.04044629 0.03498658 


Two groups of 60 can detect \(d \geq\) 0.52; 200 people can detect a \(\Delta R^2 \geq\) 0.035 over the four controls. (\(\Delta R^2\) comes from \(f^2 = \Delta R^2 / (1 - R^2_{controls} - \Delta R^2)\), solved for \(\Delta R^2\).)


Code
sens_t <- data.frame(n = seq(10, 300, by = 5))
sens_t$d <- sapply(sens_t$n, function(n) pwr.t.test(n = n, power = 0.8)$d)
sens_r2 <- data.frame(n = seq(30, 1000, by = 10))
sens_r2$dr2 <- sapply(sens_r2$n, function(n) { f <- pwr.f2.test(u = 1, v = n - k_full - 1, power = 0.8)$f2
  f * (1 - r2_controls) / (1 + f) })
s1 <- ggplot(sens_t, aes(n, d)) + geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8), linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 300, y = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8), label = c("small", "medium", "large"),
           hjust = 1, vjust = 1.4, size = 3) +
  expand_limits(y = 0.1) +                                       # room for the "small" label
  labs(title = "Two groups: smallest d\ndetectable with 80% power", x = "people per group", y = "d")
s2 <- ggplot(sens_r2, aes(n, dr2)) + geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "ΔR² step: smallest ΔR²\ndetectable with 80% power", x = "sample size", y = "ΔR²")
s1 + s2









If the smallest detectable effect is larger than any plausible effect, the study can still be useful (to estimate, or as part of a meta-analysis), but a non-significant result will say very little.

title: Power Analysis by Simulation in R: How Many People Do I Need?
text:
9. Common mistakes
“Observed” or post hoc power. Computing power after the study, from the effect size the study found, adds nothing: it is a function of the p value alone (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001). A result with p = .05 always has an “observed power” of about .50, and a non-significant result always has low observed power. For a z-test:


Code
p_values <- seq(0.001, 0.8, length.out = 300)
z_obs <- qnorm(1 - p_values / 2)
observed_power <- pnorm(z_obs - qnorm(0.975)) + pnorm(-z_obs - qnorm(0.975))
ggplot(data.frame(p = p_values, power = observed_power), aes(p, power)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.06, y = 0.55, label = sprintf("p = .05: observed power = %.2f",
           pnorm(qnorm(0.975) - qnorm(0.975)) + pnorm(-2 * qnorm(0.975))), hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "'Observed power' is just the p value in disguise", x = "p value", y = "observed power")









Power belongs to the design, before the data. After the data, report the effect size with its confidence interval.
Forgetting drop-out. If 15% of participants are expected to drop out or give unusable data, recruit \(n / (1 - 0.15)\): for 128 usable cases, 151 people.
Powering the wrong test. If the hypothesis is an interaction, power the interaction, not the main effects: interactions are usually smaller and need much larger samples (section 7). With several hypotheses, each needs enough power, and a corrected \(\alpha\) (for example Bonferroni) needs more people.
Ignoring the clustering. Planning a study of teams or classes as if the people were independent overstates the power, sometimes by a lot (section 7).
Defaults instead of thought. “Medium effect, 80% power” chosen because it is common is not a justification. Say where the effect size comes from (Lakens, 2022).

title: Power Analysis by Simulation in R: How Many People Do I Need?
section: 10. Reporting a sample-size justification in APA style
text:
10. Reporting a sample-size justification in APA style
APA 7th edition asks authors to explain how the sample size was decided. A good justification names the analysis, the effect size and where it comes from, \(\alpha\), the power, the method (formula or simulation, with \(R\)), and any allowance for drop-out. We collect the numbers from the R objects:


Code
n_t   <- ceiling(pwr.t.test(d = 0.5, power = 0.8)$n)
n_r   <- ceiling(pwr.r.test(r = 0.2, power = 0.8)$n)
n_med <- med_n80$monte_carlo[grepl("medium", med_n80$scenario)]
J_needed <- min(seq(4, 200, by = 2)[power_teams(seq(4, 200, by = 2), 10) >= 0.8])   # teams of 10, even number
set.seed(12)
power_J <- mean(replicate(R_team, summary(lme(wellbeing ~ programme, random = ~ 1 | team,
                                           data = sim_teams(J_needed, 10)))$tTable["programme", "p-value"] < 0.05))
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)


Example: sample-size justification (for the hierarchical regression of section 5):

The sample size was chosen to detect an increment of ΔR² = .02 for the new test over four control variables expected to explain 10% of the variance in job performance, f² = 0.023, the smallest increment we considered practically useful. With α = .05, a sample of 352 participants gives a power of .80 for the F-change test (pwr package; Champely, 2020). A simulation with 2,000 replications, in which the new test correlated .30 with the controls, confirmed this (power = .81, Monte Carlo SE = .009). Allowing for 15% unusable responses, we planned to recruit 415 participants.

Points to remember:

Justify the effect size: the smallest effect of interest, or earlier studies corrected for their inflation; not a default.
Give \(\alpha\), the power, the test (one- or two-sided), the method and, for a simulation, the number of replications and the assumed model.
Plan for drop-out and for the clustering of the data.
If \(n\) was fixed in advance, report a sensitivity analysis instead: the smallest effect the study could detect.
Never report “observed power” for a completed study.

title: Power Analysis by Simulation in R: How Many People Do I Need?
text:
11. Summary







Power
The chance of a significant result when the effect is real: \(1 - \beta\), usually .80 or .90


What decides it
Effect size (most of all), \(n\), \(\alpha\), and the design (clustering, number of predictors, test)


Formulas
pwr.t.test(), pwr.r.test(), pwr.f2.test() (with \(f^2 = \Delta R^2 / (1 - R^2_{full})\) and \(n = v + k + 1\)); rwf’s compute_power_r() for a correlation’s power curve


Simulation
Generate data under the assumed model, analyse as planned, repeat \(R\) times, count significant results; works for any design


Monte Carlo error
\(\sqrt{p(1 - p)/R}\): about .009 for \(R\) = 2,000 at .80


Mediation
Simulate; test \(ab\) with joint significance or a Monte Carlo CI inside the loop; the weaker path sets \(n\)


Multilevel
Plan with the design effect \(1 + (m - 1)\text{ICC}\); more groups beat more people per group for group-level effects


Fixed n
Report a sensitivity analysis: the smallest detectable effect


Avoid
Observed power, pilot-study effect sizes, default “medium” effects, forgetting drop-out

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text: A “paradox” here doesn’t mean something impossible — it means something that is mathematically true but goes against what our intuition expects. These come up constantly in real data: in medicine, sports, hiring, machine learning, and everyday probability. Each section below explains one paradox in plain language, shows the R code that simulates or visualizes it, and displays the resulting graph on its own so it’s easy to study in isolation.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text: A “paradox” here doesn’t mean something impossible — it means something that is mathematically true but goes against what our intuition expects. These come up constantly in real data: in medicine, sports, hiring, machine learning, and everyday probability. Each section below explains one paradox in plain language, shows the R code that simulates or visualizes it, and displays the resulting graph on its own so it’s easy to study in isolation.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Simpson’s Paradox
The idea: A trend can be true in every single subgroup of your data, yet completely reverse once you combine all the groups together. Imagine three schools where students who study more score higher within each school — but the school where students study most has the lowest-scoring intake, so across all schools combined, more study looks linked to lower scores. Nothing dishonest is happening; it’s just a consequence of how the groups sit relative to each other.


Code
set.seed(42)
n <- 40

# Three groups: each has a positive local slope,
# but they're staggered so the global slope is negative.
make_group <- function(mx, my, label) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean = mx, sd = 0.6)
  y <- my + 0.9 * (x - mx) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4)
  data.frame(x = x, y = y, group = label)
}

dat <- rbind(
  make_group(mx = 2, my = 8, label = "Group A"),
  make_group(mx = 5, my = 5, label = "Group B"),
  make_group(mx = 8, my = 2, label = "Group C")
)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  # Overall (aggregated) trend — negative
  geom_smooth(
    method  = "lm", se = FALSE,
    color   = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  # Per-group trends — positive
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = group),
    method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  # Points
  geom_point(aes(color = group), size = 2.8, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Group A" = "#E74C3C",
               "Group B" = "#27AE60",
               "Group C" = "#2980B9")
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 6.5, y = 8.6, label = "Overall trend\n(aggregated)",
    size = 3.5, color = "black", fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Simpson's Paradox",
    subtitle = "Within each group the slope is positive — yet the overall slope (dashed) is negative",
    x        = "X",
    y        = "Y",
    color    = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
  )









Each colored line (one per group) slopes upward. But the dashed black line — fit across all the points at once, ignoring group membership — slopes downward. Always check whether a relationship holds within subgroups before trusting an overall trend.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Infinitely Many Perfect Fits (Overfitting)
The idea: With only a handful of data points, there isn’t just one curve that fits them perfectly — there are infinitely many. Here we start with 4 points and a cubic curve that passes through all of them exactly (R² = 1, a “perfect” fit). Then we show that we can wiggle that curve in endless different ways, and every single variant still passes through all 4 points with the same perfect R². A perfect fit on tiny or noisy data doesn’t mean you’ve found the truth — it can just mean the model is flexible enough to memorize whatever points you gave it. This is the core intuition behind overfitting.


Code
# --- 4 data points ---
pts <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2, 4, 5),
  y = c(2, 5, 3, 7)
)

# --- Base: unique cubic interpolant through all 4 points ---
fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3, raw = TRUE), data = pts)

x_seq <- seq(0.3, 5.7, length.out = 600)
y_base <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = x_seq))

# --- "Wiggle" term: zero at every data point, so adding it keeps R²=1 ---
wiggle <- (x_seq - pts$x[1]) *
  (x_seq - pts$x[2]) *
  (x_seq - pts$x[3]) *
  (x_seq - pts$x[4])

# --- Build family of perfect-fit curves by varying c ---
c_vals  <- c(0, 0.25, -0.25, 0.55, -0.55)
c_labels <- c("c = 0  (cubic)", "c = 0.25", "c = -0.25", "c = 0.55", "c = -0.55")

curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(c_vals), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    x     = x_seq,
    y     = y_base + c_vals[i] * wiggle,
    curve = c_labels[i]
  )
}))

curves$curve <- factor(curves$curve, levels = c_labels)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data  = curves,
    aes(x = x, y = y, color = curve, linewidth = curve == "c = 0  (cubic)"),
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.4, `FALSE` = 0.9), guide = "none") +
  geom_point(
    data  = pts,
    aes(x = x, y = y),
    size  = 4, shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "black", stroke = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "c = 0  (cubic)" = "#E74C3C",
      "c = 0.25"       = "#3498DB",
      "c = -0.25"      = "#27AE60",
      "c = 0.55"       = "#9B59B6",
      "c = -0.55"      = "#F39C12"
    )
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 0.4, y = 20,
    label    = "All curves pass through\nevery point  (R² = 1)",
    hjust    = 0, size = 3.6, color = "grey30", fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Infinitely Many Perfect Fits",
    subtitle = expression(
      "Each curve = cubic interpolant + " * italic(c) * " · (x−x[1])(x−x[2])(x−x[3])(x−x[4])"
    ),
    x     = "x",
    y     = "y",
    color = "Curve"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 10),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









Notice how wildly the curves diverge away from the 4 known points, even though they agree perfectly at those points. Between and beyond the data, they tell completely different stories — a warning against trusting a model just because it fits your training data perfectly.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Anscombe’s Quartet
The idea: Four datasets can have nearly identical means, variances, correlations, and best-fit regression lines (equal to two or three decimal places) — while looking nothing alike when plotted. One is a clean straight-line relationship, one is a curve, one has a single outlier bending an otherwise perfect line, and one is a vertical cluster distorted by a single extreme point. The lesson: summary statistics can hide very different realities. Always plot your data.


Code
t <- theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.size = unit(0.5, "lines")
  )

data(anscombe)
al <- data.frame(
  x = c(anscombe$x1, anscombe$x2, anscombe$x3, anscombe$x4),
  y = c(anscombe$y1, anscombe$y2, anscombe$y3, anscombe$y4),
  ds = factor(rep(c("I", "II", "III", "IV"), each = 11))
)

p1 <- ggplot(al, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#E74C3C", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#2C3E50", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ds, nrow = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Anscombe's Quartet",
    subtitle = "All four: x̄=9, ȳ≈7.5, r≈0.82, same regression line",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) + t

p1









Every one of these four panels has virtually identical summary numbers. Only by plotting them do you see that dataset II is curved, dataset III has an outlier throwing off an otherwise perfect line, and dataset IV is driven entirely by one extreme x-value.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Regression to the Mean
The idea: Extremely tall parents tend to have children who are tall, but usually a bit closer to average than the parents were. This isn’t because nature is “pulling” people toward average — it happens naturally whenever a trait combines something real and inherited with a random element (luck, measurement noise, etc.). Any time you pick an extreme case, part of how extreme it was is just chance, and chance doesn’t repeat, so the next measurement tends to look more ordinary.


Code
set.seed(42)
n        <- 200
parent   <- rnorm(n, 170, 8)
child    <- 170 + 0.55 * (parent - 170) + rnorm(n, 0, 6)
rtm      <- data.frame(parent, child)

# Classify parents as short / average / tall for coloring
rtm$cat <- cut(rtm$parent,
               breaks = quantile(rtm$parent, c(0, .2, .8, 1)),
               labels = c("Short parents", "Average", "Tall parents"),
               include.lowest = TRUE)

p2 <- ggplot(rtm, aes(parent, child, color = cat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(data = rtm, aes(parent, child), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 154, y = 191,
           label = "slope = 1\n(no regression)", size = 2.9,
           color = "grey50", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 183, y = 164,
           label = "actual slope\n< 1", size = 2.9,
           color = "#E74C3C", hjust = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Short parents" = "#3498DB",
               "Average"       = "grey70",
               "Tall parents"  = "#9B59B6"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Regression to the Mean",
    subtitle = "Tall parents' children are shorter than them; short parents' children are taller",
    x = "Parent height (cm)", y = "Child height (cm)"
  ) + theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
        legend.position = "bottom")

p2









If there were no regression effect, the red best-fit line would follow the dashed “slope = 1” line exactly. Instead it’s flatter — tall parents’ children land closer to average, and short parents’ children do too.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Will Rogers Phenomenon
The idea: Named after a joke by comedian Will Rogers about migration between US states, this shows that moving a single data point from one group to another can raise the average of both groups — even though no individual value actually changed. This happens when the moved value is below the average of the group it’s leaving, but above the average of the group it’s joining.


Code
a_before <- c(6, 8, 9, 10, 12)   # mean = 9.0
b_before <- c(1, 2, 3, 4,  5)   # mean = 3.0
# Move 6 from A -> B:  new mean A = 9.75 (+0.75),  new mean B = 3.5 (+0.5)
a_after  <- c(8, 9, 10, 12)
b_after  <- c(1, 2,  3,  4,  5, 6)

make_wr <- function(vals, group, timing, moved_val = NULL) {
  data.frame(
    value  = vals,
    group  = group,
    timing = timing,
    moved  = if (!is.null(moved_val)) vals == moved_val else FALSE
  )
}

wr <- rbind(
  make_wr(a_before, "Group A", "Before", 6),
  make_wr(b_before, "Group B", "Before"),
  make_wr(a_after,  "Group A", "After"),
  make_wr(b_after,  "Group B", "After", 6)
)
wr$timing <- factor(wr$timing, levels = c("Before", "After"))

wr_means <- aggregate(value ~ group + timing, wr, mean)

p3 <- ggplot(wr, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = moved), width = 0.09, size = 3.2, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_crossbar(data = wr_means, aes(y = value, ymin = value, ymax = value),
                width = 0.45, color = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = wr_means,
            aes(y = value, label = paste0("μ = ", round(value, 2))),
            vjust = -0.7, size = 2.9, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~timing) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "#3498DB", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"),
    labels = c("Stationary", "Moved (value = 6)"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Will Rogers Phenomenon",
    subtitle = "Moving one value from A to B raises the average of BOTH groups",
    x = NULL, y = "Value"
  ) + theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
        legend.position = "bottom")

p3









The value “6” (highlighted in red) starts out below Group A’s average of 9, dragging it down. Once moved to Group B, it’s above B’s average of 3, pulling that average up too. Result: both group averages rise, purely from reclassification — nothing about the underlying data changed. This is a real concern in medicine, e.g. when improved diagnostics move borderline patients into a more severe category, apparently improving survival rates in both categories.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Berkson’s Paradox
The idea: Two traits can be completely unrelated in the general population, yet appear negatively correlated once you only look at a selected subgroup. Classic example: talent and hard work might be independent among all applicants to a competitive program, but among the people who actually got admitted, the very talented ones didn’t need to work as hard, and the very hard-working ones didn’t need as much raw talent — because admission itself required a combination of the two. The selection process manufactures a correlation that isn’t really there.


Code
set.seed(42)
n2        <- 600
talent    <- rnorm(n2)
hardwork  <- rnorm(n2)
selected  <- (talent + hardwork) > 0.7

berk <- data.frame(talent, hardwork, selected)

r_all <- round(cor(talent, hardwork), 3)
r_sel <- round(cor(talent[selected], hardwork[selected]), 3)

p4 <- ggplot(berk, aes(talent, hardwork, color = selected)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(data = berk, aes(talent, hardwork), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "grey40", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(berk, selected), aes(talent, hardwork),
              inherit.aes = FALSE,
              method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "grey75", `TRUE` = "#3498DB"),
    labels = c("Not selected", "Selected"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = -2.8, y = 2.9,
           label = paste0("Overall r = ", r_all, "  (dashed)"),
           hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.8, y = 2.4,
           label = paste0("Selected r = ", r_sel, "  (solid)"),
           hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = "#E74C3C") +
  labs(
    title    = "Berkson's Paradox",
    subtitle = "Talent & hard work are independent — but look negatively correlated among the admitted",
    x = "Talent", y = "Hard Work"
  ) + theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
        legend.position = "bottom")

p4









Across everyone (dashed line), talent and hard work have essentially zero relationship. But restrict to just the blue “selected” points, and the solid red trend line slopes clearly downward — an illusion created entirely by the selection cutoff.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
section: Range Restriction: How Narrowing Your Data Kills Correlation
text:
Range Restriction: How Narrowing Your Data Kills Correlation
The idea: If two variables have a genuinely strong relationship, but you only ever look at a narrow slice of one variable’s range, the correlation you measure can look weak or even vanish — not because the relationship changed, but because you’re only seeing a thin cross-section of it. This matters anywhere data gets filtered before analysis, e.g. studying only applicants who passed a screening test, or only patients who came back for a follow-up.

Panel 1 — The Full Picture


Code
set.seed(7)
n <- 400

# True relationship: x and y with r ~ 0.80
x   <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 15)
eps <- rnorm(n, sd = 15 * sqrt(1 - 0.80^2))
y   <- 0.80 * x + eps

dat       <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
r_full    <- cor(x, y)

lo <- 42; hi <- 58
dat$selected <- x >= lo & x <= hi
r_sub <- cor(x[dat$selected], y[dat$selected])

t <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5)
  )

p1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3498DB", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, fill = "#3498DB",
              color = "#2471A3", linewidth = 1.1, alpha = 0.15) +
  annotate("label", x = 18, y = max(y) * 0.97,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(r_full, 2)),
           size = 4, fontface = "bold", color = "#2471A3",
           fill = "white", label.size = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "Full sample  (n = 400)",
    subtitle = "Strong, clearly visible correlation",
    x = "Score (X)", y = "Outcome (Y)"
  ) + t

p1









With the full range of X visible, the strong upward relationship (r ≈ 0.80) is obvious.


Panel 2 — Zooming Into a Narrow Window


Code
p2 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
  # shade the selected window
  annotate("rect", xmin = lo, xmax = hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.07) +
  # grey out out-of-range points
  geom_point(data = subset(dat, !selected),
             color = "grey80", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.4) +
  # highlight in-range points
  geom_point(data = subset(dat, selected),
             color = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.75, size = 1.8) +
  # full-sample regression (ghost)
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "#3498DB", linewidth = 0.8,
              linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.6) +
  # subsample regression
  geom_smooth(data = subset(dat, selected), method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              fill = "#E74C3C", color = "#C0392B",
              linewidth = 1.1, alpha = 0.18) +
  # boundary markers
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lo, hi), linetype = "dotted",
             color = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("label", x = (lo + hi) / 2, y = max(y) * 0.97,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(r_sub, 2), "\n(subsample)"),
           size = 3.6, fontface = "bold", color = "#C0392B",
           fill = "white", label.size = 0, vjust = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = 18, y = max(y) * 0.97,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(r_full, 2), "\n(full)"),
           size = 3.2, color = "grey55", fill = "white",
           label.size = 0, vjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = (lo + hi) / 2, y = min(y) + 2,
           label = paste0("[", lo, " – ", hi, "]"),
           size = 3, color = "#C0392B") +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("Subsample: x ∈ [", lo, ", ", hi, "]  (n = ",
                      sum(dat$selected), ")"),
    subtitle = "Same data, narrower window — correlation collapses",
    x = "Score (X)", y = "Outcome (Y)"
  ) + t

p2









Same underlying dataset — we’ve just zoomed into the red-shaded window of X values. The correlation inside that window drops sharply from 0.8 to about 0.26, even though nothing about the true relationship changed.


Panel 3 — Correlation as a Function of Window Width


Code
half_widths <- seq(4, 44, by = 2)
curve_dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(half_widths, function(hw) {
  sub <- dat[abs(dat$x - 50) < hw, ]
  data.frame(
    window_width = hw * 2,
    r            = if (nrow(sub) >= 10) cor(sub$x, sub$y) else NA,
    n_sub        = nrow(sub)
  )
}))
curve_dat <- curve_dat[!is.na(curve_dat$r), ]

used_width <- hi - lo

p3 <- ggplot(curve_dat, aes(window_width, r)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = r_full, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#3498DB", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(color = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(color = "#E74C3C", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = used_width, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = curve_dat[curve_dat$window_width == used_width, ],
             size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "#E74C3C", color = "black", stroke = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = used_width + 1.5, y = 0.12,
           label = paste0("panel 2\n(width=", used_width, ")"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#C0392B") +
  annotate("text", x = max(curve_dat$window_width) - 1,
           y = r_full + 0.025,
           label = paste0("true r = ", round(r_full, 2)),
           hjust = 1, size = 3.2, color = "#3498DB") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Observed r vs. Range Width",
    subtitle = "Narrowing the observed range shrinks the observed correlation",
    x = "Width of observed x-window",
    y = "Observed Pearson r"
  ) + t

p3









This traces out exactly how much correlation you’d measure for every possible window width. The dashed blue line marks the “true” correlation from the full data; the red curve shows how far below that you land the more you restrict your range. The circled point marks the specific narrow window used in Panel 2.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Birthday Paradox
The idea: How many people need to be in a room before there’s a better-than-50% chance that two of them share a birthday? Most people guess somewhere near 180 (half of 365). The real answer is just 23. The trick is that you’re not comparing one person against everyone else — you’re comparing every pair of people, and the number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people.


Code
C1 <- "#E74C3C"; C2 <- "#3498DB"; C3 <- "#27AE60"
C4 <- "#9B59B6"; CG <- "grey55"

t <- theme_bw(base_size = 13) + theme(
  plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
  plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5, lineheight = 1.2),
  legend.position = "bottom",
  legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "lines"),
  legend.text     = element_text(size = 8)
)

bd <- data.frame(n = 1:70)
bd$prob <- sapply(bd$n, function(n) 1 - prod((365:(365 - n + 1)) / 365))

p1 <- ggplot(bd, aes(n, prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = prob), fill = C2, alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(color = C2, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = CG) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 23, linetype = "dotted", color = C1) +
  geom_point(data = bd[bd$n == 23, ], size = 3.5,
             shape = 21, fill = "white", color = C1, stroke = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 26, y = 0.36, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C1,
           label = "n = 23\np > 50%") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%"),
                     limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Birthday Paradox",
       subtitle = "P(≥2 shared birthdays) by group size",
       x = "People in group", y = "Probability") + t

p1









The probability curve crosses 50% at just 23 people, and by around 70 people it’s essentially guaranteed. Pairwise comparisons scale much faster than intuition expects.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
False Positive Paradox (Base Rate Fallacy)
The idea: Even a highly accurate medical test can be wrong about you as often as it’s right, or more often, if the condition it’s testing for is rare. If a test is 99% accurate (both at correctly flagging sick people and correctly clearing healthy ones), but only 1% of the population actually has the disease, roughly half of all positive results will still be false alarms. Rarity, not test quality, is what dominates here.


Code
prev_seq <- seq(0.001, 0.30, length.out = 300)
sens <- 0.99; spec <- 0.99
ppv  <- (sens * prev_seq) / (sens * prev_seq + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev_seq))
fp_dat <- data.frame(prev = prev_seq, ppv = ppv)

hit <- fp_dat[which.min(abs(fp_dat$prev - 0.01)), ]

p2 <- ggplot(fp_dat, aes(prev, ppv)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = ppv), fill = C1, alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_line(color = C1, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = CG) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.01, linetype = "dotted", color = C4) +
  geom_point(data = hit, size = 3.5,
             shape = 21, fill = "white", color = C4, stroke = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.014, y = 0.30, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C4,
           label = "1% prevalence\nPPV ≈ 50%!") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x * 100, "%")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%"),
                     limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "False Positive Paradox",
       subtitle = "P(truly sick | positive test)  [sens = spec = 99%]",
       x = "True disease prevalence", y = "Positive predictive value") + t

p2









The y-axis (positive predictive value) is the chance a positive result is a true positive. At 1% prevalence it’s only 50% — a coin flip — even though the test itself is 99% accurate. As the disease becomes more common (moving right), the test becomes far more trustworthy.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Parrondo’s Paradox
The idea: Take two gambling games that are each, individually, rigged to lose money on average. Now switch between them in a fixed pattern (A, B, B, A, B, B, …). Astonishingly, the combined strategy can win over time. This happens because Game B’s odds depend on your current capital (whether it is a multiple of 3), and the moves made in Game A knock your capital out of Game B’s unfavorable state more often than Game B alone would — their interaction creates an opportunity that neither game has on its own.


Code
play_game <- function(game, capital) {
  p <- if (game == "A") 0.495 else if (capital %% 3 == 0) 0.095 else 0.745
  capital + if (runif(1) < p) 1L else -1L
}

run_strat <- function(strategy, rounds = 300) {
  cap <- 0L
  sapply(seq_len(rounds), function(i) {
    g <- if (strategy == "A") "A"
    else if (strategy == "B") "B"
    else if (i %% 3 == 1) "A" else "B"   # repeating A, B, B pattern
    cap <<- play_game(g, cap)
    cap
  })
}

n_sims <- 40
par_dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("A", "B", "A+B (ABB pattern)"), function(strat) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_sims), function(s) {
    set.seed(s * 17)
    data.frame(round = seq_len(300), capital = run_strat(strat),
               sim = s, strategy = strat)
  }))
}))
par_mean <- aggregate(capital ~ round + strategy, par_dat, mean)
end_cap  <- with(par_mean[par_mean$round == 300, ], setNames(capital, strategy))

p3 <- ggplot(par_dat, aes(round, capital,
                          group = interaction(sim, strategy), color = strategy)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.07, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = par_mean, aes(group = strategy), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("A" = C1, "B" = CG, "A+B (ABB pattern)" = C3),
    labels = c("A" = "Game A  (losing)", "B" = "Game B  (losing)",
               "A+B (ABB pattern)" = "Switching A,B,B  (winning!)")
  ) +
  labs(title = "Parrondo's Paradox",
       subtitle = "Two losing games → winning strategy when played in an A,B,B pattern",
       x = "Round", y = "Capital", color = NULL) + t

p3









Both Game A (red) and Game B (grey) drift below zero on average — they’re losing propositions on their own (average capital after 300 rounds: -5.35 and -2.6). But playing them in the repeating pattern A, B, B (green) climbs upward, to 16.25 after 300 rounds. Note that simple one-for-one alternation (ABAB) is not enough with these parameters: it still loses slightly. Combining two “bad” strategies can beat either one alone.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Survivorship Bias
The idea: If you only study the winners — the WWII planes that made it back to base, the startups that became famous, the people who “made it” — you get a distorted picture of what actually causes success, because the failures that could tell a different story are invisible to you. Here, “outcome” depends partly on quality and partly on luck, but if we only look at data points that crossed a “survived” threshold, the relationship between quality and outcome is distorted — in this case it is flattened, because low-quality survivors are exactly the ones who got very lucky.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_surv <- 500
quality <- rnorm(n_surv, 50, 12)
luck    <- rnorm(n_surv, 0, 18)
outcome <- 0.3 * quality + luck + 20
sv_dat  <- data.frame(quality, outcome, survived = outcome > 55)
b_all   <- coef(lm(outcome ~ quality, sv_dat))[[2]]
b_sv    <- coef(lm(outcome ~ quality, subset(sv_dat, survived)))[[2]]

p4 <- ggplot(sv_dat, aes(quality, outcome)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(sv_dat, !survived),
             color = "grey82", size = 1.3, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = subset(sv_dat, survived),
             color = C2, size = 1.6, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = CG,
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(sv_dat, survived),
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = C2, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 55, linetype = "dotted", color = C1, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 17, y = 57.5, hjust = 0, size = 2.7, color = C1,
           label = "success threshold") +
  annotate("text", x = 74, y = 22,  hjust = 1, size = 2.7, color = "grey60",
           label = "unseen failures") +
  annotate("text", x = 74, y = 84,  hjust = 1, size = 2.7, color = C2,
           label = "observed survivors") +
  labs(title = "Survivorship Bias",
       subtitle = "Survivors (blue) give a distorted view of how quality relates to outcome",
       x = "Quality", y = "Outcome") + t

p4









Looking only at the blue “survivors,” quality barely seems to matter (the solid blue line is nearly flat, slope ≈ 0.13). Across everyone, including the grey failures, the true slope (dashed line) is more than twice as steep (≈ 0.29). Judging only by survivors gives a distorted picture: their outcomes are inflated by luck, which hides how quality really relates to outcome.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Inspection Paradox
The idea: If buses arrive randomly with an average gap of 10 minutes between them, and you show up at a random moment, your expected wait is not 5 minutes (half the average gap) but the full 10 minutes, because the gap you land in averages about 20 minutes. Why? Because you’re more likely to arrive during a long gap than a short one — long gaps simply take up more clock time, so they’re easier to “land in.” This is why your personal experience of waiting always seems worse than the average would suggest.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_gaps  <- 4000
gap_all <- rexp(n_gaps, rate = 1 / 10)
gap_hit <- sample(gap_all, n_gaps, replace = TRUE, prob = gap_all / sum(gap_all))

insp_dat <- data.frame(
  gap    = c(gap_all, gap_hit),
  source = rep(c(paste0("All gaps  (mean = ", round(mean(gap_all), 1), " min)"),
                 paste0("Gap you land in  (mean = ", round(mean(gap_hit), 1), " min)")),
               each = n_gaps)
)

p5 <- ggplot(insp_dat, aes(gap, fill = source, color = source)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.30, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(gap_all)), color = C2,
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(gap_hit)), color = C1,
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(gap_all) + 1, y = 0.068,
           label = paste0(round(mean(gap_all), 1), " min"), hjust = 0,
           size = 2.8, color = C2) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(gap_hit) + 1, y = 0.068,
           label = paste0(round(mean(gap_hit), 1), " min"), hjust = 0,
           size = 2.8, color = C1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 60)) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c(C2, C1), name = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(C2, C1), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Inspection Paradox",
       subtitle = "You always seem to arrive mid-gap — because longer gaps are easier to land in",
       x = "Gap length (min)", y = "Density") + t

p5









The blue curve is the true distribution of gaps between buses (mean ≈ 10.2 minutes). The red curve is the distribution of gaps that a random arrival actually experiences (mean ≈ 20.5 minutes, about double) — shifted noticeably to the right, because random arrivals are “size-biased” toward longer gaps.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Accuracy Paradox
The idea: When one outcome is much more common than the other (e.g. most patients are healthy), a model can score very high “accuracy” while being completely useless. A model that always predicts “healthy” will be right 95% of the time if 95% of patients truly are healthy — while catching exactly zero of the actual sick patients. Accuracy alone can hide a model that provides no real value; you need to also look at recall (how many true cases it actually catches).


Code
make_cm <- function(tp, fp, tn, fn, model_label) {
  total <- tp + fp + tn + fn
  data.frame(
    actual    = factor(c("Sick","Sick","Healthy","Healthy"),
                       levels = c("Sick","Healthy")),
    predicted = factor(c("Sick","Healthy","Sick","Healthy"),
                       levels = c("Sick","Healthy")),
    pct       = round(c(tp, fn, fp, tn) / total * 100, 1),
    model     = model_label
  )
}

acc_dat <- rbind(
  make_cm(0, 0, 9500, 500,
          "Model A  ('always Healthy')\nAccuracy 95%  |  Recall 0%"),
  make_cm(400, 900, 8600, 100,
          "Model B  (real classifier)\nAccuracy 90%  |  Recall 80%")
)

p6 <- ggplot(acc_dat, aes(predicted, actual, fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")), size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "white", mid = "#FFF3B0",
                       high = C1, midpoint = 30,
                       name = "% of total") +
  labs(title = "Accuracy Paradox",
       subtitle = "95%-accurate model catches zero sick patients",
       x = "Predicted", y = "Actual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 10),
        strip.text      = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "none")

p6









Model A boasts 95% accuracy but its “Sick / Predicted Sick” cell is 0% — it never identifies a single sick patient. Model B has lower accuracy (90%) but is actually useful, correctly flagging 80% of sick patients. Never judge a classifier by accuracy alone when classes are imbalanced.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Friendship Paradox
The idea: On average, your friends have more friends than you do. This isn’t a comment on your popularity — it’s a mathematical property of networks. Highly-connected people show up in many people’s friend lists, so when you average “how many friends does my friend have,” those popular people get counted repeatedly and pull the average up.


Code
edges_fp <- data.frame(
  a = c(1,1,1,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4,5,6,7,8),
  b = c(2,3,4,5,6,7,3,8,9,10,9,10,11,11,12)
)
all_n <- 1:12
deg   <- sapply(all_n, function(v) sum(edges_fp$a == v | edges_fp$b == v))

fp_dat <- data.frame(
  own = deg,
  mean_nbr = sapply(all_n, function(v) {
    nb <- union(edges_fp$b[edges_fp$a == v], edges_fp$a[edges_fp$b == v])
    if (!length(nb)) return(NA)
    mean(deg[nb])
  })
)
fp_dat <- na.omit(fp_dat)

p7 <- ggplot(fp_dat, aes(own, mean_nbr)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              color = CG, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(color = C4, size = 3.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.1, y = 5.5, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C4,
           label = "above the line:\nyour friends have\nmore friends than you") +
  labs(title = "Friendship Paradox",
       subtitle = "Mean neighbor degree > own degree for most nodes",
       x = "Your degree (# friends)",
       y = "Mean degree of your friends") + t

p7









Most points (8 of 12 people; several overlap) sit above the dashed diagonal line, meaning their friends have more connections than they do. Only the two most-connected people (degree 4 and 6, at the far right) fall below it, and two people sit exactly on it.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Braess’s Paradox
The idea: Adding a brand-new, free shortcut to a road network can make traffic worse for everyone. This happens because every driver selfishly picks whatever looks like the fastest route for themselves; once the new road exists, enough drivers pile onto it that it creates a new bottleneck, and the system settles into a “Nash equilibrium” where everyone’s total travel time is higher than before the shortcut existed.


Code
nodes_b <- data.frame(x = c(0,2,2,4), y = c(1,2,0,1), lbl = c("S","A","B","T"))

segs_before <- data.frame(
  x=c(0,2,0,2), y=c(1,2,1,0), xend=c(2,4,2,4), yend=c(2,1,0,1),
  cost=c("x/N","1","1","x/N"), new=FALSE
)
segs_after <- rbind(segs_before,
                    data.frame(x=2,y=2,xend=2,yend=0,cost="0  ← new!",new=TRUE)
)

make_net <- function(segs, nodes, title_str, cost_str, cost_col) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = segs,
                 aes(x,y,xend=xend,yend=yend,color=new,linewidth=new),
                 arrow = arrow(length=unit(0.18,"cm"),type="closed")) +
    geom_label(data = segs,
               aes((x+xend)/2 + ifelse(cost=="0  ← new!", 0.22, 0),
                   (y+yend)/2 + ifelse(cost=="0  ← new!", 0, 0),
                   label=cost, color=new),
               size=2.7, label.size=0, fill="white") +
    geom_point(data=nodes, aes(x,y), size=9, color="#2C3E50") +
    geom_text(data=nodes, aes(x,y,label=lbl),
              color="white", fontface="bold", size=3.5) +
    annotate("text", x=2, y=-0.35, label=cost_str, hjust=0.5,
             size=3.2, fontface="bold", color=cost_col) +
    scale_color_manual(values=c(`FALSE`="grey40",`TRUE`=C1), guide="none") +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values=c(`FALSE`=0.8,`TRUE`=1.4), guide="none") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-0.5, 2.5)) +
    labs(subtitle=title_str) +
    theme_void(base_size=10) +
    theme(plot.subtitle=element_text(color="grey40",size=8,hjust=0.5))
}

net1 <- make_net(segs_before, nodes_b, "Without new road", "Nash cost = 1.5", C3)
net2 <- make_net(segs_after,  nodes_b, "With free A→B road (red)", "Nash cost = 2.0  ↑", C1)

p8 <- (net1 / net2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Braess's Paradox",
    subtitle = "Adding a free road raises everyone's travel time at equilibrium",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face="bold", size=13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color="grey45", size=9)
    )
  )

p8









In the top network, drivers split evenly between the two routes (S→A→T and S→B→T), each taking 1.5 units of time. Once the free A→B shortcut is added (bottom), it becomes individually rational for everyone to route through it — but that congests the shared x/N segments, and the equilibrium travel time rises to 2.0 for everyone. More capacity, worse outcome — because no single driver has an incentive to avoid the “shortcut” unilaterally.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
P-hacking / Multiple Comparisons
The idea: If you run 100 statistical tests on data that has no real effect at all, roughly 5 of them will still come out “statistically significant” purely by chance, if you use the standard 5% significance threshold. This is exactly what that threshold means: a 5% chance of a false alarm on any single test. Run enough tests and cherry-pick the “significant” ones without accounting for how many tests you ran, and you’ll “discover” effects that are pure noise. This is a major reason many published findings fail to replicate.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_tests <- 100
pv      <- sort(runif(n_tests))
ph_dat  <- data.frame(rank = seq_len(n_tests), p = pv, sig = pv < 0.05)

p9 <- ggplot(ph_dat, aes(rank, p, fill = sig, color = sig)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, color = C1, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c(`TRUE` = C1, `FALSE` = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = C1, `FALSE` = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = 0.11, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C1,
           label = paste0(sum(ph_dat$sig), " 'significant' results\n(all truly null!)")) +
  labs(title = "P-hacking / Multiple Comparisons",
       subtitle = paste0("100 tests on pure noise — about 5 expected to cross α=0.05 by chance (",
                         sum(ph_dat$sig), " here)"),
       x = "Test (sorted by p-value)", y = "p-value") + t

p9









None of these 100 tests reflect a real effect — the underlying data was pure random noise. Yet a handful of bars dip below the red 0.05 threshold purely by chance, and in a real analysis those would be the ones that get reported as “significant findings” if you didn’t correct for the number of tests run.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Takeaway
Every one of these graphs shows the same underlying warning: statistics computed on data can mislead you unless you understand how the data was grouped, selected, filtered, or compared. Aggregation, selection bias, imbalanced classes, restricted ranges, and repeated testing can all make a relationship appear, disappear, or reverse — without any single number “lying” on its own. The fix is always the same: look at the full picture, plot your data, and think carefully about how it was collected before trusting a summary statistic.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
text:
In 2025 the US federal government lost staff in several ways at once. In January, most federal employees were offered a deferred resignation: stop working, stay on the payroll until 30 September 2025, then resign. Agencies offered early retirement, carried out reductions in force (layoffs) and dismissed staff. And people kept quitting and retiring, as they do every year.
So everyone who left federal service in 2025 left in one of six ways. This page asks: among the people who left, what made one way of leaving more likely than another? Did the young quit and the old retire? Who took the deferred resignation? Who was laid off?
The outcome is a category with six values and no natural order: quitting is not “more” or “less” than being laid off. The type of outcome decides the type of regression:



Outcome
Regression
Example




Two categories
logistic
hired or not


Ordered categories
ordinal logistic
a performance rating from 1 to 5


Unordered categories
multinomial logistic
how someone left: quit, retired, laid off…



A multinomial logistic regression picks one category as the reference and fits a logistic regression of each of the other categories against it, all at the same time. The data are real: the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) publishes a record for every federal employee who leaves.


Code
library(nnet)         # multinom(): multinomial logistic regression (comes with R)
library(nanoparquet)  # read_parquet(): reads the Parquet files that OPM publishes
library(ggplot2)

# one colour per way of leaving, the same in every chart
exits   <- c("Quit", "Retired", "Early retirement", "Deferred resignation", "Laid off", "Terminated")
colours <- setNames(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300"), exits)
ink     <- setNames(c("white", "white", "white", "#0b0b0b", "white", "white"), exits)  # labels on the bars

# number formats for the text
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
rr   <- function(x) ifelse(x >= 100, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","),
                           formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))                   # relative risk ratios

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
text:
1. The data
OPM’s Federal Workforce Data has a file for every month with one row per separation: a civilian employee leaving federal service. Each row says how the person left, their age group, years of service, agency, occupation, type of appointment and more. The files are free, need no login, and come through an API as Parquet files of one to four MB.
A monthly file holds the separations processed in that month, and some of them took effect months earlier: separations of September 2025 were still arriving in 2026. So we download every file from October 2023 to the latest one, and sort the separations by the date they took effect.


Code
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads

# the list of monthly files, with the current version of each
files <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations?current=true")
files <- files[as.integer(files$year) * 100 + as.integer(files$month) >= 202310, ]
latest <- max(as.Date(paste(files$year, files$month, "01", sep = "-")))

# the columns we need, out of the 69 in each file
columns <- c("personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm", "separation_category", "drp_indicator",
             "age_bracket", "length_of_service_years", "supervisory_status",
             "appointment_type", "stem_occupation")

# one month: download the file and read the columns; try again if OPM asks us to slow down
read_month <- function(year, month, version) {
  url  <- sprintf("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations/%s/%s/%s/download", year, month, version)
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
  for (attempt in 1:3) {
    ok <- tryCatch(download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE) == 0, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (ok) break
    Sys.sleep(10 * attempt)
  }
  if (!ok) stop("Could not download ", url)
  as.data.frame(read_parquet(path, col_select = columns))
}

raw <- do.call(rbind, Map(read_month, files$year, files$month, files$version))
nrow(raw)


[1] 808769


That is 36 monthly files, up to September 2026. The US federal fiscal year runs from October to September: fiscal year 2025 (FY2025) is October 2024 to September 2025. We keep FY2024, a year before the changes, and FY2025:


Code
ym <- as.integer(raw$personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm)   # e.g. 202509 = September 2025
raw$month       <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", ym %/% 100, ym %% 100))
raw$fiscal_year <- ym %/% 100 + (ym %% 100 >= 10)              # October 2024 to September 2025 = 2025

d <- subset(raw, fiscal_year %in% 2024:2025)
table(d$separation_category, d$fiscal_year)

  OTHER SEPARATION                    16296  17123
  QUIT                                81772 159332

  TRANSFER OUT - INDIVIDUAL TRANSFER  33003  16288
  TRANSFER OUT - MASS TRANSFER          169     84


OPM records how each separation was processed. A separate column, drp_indicator, says whether it came under the deferred resignation programme (Y):


Code
with(subset(d, fiscal_year == 2025), table(separation_category, drp_indicator))


                                    drp_indicator
separation_category                      N     Y
  OTHER SEPARATION                   17069    54
  QUIT                               94970 64362
  REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)           10416     1
  RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT              8525 12391
  RETIREMENT - OTHER                  5173    76
  RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY             69798 32692
  TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)   36907   465
  TRANSFER OUT - INDIVIDUAL TRANSFER 16259    29
  TRANSFER OUT - MASS TRANSFER          83     1


On paper, most people who took the deferred resignation quit or retired. But they took a different route from people who quit or retired in the ordinary way, so we give them a category of their own. The six ways of leaving:








Way of leaving
OPM category
What it means




Quit
QUIT
Resigned


Retired
RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY, RETIREMENT - OTHER
Retired on a pension


Early retirement
RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT
Took the agency’s offer of an early pension: age 50 with 20 years of service, or any age with 25 years


Deferred resignation
any of the above with drp_indicator = Y
Accepted the 2025 offer; most left on 30 September 2025


Laid off
REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)
The position was abolished


Terminated
TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)
A temporary appointment ended, or the agency ended the employment, for example during the probationary period



We leave out transfers to another agency (those people are still federal employees) and “other separation”, which includes deaths.


Code
exit <- c("QUIT"                             = "Quit",
          "RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY"           = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - OTHER"               = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT"           = "Early retirement",
          "REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)"         = "Laid off",
          "TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)" = "Terminated")[d$separation_category]
exit[!is.na(exit) & d$drp_indicator %in% "Y"] <- "Deferred resignation"
d$exit <- factor(exit, levels = exits)
d <- subset(d, !is.na(exit))     # drops the transfers and the other separations


The predictors are five characteristics of each person. Years of service are cut where the rules change: the first year is usually a probationary period, early retirement needs 20 or 25 years, and a full pension needs, for example, 30 years from age 55 to 57 or 20 years at age 60.


Code
age <- ifelse(d$age_bracket %in% c("LESS THAN 20", "20-24"), "Under 25",
       ifelse(d$age_bracket == "65 OR MORE", "65+", d$age_bracket))
d$age <- factor(age, levels = c("Under 25", "25-29", "30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49",
                                "50-54", "55-59", "60-64", "65+"))

years <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d$length_of_service_years))
years[years > 60] <- NA          # a few impossible values (up to 1,800 years of service)
d$service <- cut(years, c(-Inf, 1, 5, 10, 20, 25, 30, Inf), right = FALSE,
                 labels = c("Under 1", "1-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-24", "25-29", "30+"))

# supervisors and managers; team leaders count as non-supervisors
supervisors  <- c("SUPERVISOR OR MANAGER", "SUPERVISOR (CSRA)", "MANAGEMENT OFFICIAL (CSRA)")
d$supervisor <- factor(ifelse(d$supervisory_status == "INVALID", NA,
                              ifelse(d$supervisory_status %in% supervisors, "Yes", "No")),
                       levels = c("No", "Yes"))

# a permanent or a temporary (nonpermanent) appointment
d$permanent <- factor(ifelse(d$appointment_type == "INVALID", NA,
                             ifelse(grepl("NONPERMANENT", d$appointment_type), "No", "Yes")),
                      levels = c("Yes", "No"))

# STEM, health or other occupations; "UNSPECIFIED" becomes NA
d$occupation <- factor(c("ALL OTHER OCCUPATIONS" = "Other", "STEM OCCUPATIONS" = "STEM",
                         "HEALTH OCCUPATIONS" = "Health")[d$stem_occupation],
                       levels = c("Other", "STEM", "Health"))

vars <- c("exit", "age", "service", "supervisor", "permanent", "occupation")
d    <- d[complete.cases(d[vars]), ]
fy25 <- subset(d, fiscal_year == 2025)
table(d$fiscal_year)



  2024   2025 
172225 329911 


Each row is a separation, not a person: someone who left two temporary jobs in a year is in the data twice. We still call them people, for short.

In FY2025, 329,911 people left in these six ways, 1.9 times as many as in FY2024, and the most common way to leave was the deferred resignation. From here on we use FY2025. Who left which way?

# stacked bars of shares (each bar adds up to 100%), with the larger shares labelled
stacked <- function(m, y_label, x_label) {

    geom_col(width = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +

    scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +

    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(5.5, 18, 5.5, 5.5)) +  # room for "100%"

}

# how the people in each group left, in FY2025
mix <- function(group, label) {
  m <- as.data.frame(prop.table(table(group = fy25[[group]], exit = fy25$exit), 1), responseName = "share")
  stacked(m, label, "share of the people in the group who left in FY2025")
}
mix("age", "age")











Code
mix("service", "years of service")









Code
share      <- function(group) prop.table(table(fy25[[group]], fy25$exit), 1)
by_age     <- share("age")
by_service <- share("service")
by_job     <- share("occupation")
middle     <- c("30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54", "55-59", "60-64")



Quitting is the usual way out up to age 45; from 50 on, people retire.
Early retirement happens at 50 to 59 and with 20 to 29 years of service: the eligibility rules.
The deferred resignation is the odd one: between 32% and 38% of the people in every age group from 30 to 64 took it, and a similar share at every length of service from one year up. Ordinary quitting and retiring each belong to one end of a career; the deferred resignation drew from all of it.
Layoffs hit the middle of careers: 8.7% of the people aged 45 to 49 who left, 7.6% of those with 10 to 19 years of service.
Terminations belong to the young and the new: 36% of the people under 25 and 35% of those with less than a year of service.
Occupations differ too: only 4.5% of the people in health occupations took the deferred resignation, against 45% in STEM and 34% in other occupations. Agencies could exclude positions from the offer.

Age and years of service go together, so these charts cannot tell whether age or service drives an exit. The model can: it estimates each effect holding the others constant.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a reference category
Choose one way of leaving as the yardstick. We use Quit, an ordinary resignation: every other way of leaving is compared with quitting. Any category could be the reference; the predicted probabilities are the same, only the comparisons in the output change. In R the reference is the first level of the factor (levels(fy25$exit)[1] is Quit), and relevel() changes it.


Step 2: one equation for every other category
For person \(i\) and each way of leaving \(k\) other than quitting:
\[\eta_{ik} = \ln\frac{P(\text{exit}_i = k)}{P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit})} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k}x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_{pk}x_{pi}\]
That is five equations, each with its own intercept and its own slopes. The left side is the log of the relative risk: how much more likely leaving by \(k\) is than quitting. Each equation looks like a logistic regression; the difference is that the five are estimated together, so that every person’s six probabilities add up to 1.


Step 3: from the equations to probabilities
\[P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit}) = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}} \qquad P(\text{exit}_i = k) = \frac{e^{\eta_{ik}}}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}}\]
The sums run over the five categories other than Quit. Each probability is between 0 and 1, and the six add up to 1. This is the softmax function, the same formula that neural networks use to classify.


Step 4: what a coefficient means
\(e^{\beta}\) is the relative risk ratio (RRR): the number by which the ratio \(P(k)/P(\text{Quit})\) is multiplied when the predictor moves from its reference level to this level, with the other predictors held constant. An RRR of 2 means twice as likely to leave by \(k\) rather than by quitting. Some books and programs call it an odds ratio; either way it compares two categories with each other, not one category with all the others.


Step 5: how R finds the β’s
By maximum likelihood: R looks for the \(\beta\)’s that make the exits that people actually took as probable as possible,
\[\ln L = \sum_i \ln P(\text{exit}_i = \text{the exit that person } i \text{ took})\]
multinom() maximises it. It fits the model as a neural network without a hidden layer, which is why it lives in the package nnet.


Step 6: count the parameters
A predictor with \(c\) categories gets \(c - 1\) coefficients: age has 10 groups (9 coefficients), service 7 (6), supervisor and appointment 2 each (1 each) and occupation 3 (2). That is 19 slopes plus an intercept, 20 per equation, and 5 equations make 100 parameters. Multinomial models grow fast: every category needs enough people for a whole set of coefficients of its own.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
text:
4. Fitting the model
Every predictor is a category, so the 329,911 people fall into a limited number of combinations of age group, service, supervisor, appointment, occupation and exit. Fitting the model to the count of people in each combination gives the same estimates as fitting the people one by one: 300 people with the same values add the same term to the log-likelihood 300 times, which is what weights = Freq does. It takes a second instead of minutes.


Code
g <- as.data.frame(table(fy25[vars]))   # one row per combination; Freq = the number of people
g <- subset(g, Freq > 0)
nrow(g)


[1] 2416


Code
fit <- multinom(exit ~ age + service + supervisor + permanent + occupation,
                data = g, weights = Freq, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE, Hess = TRUE)
summary(fit)
