title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
text:
Since 1972 the General Social Survey (GSS) has asked Americans: “On the whole, how satisfied are you with the work you do — would you say you are very satisfied, moderately satisfied, a little dissatisfied, or very dissatisfied?” In 2022 it also asked them about the job itself: are they free to decide how to do their work, are they treated with respect, is the job secure, how often is it stressful, how often do they work from home?
This page asks: which of these go with being more satisfied with one’s job? Does working from home make people happier with their work, or is it something else?
The answer has four values in order: very dissatisfied, a little dissatisfied, moderately satisfied, very satisfied. But nobody knows how far apart they are: the step from “a little dissatisfied” to “moderately satisfied” may be bigger than the step from “moderately” to “very”. The type of outcome decides the type of regression:



Outcome
Regression
Example




Two categories
logistic
hired or not


Ordered categories
ordinal logistic
job satisfaction: very dissatisfied … very satisfied


Unordered categories
multinomial logistic
how someone left a job: quit, retired, laid off…



Three other ways to analyse the answers, and what each gets wrong:

A linear regression on the scores 1 to 4 assumes the four answers are equally far apart, and predicts answers such as 3.4 that nobody can give.
A logistic regression of satisfied against dissatisfied throws away the difference between “moderately” and “very” satisfied, where most people are.
A multinomial logistic regression ignores the order, and needs a whole set of coefficients for every answer: 27 parameters here instead of 11.

The ordinal logistic regression uses the order and needs one coefficient per predictor.


Code
library(MASS)      # polr(): ordinal logistic regression (comes with R)
library(ordinal)   # clm(), nominal_test(): checks the proportional odds assumption
library(haven)     # read_dta(): reads the Stata files of the GSS
library(ggplot2)

# one colour per answer, from red (dissatisfied) to blue (satisfied), the same in every chart
satisfaction <- c("Very dissatisfied", "A little dissatisfied", "Moderately satisfied", "Very satisfied")
colours <- setNames(c("#c23b3a", "#ec8a85", "#6da7ec", "#1c5cab"), satisfaction)
ink     <- setNames(c("white", "#0b0b0b", "#0b0b0b", "white"), satisfaction)  # labels on the bars

# number formats for the text
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
text:
1. The data
The GSS is run by NORC at the University of Chicago. Its data are free and need no login: one file per survey year. 2022 is the latest year with the Quality of Working Life module, a set of questions about work designed by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) and asked of everyone who had a job. The Stata file comes in a zip of 6 MB.


Code
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads
zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file("https://gss.norc.org/content/dam/gss/get-the-data/documents/stata/2022_stata.zip",
              zip, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
dta <- unzip(zip, files = "2022/GSS2022.dta", exdir = tempdir())

# the questions we need, out of the 1,297 columns in the file
columns <- c("satjob", "wkfreedm", "respect", "jobsecok", "stress", "wrkhome", "wrkslf", "age", "mode")
raw <- read_dta(dta, col_select = tidyselect::all_of(columns))
nrow(raw)


[1] 4149


Each answer is stored as a number with a label. “Don’t know”, “no answer”, “skipped on the web” and “not asked” (people without a job are not asked about their job) are special missing codes, which read_dta() turns into NA:


Code
attr(raw$satjob, "labels")[1:4]       # the four answers and their codes


       very satisfied  moderately satisfied a little dissatisfied     very dissatisfied 
                    1                     2                     3                     4 


Code
table(raw$satjob, useNA = "ifany")    # NA: not asked or not answered



   1    2    3    4 <NA> 
1268 1237  316  132 1196 


The codes run from very satisfied (1) to very dissatisfied (4). We turn them round, so that a higher number always means more of something: more satisfied, more freedom, more often stressed. The predictors:








Predictor
Question
Answers, coded




autonomy
I am given a lot of freedom to decide how to do my own work
1 not at all true, 2 not too true, 3 somewhat true, 4 very true


respect
At the place where I work, I am treated with respect
1 strongly disagree, 2 disagree, 3 agree, 4 strongly agree


security
The job security is good
1 not at all true … 4 very true


stress
How often do you find your work stressful?
1 never, 2 hardly ever, 3 sometimes, 4 often, 5 always


home
How often do you work at home as part of your job?
never; some days (from a few times a year to more than once a week); mainly at home


self_employed
Are you self-employed or do you work for someone else?
no, yes

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: cut the scale in three places
Four ordered answers can be split into “this answer or lower” against “higher” in three places:



Split \(j\)
Lower: \(Y \le j\)
Higher: \(Y > j\)




1
very dissatisfied
a little dissatisfied or more


2
dissatisfied (very or a little)
satisfied (moderately or very)


3
moderately satisfied or less
very satisfied



\(P(Y_i \le j)\) is a cumulative probability: the probability that person \(i\) gives answer \(j\) or a lower one.


Step 2: one logistic regression per split, with the same slopes
\[\text{logit}\,P(Y_i \le j) = \ln\frac{P(Y_i \le j)}{P(Y_i > j)} = \theta_j - (\beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_p x_{pi}), \qquad j = 1, 2, 3\]
Each split has its own intercept, \(\theta_j\), called a threshold or cut-point. The slopes \(\beta\) are the same at all three splits: a predictor changes the odds of a higher answer by the same factor wherever the scale is cut. This is the proportional odds assumption, and the model is also called the proportional odds model.
The thresholds increase, \(\theta_1 < \theta_2 < \theta_3\), because \(P(Y \le j)\) can only grow with \(j\). The minus sign makes a positive \(\beta\) mean higher answers: here, more satisfied. R’s polr() and clm() and SPSS’s PLUM write the model this way; some programs, for example SAS, write it with a plus sign, and their coefficients have the opposite sign.


Step 3: from the splits to the four answers
Write \(\eta_i = \beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_p x_{pi}\). Then
\[P(Y_i \le j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\theta_j - \eta_i)}}\]
and the probability of each answer is the difference between two cumulative probabilities:
\[P(Y_i = 1) = P(Y_i \le 1) \qquad P(Y_i = j) = P(Y_i \le j) - P(Y_i \le j - 1) \qquad P(Y_i = 4) = 1 - P(Y_i \le 3)\]
The four probabilities are between 0 and 1 and add up to 1.


Step 4: what a coefficient means
\(e^{\beta}\) is a cumulative odds ratio: the number by which the odds of a higher answer rather than a lower one are multiplied for each step up the predictor, with the other predictors held constant. With proportional odds the same number holds at every split. An odds ratio of 2 for respect means that one step up the respect scale doubles the odds of being very satisfied rather than less satisfied, and doubles the odds of being satisfied rather than dissatisfied, and doubles the odds of being anything but very dissatisfied.


Step 5: the picture behind the model, a hidden satisfaction scale
Imagine that each person has a hidden, continuous satisfaction, \(Y^*\), which depends on the predictors plus a random part:
\[Y^*_i = \eta_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \text{logistic}(0, 1)\]
The person answers by where \(Y^*\) falls among the thresholds: “very dissatisfied” below \(\theta_1\), “a little dissatisfied” between \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\), “moderately satisfied” between \(\theta_2\) and \(\theta_3\), “very satisfied” above \(\theta_3\). The predictors move the whole distribution of \(Y^*\) to the right or to the left; the thresholds stay where they are. This gives exactly the formulas of steps 2 and 3. With a normal \(\varepsilon\) instead of a logistic one, it is the ordinal probit model (polr(..., method = "probit")). Section 5 draws the picture with the fitted numbers.


Step 6: how R finds the numbers
By maximum likelihood: R looks for the thresholds and the \(\beta\)’s that make the answers people actually gave as probable as possible,
\[\ln L = \sum_i \ln P(Y_i = \text{the answer that person } i \text{ gave})\]


Step 7: count the parameters
Three thresholds, plus one slope for each of autonomy, respect, security, stress, self-employment and age, plus two for working from home (three groups): 11 parameters. A multinomial model with the same predictors needs 9 coefficients for each of the three answers other than the reference: 27.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?

            data = d, Hess = TRUE)
summary(fit)

    stress + home + self_employed + age10, data = d, Hess = TRUE)

Hess = TRUE keeps the matrix that summary() needs for the standard errors; without it, summary() fits the model again.

How to read the output


Code
b     <- coef(fit)                          # the slopes
theta <- fit$zeta                           # the thresholds
se    <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[names(b)]
z     <- b / se
p     <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))                 # summary() prints no p values: compute them
or    <- exp(b)                             # odds ratios
ci    <- exp(confint(fit))                  # their 95% confidence intervals (profile likelihood)










Part
Meaning
Here




Coefficients
One slope \(\beta\) per predictor term, with its standard error and \(t = \beta / SE\). Positive: more satisfied
respect: \(\beta\) = 0.73, SE = 0.07


Intercepts
The thresholds \(\theta_j\), named after the two answers they separate
Moderately satisfied|Very satisfied: 4.87


Residual Deviance
\(-2 \ln L\): how badly the model fits; smaller is better. Used for the tests in section 6
4,065


AIC
The deviance plus 2 for every parameter, for comparing models fitted to the same data
4,087




There are no p values. The t value is really a \(z\): compare it with the normal distribution. For respect, z = 10.03, p < .001.
The thresholds are the cut-points on the hidden scale for someone with every predictor at 0. Here that person does not exist (autonomy and respect start at 1, age at 18), so the thresholds mean little on their own; they are needed for the predicted probabilities.
One coefficient per predictor, not one per answer: that is the gain over the multinomial model.

The odds ratios:

All at the same values of the other predictors:

Respect matters most: each step up the scale, for example from “agree” to “strongly agree”, multiplies the odds of a higher satisfaction answer by 2.07.
Autonomy (1.48 per step) and job security (1.47) also go with more satisfaction.
Stress goes the other way: each step more often stressful cuts the odds of a higher answer by 31% (odds ratio 0.69).

Working from home alone does go with more satisfaction, as section 2 showed:

round(exp(coef(home_alone)), 2)

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
section: 5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model
text:
5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model

The hidden scale
Step 5 of section 3, with the fitted numbers: the hidden satisfaction of the typical worker if they disagree, and if they strongly agree, that they are treated with respect. Everything else stays the same.


Code
two <- people(autonomy = 3, respect = c(2, 4), security = 4, stress = 3, home = "Never",
              self_employed = "No", age10 = 4.1)
person <- c("Disagrees that they are treated with respect", "Strongly agrees that they are treated with respect")
centre <- eta + b[["respect"]] * (c(2, 4) - 3)        # eta of each: the typical worker has respect = 3
probs2 <- predict(fit, newdata = two, type = "probs")

grid   <- seq(-2.5, 11, by = 0.01)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(k)
  data.frame(person = person[k], y = grid, density = dlogis(grid, centre[k]),
             answer = cut(grid, c(-Inf, theta, Inf), labels = satisfaction))))
curves$person <- factor(curves$person, levels = person)

# the probability of each answer, printed above its part of the scale
middle <- c(theta[1] - 0.9, (theta[1] + theta[2]) / 2, (theta[2] + theta[3]) / 2, theta[3] + 1.6)
labels <- data.frame(person = factor(rep(person, each = 4), levels = person),
                     y = rep(middle, 2), share = as.vector(t(probs2)))

ggplot(curves, aes(y, density)) +
  geom_area(aes(fill = answer, group = answer), position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey20") +
  # the thresholds stop below their names, the centre at the top of the curve
  geom_segment(data = data.frame(x = theta), aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = 0.31),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_segment(data = data.frame(person = factor(person, levels = person), x = centre),
               aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = dlogis(0)), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(y, 0.29, label = pct(share)), size = 3.2, colour = "grey15") +
  geom_text(data = data.frame(person = factor(rep(person, each = 3), levels = person), y = rep(theta, 2),
                              label = rep(paste0("theta[", 1:3, "]"), 2)),
            aes(y, 0.33, label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 3.4, colour = "grey30") +
  facet_wrap(~ person, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.345), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Where the hidden satisfaction of the typical worker falls",
       subtitle = "Dashed lines: the thresholds. Solid line: the centre of the distribution, eta.\nThe percentages are the areas: the probability of each answer.",
       x = "hidden satisfaction (Y*)", y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))









Strongly agreeing instead of disagreeing moves the centre of the distribution by \(2\beta\) = 1.45 to the right. The thresholds stay where they are, so more of the area falls above \(\theta_3\): the probability of “very satisfied” goes from 23% to 56%.


Predicted probabilities, one predictor at a time
The typical worker again, changing one predictor at a time:


Code
vary <- function(v, values) {
  x <- typical[rep(1, length(values)), ]
  x[[v]] <- values
  pr <- predict(fit, newdata = x, type = "probs")
  labels <- paste0(questions[[v]], ": ", answers[[v]][values])
  data.frame(question = factor(questions[[v]], levels = questions),
             answer = factor(rep(labels, 4), levels = rev(labels)),
             satisfaction = factor(rep(satisfaction, each = length(values)), levels = satisfaction),
             share = as.vector(pr))
}
predicted <- rbind(vary("respect", 1:4), vary("autonomy", 1:4), vary("stress", 1:5))
predicted$question <- droplevels(predicted$question)
stacked(predicted, "predicted probability of each answer, for the typical worker")









Code
p_resp   <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(typical[rep(1, 4), ], respect = 1:4), type = "probs")
p_stress <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(typical[rep(1, 5), ], stress = 1:5), type = "probs")



From “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” that they are treated with respect, the probability that the typical worker is very satisfied rises from 13% to 56%, and the probability of being dissatisfied (very or a little) falls from 35% to 6%.
From work that is never stressful to work that is always stressful, “very satisfied” falls from 57% to 22%.
The odds ratio is the same at every step, the change in probability is not. Each step up the respect scale multiplies the odds by 2.07, but moves the probability of “very satisfied” by 10, 15, 18 percentage points: the effect on a probability depends on where a person starts.

Unlike the observed shares of section 2, these predictions follow the pattern of the model: every step up the respect scale helps, including the step from “strongly disagree” to “disagree”, which the few people who strongly disagree did not show.

text:
6. Testing the predictors and the model
The likelihood-ratio test compares the deviances of two nested models. First the whole model against a model with thresholds only, then each predictor: drop it and see how much worse the model gets.


Code
null <- polr(satisfaction ~ 1, data = d)
model_test <- anova(null, fit)
model_test

2 autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10      2156   4065.195 1 vs 2     8 566.9527       0


Code
tests <- drop1(fit, test = "Chisq")
tests


Single term deletions

Model:
satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + 
    self_employed + age10
              Df    AIC     LRT  Pr(>Chi)    
<none>           4087.2                      
autonomy       1 4128.6  43.387 4.491e-11 ***
respect        1 4188.0 102.836 < 2.2e-16 ***
security       1 4127.8  42.591 6.748e-11 ***
stress         1 4148.2  62.972 2.096e-15 ***
home           2 4086.9   3.657  0.160641    
self_employed  1 4095.6  10.395  0.001264 ** 
age10          1 4108.2  23.048 1.580e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
mcfadden <- 1 - deviance(fit) / deviance(null)   # McFadden's pseudo-R squared
mcfadden


[1] 0.1223952



Every predictor except working from home is significant. The \(\chi^2\) values rank them: respect (102.84), stress (62.97), autonomy (43.39) and job security (42.59), then age and self-employment. Working from home: \(\chi^2\)(2) = 3.66, p = .161.
McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) = 0.12: one minus the deviance of the model divided by the deviance of the model with thresholds only. It runs much lower than the \(R^2\) of a linear regression; use it to compare models fitted to the same data.

Is the order worth using? The same predictors in a multinomial model, which ignores the order:


Code
multi <- nnet::multinom(formula(fit), data = d, trace = FALSE)
data.frame(model      = c("ordinal (polr)", "multinomial (multinom)"),
           parameters = c(length(b) + length(theta), length(coef(multi))),
           AIC        = round(c(AIC(fit), AIC(multi)), 1))


                   model parameters    AIC
1         ordinal (polr)         11 4087.2
2 multinomial (multinom)         27 4115.9


The ordinal model fits better by AIC, with 11 parameters instead of 27: the multinomial model spends 16 more parameters and gains less than they cost.
How often does the model pick the right answer, if it picks the most likely one for each person?


Code
guess <- predict(fit, type = "class")
table(observed = d$satisfaction, predicted = guess)


                       predicted
observed                Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied Moderately satisfied Very satisfied
  Very dissatisfied                     6                    12                   48              9
  A little dissatisfied                 4                    10                  165             34
  Moderately satisfied                  1                    16                  574            323
  Very satisfied                        1                     8                  289            667


Code
accuracy  <- mean(as.character(guess) == as.character(d$satisfaction))
base_rate <- max(overall)   # always guessing the most common answer
c(model = accuracy, most_common_answer = base_rate)


             model most_common_answer 
         0.5800646          0.4453161 


58% right, against 45% for always guessing the most common answer. The model almost never predicts the two dissatisfied answers: they are rare, so for almost nobody are they the most likely answer. As in the multinomial example, the predicted probabilities carry the information, not the single best guess.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
text:
7. The proportional odds assumption
The model gives each predictor one slope for all three splits. Does it need three? A visual check first: fit a separate logistic regression at each split and compare the slopes.


Code
splits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(j) {
  dj <- transform(d, higher = as.integer(satisfaction) > j)   # TRUE above split j
  m  <- glm(update(formula(fit), higher ~ .), family = binomial, data = dj)
  data.frame(split = j, term = names(coef(m))[-1], b = coef(m)[-1], se = sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[-1])
}))
short <- c(autonomy = "Autonomy", respect = "Respect", security = "Job security", stress = "Stress",
           "homeSome days" = "Home: some days", homeMainly = "Home: mainly",
           self_employedYes = "Self-employed", age10 = "Age (10 years)")
splits$term <- factor(short[splits$term], levels = short)
common      <- data.frame(term = factor(short, levels = short), b = b[names(short)])

ggplot(splits, aes(split, b)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_hline(data = common, aes(yintercept = b), colour = "#1c5cab", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = b - 1.96 * se, ymax = b + 1.96 * se), width = 0.15, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = "grey15") +
  facet_wrap(~ term, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3, limits = c(0.6, 3.4)) +
  labs(title = "The slope of each predictor at each split",
       subtitle = "Points: the slope from a separate logistic regression, with its 95% CI.\nDashed line: the one slope of the ordinal model.\nSplits: 1 very dissatisfied | the rest, 2 dissatisfied | satisfied, 3 very satisfied | the rest",
       x = "split", y = "slope (log odds of a higher answer)") +
  theme_bw()









Code
security_splits <- splits$b[splits$term == short[["security"]]]


If the proportional odds assumption holds, the three points of each panel scatter around the dashed line, within their error bars. Most do. The clearest exception is job security: its slope grows from 0.07 at the first split to 0.45 at the third. Good job security seems to separate the very satisfied from the moderately satisfied more than it protects against being very dissatisfied. The confidence intervals are wide at the first split, though: only 75 people are very dissatisfied.
The formal test: fit the same model with clm() from the package ordinal, which can relax the assumption one predictor at a time. nominal_test() does that for each predictor and compares the two models with a likelihood-ratio test:


Code
# the same model as polr(), with the same estimates
clm_fit <- clm(satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10, data = d)
nominal <- nominal_test(clm_fit)
nominal


Tests of nominal effects

formula: satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10
              Df  logLik    AIC    LRT Pr(>Chi)
<none>           -2032.6 4087.2                
autonomy       2 -2032.5 4091.0 0.1898   0.9095
respect        2 -2031.5 4088.9 2.2979   0.3170
security       2 -2030.8 4087.6 3.5963   0.1656
stress         2 -2032.3 4090.7 0.4917   0.7821
home           4 -2031.4 4092.9 2.3305   0.6752
self_employed  2 -2032.5 4090.9 0.2827   0.8682
age10          2 -2032.2 4090.4 0.7607   0.6836


No predictor needs its own slopes: the smallest p is .166, for job security. The differences that the chart shows could be chance. The Brant test (Brant, 1990), in the package brant, is a common alternative that answers the same question.

If the assumption fails: a partial proportional odds model
If a predictor did fail the test, it could get one slope per split while the others keep one slope: a partial proportional odds model (Peterson & Harrell, 1990). In clm(), the predictors in nominal get their own slopes:


Code
partial <- clm(satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + stress + home + self_employed + age10,
               nominal = ~ security, data = d)
coef(partial)[grep("security", names(coef(partial)))]


   Very dissatisfied|A little dissatisfied.security A little dissatisfied|Moderately satisfied.security        Moderately satisfied|Very satisfied.security 
                                         -0.1968220                                          -0.3232832                                          -0.4471662 


Code
anova(clm_fit, partial)


Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models:
 
        formula:                                                                             nominal:  link: threshold:
clm_fit satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10 ~1        logit flexible  
partial satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + stress + home + self_employed + age10            ~security logit flexible  

        no.par    AIC  logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq)
clm_fit     11 4087.2 -2032.6                      
partial     13 4087.6 -2030.8  3.5963  2     0.1656


clm() writes these slopes as shifts of the thresholds, so the effect of security on a higher answer is the number shown with its sign changed: 0.20, 0.32, 0.45 at the three splits. The likelihood-ratio test is the same as the security row of nominal_test(), and the AIC is a little worse: two more parameters that do not pay for themselves. We keep the simple model. If several predictors failed, the alternatives are a model with every slope free (nominal = ~ ., the generalized ordered logit) or the multinomial model.


Four more things to keep in mind


Code
# answers given as categories instead of numbers: one coefficient per answer
fit_steps <- update(fit, . ~ . - autonomy - respect - security - stress +
                      factor(autonomy) + factor(respect) + factor(security) + factor(stress))
steps_test <- anova(fit, fit_steps)
stress_steps <- coef(fit_steps)[paste0("factor(stress)", 2:5)]   # hardly ever ... always, against never

# the people who answered on the web against those interviewed in person or by phone
very_by_mode <- prop.table(table(d$web, d$satisfaction), 1)[, "Very satisfied"]
fit_mode <- update(fit, . ~ . + web)
round(cbind(without_mode = coef(fit), with_mode = coef(fit_mode)[names(coef(fit))]), 2)


                 without_mode with_mode
autonomy                 0.39      0.39
respect                  0.73      0.73
security                 0.38      0.37
stress                  -0.38     -0.37
homeSome days            0.16      0.17
homeMainly              -0.08     -0.06
self_employedYes         0.45      0.44
age10                    0.15      0.15



Equal steps. The four scored questions count each step up the scale the same. Treating the answers as categories instead, with a coefficient for each answer, fits somewhat better, \(\chi^2\)(9) = 21.73, p = .010: the steps are not all equal. For stress, for example, the coefficients of “hardly ever”, “sometimes”, “often” and “always” against “never” are -0.64, -0.83, -1.41, -1.59, not evenly spaced. The scored model is easier to read and tells the same story.
Web or interview. In 2022 most people answered the GSS on the web. 41% of them said “very satisfied”, against 49% of those interviewed in person or by phone, as people often give more positive answers when an interviewer is listening. Adding the mode to the model leaves the other coefficients almost unchanged (above).
The sample, not the population. These are unweighted estimates for the people in the survey. To describe all US workers, use the GSS weights (wtssps) and the design of the survey, for example with svyolr() in the package survey (Lumley, 2010).
Association, not cause. People who like their work may also see their workplace in a better light, and judge it more respectful and more secure. One survey at one point in time cannot tell which comes first.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the outcome and its order, the predictors and how they were scored, the model test, the check of the proportional odds assumption and the odds ratios with their uncertainty. The numbers come from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:


Code
n_model <- nrow(d)
lr      <- model_test$"LR stat."[2]
lr_df   <- model_test$"   Df"[2]
lr_p    <- model_test$"Pr(Chi)"[2]
ci_text <- function(t) paste0("95% CI [", f2(ci[t, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[t, 2]), "]")


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 2,167 employed respondents to the 2022 General Social Survey (Davern et al., 2024) who answered the job satisfaction question and the Quality of Working Life questions used here. Job satisfaction (very dissatisfied, a little dissatisfied, moderately satisfied, very satisfied) was analysed with an ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds model). The predictors were autonomy, respect at work and job security (each scored 1–4) and work stress (scored 1–5), with higher scores meaning more; how often the respondent worked from home (never, some days, mainly); self-employment; and age. The proportional odds assumption was checked with likelihood-ratio tests of nominal effects. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the MASS (Venables & Ripley, 2002) and ordinal (Christensen, 2026) packages.

Results:

The predictors improved the fit over a thresholds-only model, χ²(8) = 566.95, p < .001, McFadden’s R² = .12, and no predictor departed from the proportional odds assumption (smallest p = .166). Holding the other predictors constant, respondents who felt more respected at work were more satisfied with their job, OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.80, 2.39], as were those with more autonomy, OR = 1.48, 95% CI [1.32, 1.67], and better job security, OR = 1.47, 95% CI [1.31, 1.64]. More frequent stress went with lower satisfaction, OR = 0.69, 95% CI [0.62, 0.75]. Self-employed and older respondents were more satisfied (Table 1). How often respondents worked from home was not related to job satisfaction once the other predictors were held constant, χ²(2) = 3.66, p = .161.

Points to remember:

Say which way the outcome runs, and whether an odds ratio above 1 means a higher or a lower answer: programs differ.
Report odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and say that they hold the other predictors constant.
Give the model test (\(\chi^2\) with its degrees of freedom) and a pseudo-\(R^2\), and say which one.
Report the check of the proportional odds assumption, and what you did if it failed.
Predicted probabilities for typical people are easier to understand than odds ratios; show them where they help.
Cite R and the packages; citation("MASS") and citation("ordinal") give the references.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
text:
9. Summary







When
The outcome is a category with three or more values in a natural order


Why not linear regression
It assumes equal steps between the answers and predicts values nobody can give


Why not multinomial logistic regression
It ignores the order and needs a set of coefficients for every answer


How (R)
MASS::polr(y ~ x, data, Hess = TRUE), with y an ordered factor; or ordinal::clm()


Output
Thresholds (one per split) and one slope per predictor; exp() of a slope is a cumulative odds ratio


Easiest to read
Predicted probabilities: predict(fit, newdata, type = "probs")


Tests
Likelihood-ratio tests with anova() and drop1(); McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\)


Assumptions
Independent observations; proportional odds (the same slopes at every split)


If proportional odds fails
A partial proportional odds model, clm(..., nominal = ~ x); or a multinomial model

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
In March 1958 Charles David Keeling started measuring carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the air on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii, far from cities and forests. The record has run every month since. It is the longest direct record of CO₂ in the atmosphere.
The amount of CO₂ has gone up every year. This page asks: is it going up by about the same amount every year, or by more and more? If the yearly rise is constant, the record is a straight line. If the rise itself grows, the record bends upwards: a curve.
Polynomial regression fits curves with an ordinary regression, by adding powers of the predictor:








Degree
Model
Shape




1
\(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)
a straight line


2
\(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2\)
a parabola: one bend, a steady acceleration


3
\(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3\)
up to two bends: the acceleration itself can change


\(k\)
… \(+ \beta_k x^k\)
up to \(k - 1\) bends



The model is a curve in \(x\), but it is linear in the coefficients \(\beta\): each power of \(x\) is just another predictor. So lm() fits it, and everything known about linear regression (standard errors, F tests, \(R^2\)) still applies.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(nlme)   # gls(): regression with autocorrelated errors (comes with R)

# one colour per degree of polynomial, the same in every chart
degree_colours <- c("1" = "#2a78d6", "2" = "#eb6834", "3" = "#1baf7a", "5" = "#eda100")

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
1. The data
The NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory publishes the monthly means as a small CSV file, free and with no login. The first 16 years come from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, where Keeling worked.


Code
raw <- read.csv("https://gml.noaa.gov/webdata/ccgg/trends/co2/co2_mm_mlo.csv",
                comment.char = "#")   # the notes at the top start with #
head(raw, 3)


  year month decimal.date average deseasonalized ndays  sdev   unc
1 1958     3     1958.203  315.71         314.44    -1 -9.99 -0.99
2 1958     4     1958.288  317.45         315.16    -1 -9.99 -0.99
3 1958     5     1958.370  317.51         314.69    -1 -9.99 -0.99


average is the monthly mean in parts per million (ppm): molecules of CO₂ per million molecules of dry air. decimal.date is the middle of the month as a year with decimals (1958.2027 is mid-March 1958). We keep those two, plus the year and month:


Code
co2 <- data.frame(date  = raw$decimal.date, year = raw$year, month = raw$month,
                  ppm   = raw$average)
co2$t <- co2$date - 2000    # years since the start of 2000: negative before, positive after
nrow(co2)


[1] 824


Code
range(co2$ppm)


[1] 312.42 432.34


That is 824 months, from March 1958 to October 2026. NOAA filled the few missing months by interpolation. After the eruption of Mauna Loa in November 2022, the measurements came from Maunakea, 34 km to the north, until July 2023. Why we use years since 2000, t, rather than the year itself, is explained in section 4.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
linear <- lm(ppm ~ t, data = co2)

ggplot(co2, aes(date, ppm)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted(linear)), colour = degree_colours[["1"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 10)) +
  labs(title = "CO₂ at Mauna Loa, monthly means, with a straight line",
       x = NULL, y = "CO₂ (ppm)") +
  theme_bw()









Two things stand out. The record wiggles up and down every year: that is the seasonal cycle, which section 6 deals with. And the straight line does not follow the record: it is too low at both ends and too high in the middle. The residuals of the straight line, the measured values minus the line, make this plain:


Code
ggplot(co2, aes(date, resid(linear))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 10)) +
  labs(title = "What the straight line misses",
       subtitle = "Residuals: measured CO₂ minus the straight line",
       x = NULL, y = "residual (ppm)") +
  theme_bw()









A U shape in the residuals is the classic sign that a straight line is not enough and a quadratic term is needed. The yearly rise tells the same story:


Code
# the mean of each complete year, and the rise from one year to the next
complete <- as.integer(names(which(table(co2$year) == 12)))
annual   <- aggregate(ppm ~ year, data = subset(co2, year %in% complete), FUN = mean)
growth   <- data.frame(year = annual$year[-1], rise = diff(annual$ppm))
head(growth, 3)


  year      rise
1 1960 0.9266667
2 1961 0.7350000
3 1962 0.8100000


Code
tail(growth, 3)


   year     rise
64 2023 2.551667
65 2024 3.524167
66 2025 2.745000


Code
early  <- mean(growth$rise[growth$year <= 1969])
recent <- mean(growth$rise[growth$year >= 2016])


In the 1960s CO₂ rose by 0.86 ppm a year on average; in the last ten years, by 2.63 ppm a year. The rise is speeding up.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the quadratic model
\[\text{ppm}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t_i + \beta_2 t_i^2 + \varepsilon_i\]
where \(t_i\) is the time of month \(i\) in years since the start of 2000. \(t\) and \(t^2\) are two predictors; least squares finds the \(\beta\)’s that make the sum of squared residuals, \(\sum_i \varepsilon_i^2\), as small as possible, exactly as in any linear regression.


Step 2: what the coefficients mean
The slope of a curve changes along it. The slope at time \(t\) is the derivative:
\[\frac{d\,\text{ppm}}{dt} = \beta_1 + 2\beta_2 t\]
So, with \(t\) measured from 2000:

\(\beta_0\) is the level of CO₂ at the start of 2000;
\(\beta_1\) is the yearly rise at the start of 2000;
\(2\beta_2\) is the acceleration: how much the yearly rise grows every year. A positive \(\beta_2\) means the rise speeds up.

\(\beta_2\) is not “the effect of \(t^2\) holding \(t\) constant”: \(t^2\) cannot change while \(t\) stays the same. The terms of a polynomial are read together, through the slope or through the fitted curve.


Step 3: higher degrees
A cubic adds \(\beta_3 t^3\), and the slope becomes \(\beta_1 + 2\beta_2 t + 3\beta_3 t^2\): now the acceleration itself can change over time. Each extra degree lets the curve bend once more. With \(n\) points, a polynomial of degree \(n - 1\) passes through every one of them, and predicts nothing.


Step 4: keep the lower terms
A model with \(t^2\) should also have \(t\), and a model with \(t^3\) should have \(t\) and \(t^2\). Without \(t\), the model \(\beta_0 + \beta_2 t^2\) forces the bottom of the parabola to sit exactly at \(t = 0\), which here is the arbitrary start of 2000. A different choice of zero would give a different model.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
4. Fitting the model


Code
quadratic <- lm(ppm ~ t + I(t^2), data = co2)
summary(quadratic)



Call:
lm(formula = ppm ~ t + I(t^2), data = co2)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-4.842 -1.863  0.132  1.793  4.883 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 3.695e+02  1.122e-01 3293.15   <2e-16 ***
t           1.874e+00  5.165e-03  362.87   <2e-16 ***
I(t^2)      1.351e-02  2.224e-04   60.76   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.244 on 821 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9955,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9955 
F-statistic: 9.17e+04 on 2 and 821 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


I(t^2), not t^2. In an R formula ^ has its own meaning: (a + b)^2 means “a, b and their interaction”. I() tells R to compute the square as arithmetic. poly(t, 2, raw = TRUE) builds the same two columns.


Code
b   <- coef(quadratic)
ci  <- confint(quadratic)
rise_at <- function(year) b[["t"]] + 2 * b[["I(t^2)"]] * (year - 2000)   # the slope, step 2
r2  <- c(linear = summary(linear)$r.squared, quadratic = summary(quadratic)$r.squared)
r2


   linear quadratic 
0.9755062 0.9955435 










Coefficient
Estimate
Meaning




(Intercept)
369.51
CO₂ at the start of 2000, in ppm


t
1.87

I(t^2)
0.0135
half the acceleration: the yearly rise grows by \(2 \times\) 0.0135 = 0.027 ppm per year, every year




By the quadratic, CO₂ rose by 0.79 ppm a year in 1960 and by 2.55 ppm a year in 2025.
The quadratic term is far from zero: t = 60.8, 95% CI [0.0131, 0.0139]. Section 7 shows that this t is too big, though the conclusion stands.
\(R^2\) rises from .976 to .996, and the residual standard deviation falls from 5.26 to 2.24 ppm. \(R^2\) is high even for the straight line, because CO₂ rises so steadily: with trends, compare the residuals rather than \(R^2\).

The yearly rise that each model implies, against the measured rise:


Code
bc <- coef(lm(ppm ~ t + I(t^2) + I(t^3), data = co2))
s  <- growth$year - 2000
implied <- rbind(data.frame(year = growth$year, rise = rise_at(growth$year), model = "Quadratic"),
                 data.frame(year = growth$year, rise = bc[2] + 2 * bc[3] * s + 3 * bc[4] * s^2,
                            model = "Cubic"))
implied$model <- factor(implied$model, levels = c("Quadratic", "Cubic"))

ggplot(growth, aes(year, rise)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey45", size = 1.6) +
  geom_line(data = implied, aes(colour = model), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Quadratic = degree_colours[["2"]], Cubic = degree_colours[["3"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 10)) +
  labs(title = "How much CO₂ rises each year",
       subtitle = "Points: the measured rise from one year's mean to the next. Lines: the slope of each model.",
       x = NULL, y = "rise (ppm per year)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The quadratic says that the yearly rise grows in a straight line; the cubic lets it bend. Both run through the middle of the measured rises. The points scatter around them because the rise varies from year to year: El Niño years, for example, have bigger rises.

Raw years, centred years and orthogonal polynomials
Why years since 2000, and not the year itself? Fit the same quadratic three ways:


Code
raw_year   <- lm(ppm ~ date + I(date^2), data = co2)   # the year itself: 1958.2 ... 2026.8
orthogonal <- lm(ppm ~ poly(date, 2), data = co2)      # orthogonal polynomials
rbind(raw_year = coef(raw_year), centred = coef(quadratic), orthogonal = coef(orthogonal))


           (Intercept)       date    I(date^2)
raw_year    50665.7275 -52.170443   0.01351117
centred       369.5066   1.874223   0.01351117
orthogonal    361.5182 951.146262 136.31748786


Code
# the three give the same fitted curve
c(max(abs(fitted(raw_year) - fitted(quadratic))), max(abs(fitted(orthogonal) - fitted(quadratic))))


[1] 4.033609e-10 2.842171e-13


Code
# but their predictors are very different
c(raw_year = cor(co2$date, co2$date^2), centred = cor(co2$t, co2$t^2))


  raw_year    centred 
 0.9999901 -0.6459394 


Code
c(raw_year = kappa(model.matrix(raw_year)), centred = kappa(model.matrix(quadratic)),
  orthogonal = kappa(model.matrix(orthogonal)))


    raw_year      centred   orthogonal 
4.538131e+10 9.959183e+02 2.823108e+01 



The fitted curve is the same in all three: they are the same model, written differently.
With the year itself, the coefficients are -52.17 and 50,665.73: the slope and level in the year 0, two thousand years before the data. The year and its square correlate at 0.99999, and the condition number of the predictors, a measure of how close they are to being redundant, is about 4.5e+10. Numbers that large make computations unstable, and higher degrees soon fail.
Centring, here subtracting 2000, makes the coefficients mean something (the level and the rise in 2000) and brings the condition number down to 996.
poly(date, 2) builds orthogonal polynomials: columns that are uncorrelated with each other. The computation is as stable as it gets (condition number 28.2), and the test of the last column is the test of the highest degree, but the coefficients are not in ppm per year. Use poly() to choose the degree and centred raw powers to report what the curve means.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
5. Choosing the degree

F tests and information criteria
Fit degrees 1 to 6 and compare each with the one before:


Code
# ppm ~ poly(t, 1, raw = TRUE), ppm ~ poly(t, 2, raw = TRUE), ...: raw powers of t
formulas <- lapply(1:8, function(k) as.formula(paste0("ppm ~ poly(t, ", k, ", raw = TRUE)")))
fits     <- lapply(formulas[1:6], lm, data = co2)
f_tests  <- do.call(anova, fits)
f_tests


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: ppm ~ poly(t, 1, raw = TRUE)
Model 2: ppm ~ poly(t, 2, raw = TRUE)
Model 3: ppm ~ poly(t, 3, raw = TRUE)
Model 4: ppm ~ poly(t, 4, raw = TRUE)
Model 5: ppm ~ poly(t, 5, raw = TRUE)
Model 6: ppm ~ poly(t, 6, raw = TRUE)
  Res.Df     RSS Df Sum of Sq         F    Pr(>F)    
1    822 22715.4                                     
2    821  4132.9  1   18582.5 3921.5677 < 2.2e-16 ***
3    820  4081.0  1      52.0   10.9685 0.0009674 ***
4    819  3960.9  1     120.1   25.3458 5.898e-07 ***
5    818  3885.9  1      74.9   15.8134 7.610e-05 ***
6    817  3871.4  1      14.5    3.0694 0.0801551 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
degrees <- data.frame(degree = 1:6,
                      R2     = sapply(fits, function(f) summary(f)$r.squared),
                      sd     = sapply(fits, sigma),
                      AIC    = sapply(fits, AIC),
                      BIC    = sapply(fits, BIC))
degrees


  degree        R2       sd      AIC      BIC
1      1 0.9755062 5.256833 5077.312 5091.454
2      2 0.9955435 2.243662 3675.169 3694.026
3      3 0.9955995 2.230869 3666.741 3690.312
4      4 0.9957291 2.199138 3644.127 3672.412
5      5 0.9958099 2.179568 3630.389 3663.389
6      6 0.9958255 2.176816 3629.299 3667.013


Every extra degree is “significant” up to degree 5, and AIC keeps falling. But look at the size of the gains: the residual standard deviation goes from 5.26 ppm for the straight line to 2.24 for the quadratic, and then only to 2.18 at degree 6. With 824 months even tiny improvements are significant, and section 7 shows that these p values are too small anyway. The extra degrees bend the curve around wiggles of the past, such as the slower rise of the early 1990s.


Forward validation: does the curve predict the future?
A trend is useful if it predicts years it has not seen. Fit each degree to the record up to 2006, and predict 2007 to 2026:


Code
past   <- subset(co2, date < 2007)
future <- subset(co2, date >= 2007)
forward_fits <- lapply(formulas, lm, data = past)
forward_rmse <- sapply(forward_fits, function(f) sqrt(mean((future$ppm - predict(f, future))^2)))
round(setNames(forward_rmse, paste("degree", 1:8)), 1)


degree 1 degree 2 degree 3 degree 4 degree 5 degree 6 degree 7 degree 8 
    15.0      3.0      8.2     10.0     42.7     10.4    286.6    637.0 


Code
best <- which.min(forward_rmse)




Code
grid <- data.frame(date = seq(1958.2, 2030, by = 0.1))
grid$t <- grid$date - 2000
shown <- c(1, 2, 3, 5)
paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(shown, function(k)
  data.frame(date = grid$date, ppm = predict(forward_fits[[k]], grid), degree = as.character(k))))
paths$degree <- factor(paths$degree, levels = as.character(shown))

ggplot(co2, aes(date, ppm)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2007, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = paths, aes(colour = degree), linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 2006, y = 445, label = "fitted", hjust = 1, size = 3.3, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 2008, y = 445, label = "predicted", hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = degree_colours) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(305, 450)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2030, 10)) +
  labs(title = "Polynomials fitted to 1958–2006, continued to 2030",
       subtitle = "Grey: the measured record. A line that leaves the chart has run off.",
       x = NULL, y = "CO₂ (ppm)", colour = "degree") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The quadratic predicts the next 20 years best, with a root mean squared error of 3.0 ppm. The straight line falls behind (15.0 ppm), and the higher degrees, which fitted the past a little better, predict the future worse: 8.2 ppm for the cubic and 42.7 ppm for degree 5. Beyond the data, a polynomial follows its highest power, and nothing holds it back.
The same problem, with the whole record: what each degree says about the year 2050.


Code
in_2050 <- sapply(fits, function(f) predict(f, data.frame(t = 50)))
round(setNames(in_2050, paste("degree", 1:6)), 1)


degree 1 degree 2 degree 3 degree 4 degree 5 degree 6 
   457.6    497.0    503.1    530.9    465.1    378.1 


Six curves that all fit 1958 to 2026 well disagree about 2050 by 152.9 ppm. A polynomial describes the record; it knows nothing about what drives it. What CO₂ will be in 2050 depends on emissions, not on the shape of a curve.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
6. The seasonal cycle
The residuals of the quadratic, month by month:


Code
co2$trend_residual <- resid(quadratic)
co2$month_name     <- factor(month.abb[co2$month], levels = month.abb)

ggplot(co2, aes(month_name, trend_residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90", colour = "grey30", outlier.size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "The residuals of the quadratic trend, by month",
       x = NULL, y = "residual (ppm)") +
  theme_bw()









Code
cycle <- tapply(co2$trend_residual, co2$month, mean)   # the mean residual of each month, 1 to 12


CO₂ peaks in May and is lowest in October, 6.3 ppm apart on average. In the Northern Hemisphere, which holds most of the world’s land and plants, plants take up CO₂ as they grow in spring and summer, and release it as leaves decay in autumn and winter.
A wave can join the model as more predictors, a sine and a cosine with a period of one year (and two more with a period of six months, for the uneven shape). The model is still linear in its coefficients:


Code
seasonal <- lm(ppm ~ t + I(t^2) + sin(2 * pi * date) + cos(2 * pi * date) +
                 sin(4 * pi * date) + cos(4 * pi * date), data = co2)
c(quadratic = sigma(quadratic), with_seasons = sigma(seasonal))


   quadratic with_seasons 
   2.2436621    0.8153083 


Code
round(coef(seasonal)[1:3], 4)


(Intercept)           t      I(t^2) 
   369.5148      1.8746      0.0135 


The residual standard deviation falls from 2.24 to 0.82 ppm, and the trend coefficients hardly move: the seasonal wave was noise around the trend, not part of it.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

Neighbouring months are not independent
Regression assumes that the residuals are independent. In a time series they rarely are: a month above the trend is usually followed by another month above the trend.


Code
lag1 <- acf(resid(seasonal), plot = FALSE)$acf[2]   # correlation of each residual with the next
lag1


[1] 0.9057675


The correlation of each residual with the next month’s is 0.91. Then lm() acts as if it had far more independent information than it has, and its standard errors are too small. Generalized least squares (gls() from the package nlme) can estimate the same model with autoregressive errors, where each residual depends on the one before:


Code
ar1 <- gls(formula(seasonal), data = co2, correlation = corAR1())
se  <- c(ols = summary(seasonal)$coefficients["I(t^2)", "Std. Error"],
         ar1 = summary(ar1)$tTable["I(t^2)", "Std.Error"])
se


         ols          ar1 
0.0000808181 0.0003658653 


Code
# is the cubic term needed, once the errors are autocorrelated? (ML for a likelihood-ratio test)
ar1_ml    <- update(ar1, method = "ML")
ar1_cubic <- update(ar1_ml, . ~ . + I(t^3))
cubic_test <- anova(ar1_ml, ar1_cubic)
cubic_test


          Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test  L.Ratio p-value
ar1_ml        1  9 596.7898 639.2173 -289.3949                        
ar1_cubic     2 10 593.3422 640.4839 -286.6711 1 vs 2 5.447584  0.0196



The standard error of the quadratic term is 4.5 times larger with autocorrelated errors. The acceleration is still clear, t = 36.9, but every p value from lm() on this page is too small.
The cubic term is weaker than the F test of section 5 suggested: likelihood-ratio \(\chi^2\)(1) = 5.45, p = .020.
The estimates themselves hardly change: autocorrelation affects the uncertainty more than the curve.



Other ways to draw a curve

Splines join several low-degree polynomials at chosen points, so the curve can bend where the data bend without swinging wildly at the ends. They are usually the better choice when the aim is a flexible curve rather than a few interpretable coefficients (Harrell, 2015).
A curve with a mechanism. CO₂ was about 280 ppm before industry. A rise of the excess above 280 ppm by a constant percentage each year is an exponential curve, fitted with nonlinear least squares (nls()). Its parameters mean something physical; a polynomial’s do not.
A polynomial has no memory of its purpose. It fits the range of the data, and only that range.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the variables and their units, how time was coded, how the degree was chosen, the coefficients with their uncertainty, and what was done about autocorrelation. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
quad_vs_linear <- anova(linear, quadratic)
delta_r2 <- r2[["quadratic"]] - r2[["linear"]]
ci_ar1   <- intervals(ar1, which = "coef")$coef        # 95% CIs with AR(1) errors
b_ar1    <- coef(ar1)

degree_table <- data.frame(
  Degree         = 1:6,
  `R²`           = nz(degrees$R2, 4),
  `Residual SD`  = f2(degrees$sd),
  `F test p`     = c("—", sapply(f_tests$"Pr(>F)"[-1], function(p) sub("= ", "", pval(p)))),
  AIC            = f1(degrees$AIC),
  `Forecast RMSE` = f1(forward_rmse[1:6]),
  check.names = FALSE)


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the monthly mean CO₂ concentrations measured at Mauna Loa Observatory from March 1958 to October 2026 (N = 824 months; Lan & Keeling, 2026) with polynomial regressions of concentration (ppm) on time, in years since 1 January 2000. Polynomials of degree 1 to 6 were compared with F tests and with forward validation: each was fitted to 1958–2006 and its predictions for 2007–2026 were compared with the measurements. The final model added sine and cosine terms with periods of 12 and 6 months for the seasonal cycle, and was estimated by generalized least squares with first-order autoregressive errors (Pinheiro & Bates, 2000). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

A quadratic trend fitted the record better than a linear trend, ΔR² = .020, F(1, 821) = 3,691.4, p < .001, and predicted 2007–2026 more accurately than polynomials of degree 1 and 3 to 6 (Table 1). In the final model, CO₂ was 369.52 ppm at the start of 2000, 95% CI [369.14, 369.90], and rose by 1.88 ppm per year at that point, 95% CI [1.86, 1.89]. The yearly rise increased by 0.027 ppm per year each year, 95% CI [0.026, 0.028], from about 0.8 ppm per year in 1960 to 2.5 ppm per year in 2025. With autocorrelated errors, adding a cubic term gave a smaller improvement than under independent errors, χ²(1) = 5.45, p = .020, and the cubic predicted 2007–2026 less accurately than the quadratic (RMSE 8.2 against 3.0 ppm), so we kept the quadratic.

Points to remember:

Say how the predictor was coded (here, centred at 2000), because the lower coefficients depend on it.
Read the terms of a polynomial together: report the slope at chosen values (here, the yearly rise in 1960 and 2025), or show the curve.
Choose the degree by more than p values: by the size of the improvement, by validation on data the model has not seen, and by what makes sense.
Do not extrapolate a polynomial beyond the data.
With a time series, check the residuals for autocorrelation, and say how you handled it.

title: Polynomial Regression: Is the Rise of CO₂ Speeding Up?
text:
9. Summary







When
The outcome follows a curve in a continuous predictor, with one or two bends


The model
\(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \dots\): a curve in \(x\), linear in the \(\beta\)’s


How (R)
lm(y ~ x + I(x^2)), or lm(y ~ poly(x, 2)) for orthogonal polynomials


Coding
Centre \(x\) (subtract a meaningful value) before taking powers


Reading it
The slope at \(x\) is \(\beta_1 + 2\beta_2 x\); read the terms together, never \(\beta_2\) alone


Choosing the degree
Nested F tests, AIC or BIC, and above all validation on new data; usually 2 or 3 is enough


Dangers
Wild behaviour at the ends and beyond the data; high degrees fit noise


Alternatives
Splines and GAMs for flexible curves; nonlinear models when a mechanism is known

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
A detached house costs more than a terraced house, and a home in London costs more than one elsewhere. Everybody knows that. The question for this page is: by how much, and is it the same amount for cheap homes and for expensive ones?
An ordinary regression (OLS) answers with one number per predictor: the difference in the mean price. But house prices are strongly skewed: most homes sell for a modest sum and a few sell for millions. A predictor can move the cheap end of the market by a little, the middle by more, and the expensive end by far more. The mean blends all of that into one figure that describes nobody in particular.
Quantile regression (Koenker & Bassett, 1978) fits a separate line for any quantile of the outcome: the 10th percentile (the cheapest tenth of homes), the median, the 90th percentile, and so on. The model is a family of regressions, one for each quantile \(\tau\) (the Greek letter tau):








Quantile \(\tau\)
What the line describes
In this example




0.1
the lower tail
the price below which 10% of comparable homes sell


0.5
the median
the middle price


0.9
the upper tail
the price below which 90% of comparable homes sell



Where a predictor’s coefficient is the same at every \(\tau\), it only shifts the distribution. Where it changes with \(\tau\), the predictor changes the shape of the distribution: its spread, its skew.


Code
library(quantreg)   # rq(): quantile regression
library(ggplot2)

# the site's colours, in order
blue <- "#2a78d6"; orange <- "#eb6834"; green <- "#1baf7a"; yellow <- "#eda100"; pink <- "#e87ba4"

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
k    <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "£", f0(abs(x)), "k")   # a price in thousands of pounds, for the text

text:
1. The data
HM Land Registry, the government register of property ownership in England and Wales, publishes the Price Paid Data: one row for every residential sale registered since 1995, free, with no login, under the Open Government Licence v3.0. The yearly files are large (about 170 MB each), so this page uses the small monthly update file, the sales registered with the Land Registry in the latest month.


Code
url  <- "https://price-paid-data.publicdata.landregistry.gov.uk/pp-monthly-update-new-version.csv"
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
download_time <- system.time(download.file(url, file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE))[["elapsed"]]
file_mb <- file.size(file) / 1e6


The download is 17.1 MB and took 0.2 seconds. The file has no header row. The columns are documented on the Land Registry’s about the Price Paid Data page, and we read only the ones we need:







Column
Meaning (from the documentation)




2
Price: the sale price stated on the transfer deed, in pounds


3
Date of transfer: when the sale was completed, as stated on the deed


5
Property type: D detached, S semi-detached, T terraced (including end-of-terrace), F flat or maisonette, O other. Bungalows are not separate


6
Old/new: Y a newly built property, N an established one


14
County


15
PPD category: A a standard sale of a single residential property; B additional transactions, such as repossessions, buy-to-lets identified by a mortgage and transfers to non-private individuals


16
Record status (monthly file only): A added, C changed, D deleted





Code
columns <- rep("NULL", 16)                      # "NULL" skips a column
columns[c(2, 3, 5, 6, 14, 15, 16)] <- "character"
raw <- read.csv(file, header = FALSE, colClasses = columns)
names(raw) <- c("price", "date", "type", "new", "county", "category", "status")
nrow(raw)


[1] 98103


Code
table(raw$status)



    A     C     D 
93495  3056  1552 


The file holds 98,103 rows. We keep what the question needs:


Code
raw$date <- as.Date(substr(raw$date, 1, 10))
homes <- subset(raw, status == "A" &                          # added records, not changes or deletions
                  category == "A" &                           # standard sales of a single home
                  type %in% c("T", "F", "S", "D") &           # the four named types of home
                  date > max(date) - 365)                     # sales completed in the last 12 months

homes$k      <- as.numeric(homes$price) / 1000                # price in £ thousand
homes$type   <- factor(homes$type, levels = c("T", "F", "S", "D"),
                       labels = c("Terraced", "Flat", "Semi-detached", "Detached"))
homes$new    <- factor(homes$new, levels = c("N", "Y"), labels = c("Established", "New build"))
homes$london <- factor(ifelse(homes$county == "GREATER LONDON", "London", "Elsewhere"),
                       levels = c("Elsewhere", "London"))
n <- nrow(homes)


That leaves 73,902 sales completed between 01 October 2025 and 30 September 2026 (61% of them in the last two months, because sales are registered some weeks after completion). The three predictors:

type: the type of home, with terraced as the reference, because it is the most common type;
new: newly built or established;
london: in Greater London, or elsewhere in England and Wales.
the outcome k is the price in thousands of pounds, so a coefficient of 50 means £50,000.



Code
table(homes$type, homes$london)


               
                Elsewhere London
  Terraced          17611   2258
  Flat               7637   3926
  Semi-detached     21311   1283
  Detached          19492    384


What these data cannot say. The Price Paid Data has no floor area, number of bedrooms, condition or street-level location. A detached house in the data is bigger than a terraced one, and the coefficient on type includes that. Nor does one monthly file cover all sales in England and Wales in a year: it holds the ones registered in one month, which is a large and mixed set, but not a random sample of the year. This page is a worked example of a method, not a house price index.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
mean_k   <- mean(homes$k)
median_k <- median(homes$k)

ggplot(homes, aes(k)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, boundary = 0, fill = "grey80", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median_k, colour = "Median", linetype = "Median"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_k, colour = "Mean", linetype = "Mean"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Median = blue, Mean = orange)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Median = "solid", Mean = "dashed")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1500)) +
  labs(title = "Sale prices of homes, England and Wales",
       subtitle = "The chart stops at £1.5 million",
       x = "price (£ thousand)", y = "sales", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
qs <- quantile(homes$k, c(.1, .5, .9, .99))
over <- mean(homes$k > 1500)


Prices pile up on the left and trail off to the right. The median is £300k, the mean £376k: a few very expensive sales pull the mean up. The cheapest tenth of homes sold for up to £145k, and the dearest tenth for £653k or more. The chart cuts off 1.1% of the sales, those above £1.5 million; the dearest sale in the data is £25,400k.
The skew matters because the London gap is not one number. The same quantiles in the two areas:


Code
taus <- seq(.05, .95, by = .05)
by_area <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(homes$london), function(a)
  data.frame(area = a, tau = taus, price = quantile(homes$k[homes$london == a], taus, names = FALSE))))
by_area$area <- factor(by_area$area, levels = c("Elsewhere", "London"))

ggplot(by_area, aes(tau, price, colour = area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Elsewhere = blue, London = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  labs(title = "Sale price quantiles, London and elsewhere",
       x = expression("quantile " * tau), y = "price (£ thousand)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
q_area <- tapply(homes$k, homes$london, quantile, probs = c(.1, .5, .9))


At the 10th percentile, a London home sells for £295k against £140k elsewhere, a difference of £155k. At the median the difference is £246k, and at the 90th percentile £670k. The London premium grows steadily from the bottom of the market to the top. An OLS coefficient would report one number, somewhere in the middle of those, and say nothing about this.
These are the raw differences. Quantile regression does the same thing while holding the type of home, and whether it is new, fixed.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: one line per quantile
For a quantile \(\tau\) between 0 and 1, the model says that the \(\tau\)-th quantile of the price, given the predictors \(x_i\), is a linear function of them:
\[Q_\tau(y_i \mid x_i) = \beta_0(\tau) + \beta_1(\tau)\,x_{i1} + \dots + \beta_p(\tau)\,x_{ip}\]
The coefficients carry \((\tau)\) because each quantile has its own. The conditional quantile \(Q_\tau(y_i \mid x_i)\) is the price below which a fraction \(\tau\) of the homes with these characteristics sell. OLS models the conditional mean, \(E(y_i \mid x_i)\), in the same way, with one set of coefficients.


Step 2: the check (pinball) loss
OLS finds the coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals. Quantile regression minimises a different sum, with the check loss (also called the pinball loss because of its shape). For a residual \(u = y - \hat y\):
\[\rho_\tau(u) = u\,\bigl(\tau - I(u < 0)\bigr) = \begin{cases} \tau\,u & \text{if } u \ge 0 \text{ (the price is above the line)}\\ (\tau - 1)\,u = (1-\tau)\,|u| & \text{if } u < 0 \text{ (the price is below the line)}\end{cases}\]
where \(I(u < 0)\) is 1 when the residual is negative and 0 otherwise. The coefficients are
\[\hat\beta(\tau) = \arg\min_{\beta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \rho_\tau\bigl(y_i - x_i^\top \beta\bigr)\]
The loss is a pair of straight lines: a point above the fitted line costs \(\tau\) per unit of distance, a point below it costs \(1-\tau\). Three cases:

\(\tau = 0.5\): both sides cost 0.5, so the loss is half the absolute residual, \(\tfrac12|u|\). This is median regression, or least absolute deviations (LAD): the line that minimises the sum of the absolute residuals.
\(\tau = 0.9\): a point above the line costs 0.9, a point below costs only 0.1. The line is pushed up until 90% of the points are below it.
\(\tau = 0.1\): the reverse: the line is pushed down until 10% of the points are below it.



Step 3: why minimising it gives the quantile
Start with no predictors, only a single number \(c\) as the fit. The expected loss is
\[E\,\rho_\tau(y - c) = (\tau - 1)\int_{-\infty}^{c} (y - c)\,dF(y) + \tau \int_{c}^{\infty} (y - c)\,dF(y)\]
where \(F\) is the distribution function of \(y\). Differentiating with respect to \(c\) gives
\[\frac{d}{dc}\,E\,\rho_\tau(y - c) = (1 - \tau)\,F(c) - \tau\,\bigl(1 - F(c)\bigr) = F(c) - \tau\]
which is zero when \(F(c) = \tau\): the value \(c\) below which a fraction \(\tau\) of the data lies, which is the \(\tau\)-th quantile. In the same way, squared loss gives the mean, and absolute loss gives the median. A small numeric check with 11 real sales, drawn at random from the data:


Code
rho <- function(u, tau) u * (tau - (u < 0))     # the check loss

set.seed(2026)
few    <- sort(sample(homes$k, 11))
cand   <- seq(0, max(few) * 1.05, length.out = 1500)
tau_set <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)

loss <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tau_set, function(t)
  data.frame(tau = t, c = cand, loss = sapply(cand, function(cc) mean(rho(few - cc, t))))))
best <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tau_set, function(t)
  data.frame(tau = t, c = loss$c[loss$tau == t][which.min(loss$loss[loss$tau == t])],
             loss = min(loss$loss[loss$tau == t]))))
best$quantile <- sapply(tau_set, function(t) quantile(few, t, type = 1, names = FALSE))
best


  tau        c      loss quantile
1 0.1 206.4977  9.904112    206.5
2 0.5 240.0150 38.089319    240.0
3 0.9 390.2652 23.584683    390.0




Code
loss$panel <- factor(paste("τ =", loss$tau), levels = paste("τ =", tau_set))
best$panel <- factor(paste("τ =", best$tau), levels = paste("τ =", tau_set))
pts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tau_set, function(t)
  data.frame(panel = paste("τ =", t), x = few)))
pts$panel <- factor(pts$panel, levels = paste("τ =", tau_set))

ggplot(loss, aes(c, loss)) +
  geom_line(colour = blue, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = best, colour = orange, size = 3) +
  geom_rug(data = pts, aes(x = x, y = NULL), colour = "grey35", sides = "b") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Average check loss for a single fitted value c",
       subtitle = "Orange: the lowest point. Grey ticks: the 11 sale prices.",
       x = "c, the fitted price (£ thousand)", y = "average check loss") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.08))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "lines"))









The loss curve is made of straight pieces that bend at the data points, and its lowest point (orange) sits on a data value: £206k for \(\tau\) = 0.1, £240k for the median and £390k for \(\tau\) = 0.9. Those are the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of the 11 prices (£206k, £240k and £390k). The same check on all 73,902 sales, by trying every candidate price on a fine grid:


Code
grid <- seq(0, 1500, by = 0.5)
by_search <- sapply(tau_set, function(t) grid[which.min(sapply(grid, function(cc) mean(rho(homes$k - cc, t))))])
rbind(`minimising the loss` = by_search,
      `quantile()` = quantile(homes$k, tau_set, type = 1, names = FALSE))


                    [,1] [,2] [,3]
minimising the loss  145  300  653
quantile()           145  300  653




Step 4: how the line is found
The check loss has a corner at zero, so there is no formula like the normal equations of OLS. rq() solves the problem as a linear programme (the Barrodale and Roberts simplex algorithm, method = "br", the default), which is fast for samples up to a few thousand rows; for very large data method = "fn" (an interior point method) is quicker. When the minimum is a flat stretch rather than a single point, as happens when many prices are the same round number, R warns “Solution may be nonunique”. The warning is harmless here: any value on the flat stretch fits equally well.


Step 5: what the coefficients mean
\(\beta_j(\tau)\) is the change in the \(\tau\)-th conditional quantile of the price when \(x_j\) goes up by one unit, with the other predictors fixed. With a categorical predictor, it is the difference between the \(\tau\)-th quantiles of the two groups, adjusting for the other predictors. Section 7 spells out what this does and does not mean.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 4. Fitting the model and reading the output
text:
4. Fitting the model and reading the output
The model is k ~ type + new + london. rq() takes a formula, the data and the quantile or quantiles in tau:


Code
f <- k ~ type + new + london

fit_ols <- lm(f, data = homes)
fit10   <- rq(f, tau = 0.1, data = homes)
fit50   <- rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = homes)
fit90   <- rq(f, tau = 0.9, data = homes)
summary(fit50, se = "nid")



Call: rq(formula = f, tau = 0.5, data = homes)

tau: [1] 0.5

Coefficients:
                  Value     Std. Error t value   Pr(>|t|) 
(Intercept)       229.50000   1.21415  189.02077   0.00000
typeFlat          -59.50000   1.91511  -31.06868   0.00000
typeSemi-detached  40.49900   1.58774   25.50729   0.00000
typeDetached      190.50000   1.95280   97.55209   0.00000
newNew build       29.20400   2.23098   13.09024   0.00000
londonLondon      310.50000   3.80080   81.69333   0.00000


The output looks like lm(): Value is the coefficient, then its standard error, t and p. The intercept is the median price of the reference home: an established terraced house elsewhere in England and Wales (the £230k, which is also the median of that group). The other lines are the differences from it:


Code
coefs <- cbind(`τ = 0.1` = coef(fit10), `τ = 0.5` = coef(fit50), `τ = 0.9` = coef(fit90), OLS = coef(fit_ols))
round(coefs, 1)


                  τ = 0.1 τ = 0.5 τ = 0.9    OLS
(Intercept)           120   229.5   415.0  260.9
typeFlat              -42   -59.5   -89.6 -101.7
typeSemi-detached      40    40.5    65.0   45.1
typeDetached          130   190.5   410.0  247.1
newNew build           50    29.2    -1.8    8.5
londonLondon          205   310.5   799.6  475.9


Code
b10 <- coef(fit10); b50 <- coef(fit50); b90 <- coef(fit90); bo <- coef(fit_ols)






\(\tau\) = 0.1
Median
\(\tau\) = 0.9
OLS (mean)




Detached (against terraced)

London (against elsewhere)
£205k

£50k
