London. The London difference is £205k in the cheap end of the market, £310k at the median and £800k in the expensive end: about 3.9 times bigger at the top than at the bottom. OLS reports £476k, a number that is not the London difference for any group of homes: it is above the median difference because the mean follows the long right tail.
Detached. A detached house costs £130k more than a terraced one at \(\tau\) = 0.1, £190k more at the median and £410k more at \(\tau\) = 0.9.
New build. This is where the mean misleads the most. The new-build difference is £50k in the cheap end, £29k at the median, and -£2k at \(\tau\) = 0.9: new homes sell for more than established ones at the bottom of the market, and for a little less at the top. OLS says £8k, which hides the sign change. The data cannot say why: they have no information on size or exact location, which may differ between new and established homes.
Flat. Flats are cheaper than terraced houses, by £42k at \(\tau\) = 0.1 and £90k at \(\tau\) = 0.9.

All the models here have categorical predictors only. The fitted lines are then the quantiles of price within each combination of type, new and London, tied together by the model’s additive form (no interactions). With a continuous predictor, such as floor area, each \(\tau\) would give a slope instead of a gap: the reading is the same.

Three ways to calculate the standard errors
summary.rq() offers several methods for the standard errors, set with se =:








se =
The idea
When it fits




"iid"
Assumes the errors have the same distribution for every observation: one common density at the quantile
Only if the spread of the outcome is the same for all values of the predictors. Not here


"nid"
A sandwich estimator (Hendricks & Koenker, 1992) that allows the density at the quantile to differ from one observation to the next. The default for samples above 1,000
The usual choice with heteroscedastic data


"ker"
A sandwich estimator that estimates the density with a kernel (Powell, 1991)
An alternative to "nid"


"boot"
Bootstrap: resample the rows with replacement (the default bsmethod = "xy" resamples (x, y) pairs), refit, and take the standard deviation of the estimates
Needs no density at all, but slow: each bootstrap sample is a new fit



The standard error of a quantile depends on how thinly the data are spread around that quantile, since a coefficient is more uncertain where observations are sparse. The sandwich methods estimate this density, and "iid" takes it to be the same everywhere, which is wrong when the spread of price differs between London and elsewhere. A comparison on a random subsample of 5,000 sales (a bootstrap of the full 73,902 sales would be much slower), at \(\tau\) = 0.9:


Code
set.seed(2026)
sub   <- homes[sample(n, 5000), ]
fit_s <- rq(f, tau = 0.9, data = sub)
se_methods <- sapply(c("iid", "nid", "ker", "boot"), function(m) {
  s <- if (m == "boot") summary(fit_s, se = m, R = 200) else summary(fit_s, se = m)
  s$coefficients[, "Std. Error"]
})
round(se_methods, 1)


                   iid  nid  ker boot
(Intercept)       15.5  8.8  9.5  9.5
typeFlat          25.9 19.0 15.5 18.3
typeSemi-detached 21.1 16.8 17.2 16.3
typeDetached      22.3 21.6 21.6 24.6
newNew build      34.0 36.3 23.0 33.9
londonLondon      27.3 77.5 70.0 80.9


For the London coefficient the standard error is 27.3 with "iid" and 77.5 with "nid", 70.0 with "ker" and 80.9 with the bootstrap. "iid" is 2.8 times too small: London prices are much more spread out than prices elsewhere, which the "iid" method does not allow. The three methods that allow unequal spread are in the same range for London, but they do not agree exactly: for the new-build coefficient the standard errors run from 23.0 to 36.3. The bootstrap makes the fewest assumptions. A quick rule: use "nid" for large samples (it is the default) and "boot" for the final results of a smaller study, with a larger R (1,000 or more).
The rest of the page uses "nid" on the full data.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 5. The classic chart: coefficients across the quantiles
text:
5. The classic chart: coefficients across the quantiles
Three quantiles tell the story in a table. The whole story is a chart: fit the model at 19 quantiles from \(\tau\) = 0.05 to 0.95, and draw each coefficient against \(\tau\), with its 95% confidence band. The OLS estimate, with its interval, is a single horizontal line: if the quantile coefficients stay near the OLS line, the mean tells the story; if they drift away from it, it does not.


Code
fits_path <- rq(f, tau = taus, data = homes)
sums_path <- summary(fits_path, se = "nid")

names_short <- c(typeFlat = "Flat (vs terraced)", `typeSemi-detached` = "Semi-detached (vs terraced)",
                 typeDetached = "Detached (vs terraced)", `newNew build` = "New build (vs established)",
                 londonLondon = "London (vs elsewhere)")
terms <- names(names_short)

path <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(taus), function(i) {
  cm <- sums_path[[i]]$coefficients[terms, , drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(tau = taus[i], term = terms, est = cm[, "Value"],
             lo = cm[, "Value"] - qnorm(.975) * cm[, "Std. Error"],
             hi = cm[, "Value"] + qnorm(.975) * cm[, "Std. Error"])
}))
path$term <- factor(names_short[path$term], levels = names_short)

ols_ci  <- confint(fit_ols)
ols_ref <- data.frame(term = factor(names_short, levels = names_short),
                      est = coef(fit_ols)[terms], lo = ols_ci[terms, 1], hi = ols_ci[terms, 2])

ggplot(path, aes(tau)) +
  geom_rect(data = ols_ref, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "OLS (mean)"),
            alpha = 0.18, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(data = ols_ref, aes(yintercept = est, colour = "OLS (mean)"), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "Quantile regression"), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = est, colour = "Quantile regression"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = est, colour = "Quantile regression"), size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ term, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Quantile regression` = blue, `OLS (mean)` = orange)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Quantile regression` = blue, `OLS (mean)` = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)) +
  labs(title = "How each coefficient changes along the price distribution",
       subtitle = "Bands: 95% confidence intervals (standard errors by nid)",
       x = expression("quantile " * tau), y = "difference in price (£ thousand)",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









(The base R version is plot(summary(rq(f, tau = taus, data = homes))), which draws the same panels, with the OLS line in red.) Reading the panels:


Code
p <- function(term, t) path$est[path$term == names_short[[term]] & abs(path$tau - t) < 1e-9]
inside <- tapply(seq_len(nrow(path)), path$term, function(i) {
  o <- ols_ref[ols_ref$term == path$term[i[1]], ]
  mean(path$est[i] >= o$lo & path$est[i] <= o$hi)
})



London and Detached: the coefficient climbs steadily with \(\tau\), from £170k and £121k at \(\tau\) = 0.05 to £1,105k and £545k at \(\tau\) = 0.95. The OLS line cuts across the middle and describes none of the ends.
New build: the coefficient falls from £55k at \(\tau\) = 0.05 to -£10k at \(\tau\) = 0.95, and first drops below zero at \(\tau\) = .90. OLS is a small positive number, £8k, for all.
Flat: the gap against terraced homes widens from £32k to £90k. The OLS gap, £102k, is bigger than the quantile gap at 19 of the 19 quantiles: here the mean gap is larger than the gap at the quantiles, because the few very dear sales pull the mean.
Semi-detached: changes least. It is £40k at \(\tau\) = 0.05 and £40k at the median, and rises only in the top tail, to £95k at \(\tau\) = 0.95. For most of the market, OLS (£45k) is not misleading for this predictor.

The confidence bands widen at the extremes: there are fewer observations near the 5th and 95th percentiles to pin the line down. Remember that the bands are for each \(\tau\) separately; they are not a simultaneous band for the whole curve.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 6. Do the slopes differ across quantiles?
text:
6. Do the slopes differ across quantiles?
The chart suggests that they do. anova() on rq fits at several quantiles tests it (Koenker & Bassett, 1982): the null hypothesis is that the coefficients of the predictors are the same at every \(\tau\) in the set, which is the pure location-shift model in which the predictors move the whole distribution up or down by the same amount and leave its shape alone.


Code
test_joint <- anova(fit10, fit50, fit90)
test_joint


Quantile Regression Analysis of Deviance Table

Model: k ~ type + new + london
Joint Test of Equality of Slopes: tau in {  0.1 0.5 0.9  }

  Df Resid Df F value    Pr(>F)    
1 10   221696   419.3 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
test_terms <- anova(fit10, fit50, fit90, joint = FALSE)
test_terms


Quantile Regression Analysis of Deviance Table

Model: k ~ type + new + london
Tests of Equality of Distinct Slopes: tau in {  0.1 0.5 0.9  }

                  Df Resid Df  F value    Pr(>F)    
typeFlat           2   221704   77.187 < 2.2e-16 ***
typeSemi-detached  2   221704   25.654 7.239e-12 ***
typeDetached       2   221704 1160.060 < 2.2e-16 ***
newNew build       2   221704   41.665 < 2.2e-16 ***
londonLondon       2   221704  658.493 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The first test is a joint test of all five predictors at the three quantiles (10 restrictions: each predictor’s coefficient at \(\tau\) = 0.1 and at 0.9 equal to the median’s): F(10, 221,696) = 419.3, p < .001. The slopes are not the same at the three quantiles. The second test takes one predictor at a time: all five are significant, with the largest statistics for Detached (vs terraced) (1,160.1) and London (vs elsewhere) (658.5), and the smallest for Semi-detached (vs terraced) (25.7).
Two cautions. With 73,902 sales, even a small difference is “significant”, so the size of the differences (the chart) matters more than the p value. And the test compares only the quantiles you give it: a set of \(\tau\) values such as 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 can miss differences elsewhere.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
7. Interpretation: a conditional quantile effect
A coefficient at \(\tau\) = 0.9 is easy to misread. It is not “the effect of being in London on the people at the top of the market”. Two ideas separate:

A conditional quantile is a quantile of price among homes that share the same values of the predictors. \(\beta_{\text{London}}(0.9)\) is the gap between the 90th percentile of London homes and the 90th percentile of the other homes of the same type and age. A 90th-percentile London flat is not the same home as a 90th-percentile detached house elsewhere: “the top” is defined within each group of comparable homes.
An unconditional quantile is a quantile of the whole market: the dearest 10% of all sales in the country, whatever their type or location. A coefficient at \(\tau\) = 0.9 does not say what would happen to the dearest 10% of the whole market if the predictor changed. That is a different question, with a different method (Firpo et al., 2009).

In plain words: the median regression tells you how the typical London home compares with the typical home elsewhere, and the 90th percentile regression tells you how an expensive London home compares with an expensive home elsewhere. Nothing is said about individual homes: a person who buys at the 90th percentile of a cheap area does not move to the 90th percentile of London by moving there.
The numbers are also differences between groups, not changes in a home: the Price Paid Data holds one sale per home, so the coefficients describe how the groups differ, not what would happen to a given house if it were in London.
A chart of the model’s predictions for six typical homes, all established, makes the point concrete: the middle 80% of the predicted prices (from \(\tau\) = 0.1 to 0.9) with the median and, for contrast, the OLS mean.


Code
cases <- expand.grid(type = c("Terraced", "Flat", "Detached"), london = c("Elsewhere", "London"),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cases$new    <- "Established"
cases$type   <- factor(cases$type, levels = levels(homes$type))
cases$new    <- factor(cases$new, levels = levels(homes$new))
cases$london <- factor(cases$london, levels = levels(homes$london))
cases$label  <- paste0(cases$type, ", ", ifelse(cases$london == "London", "London", "elsewhere"))
cases <- cases[order(cases$london, match(cases$type, c("Flat", "Terraced", "Detached"))), ]

pred <- data.frame(label = cases$label,
                   q10 = predict(fit10, cases), q50 = predict(fit50, cases), q90 = predict(fit90, cases),
                   mean = predict(fit_ols, cases))
pred$label <- factor(pred$label, levels = rev(pred$label))
round(pred[, -1], 0)


  q10 q50  q90 mean
2  78 170  325  159

Code
ggplot(pred, aes(y = label)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = q10, xmax = q90), colour = "grey55", linewidth = 2.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = q50, colour = "Median"), size = 3.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean, colour = "Mean (OLS)"), size = 3.2, shape = 18) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Median = blue, `Mean (OLS)` = orange)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted prices of six typical homes",
       subtitle = "Grey bar: the 10th to the 90th percentile of the quantile regression",
       x = "price (£ thousand)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The grey bars say what OLS cannot: the range of prices to expect. A detached home in London has a predicted median of £730k, and the middle 80% of its predicted prices runs from £455k to £1,625k; a flat elsewhere is far tighter, from £78k to £325k. The OLS mean for the detached home in London, £984k, is above the median: the mean is pulled up by the right tail.
How well do the fitted lines do their job? By definition, a fraction \(\tau\) of the sales should lie below the line at \(\tau\). The check:


Code
below <- sapply(list(fit10, fit50, fit90), function(m) mean(homes$k < fitted(m)))
setNames(round(below, 3), c("τ = 0.1", "τ = 0.5", "τ = 0.9"))


τ = 0.1 τ = 0.5 τ = 0.9 
  0.097   0.499   0.899 


The shares below the lines are 9.7%, 49.9% and 89.9%, close to 10%, 50% and 90% (not exactly so because many prices are round numbers, such as £250,000, and tie with the fitted values).

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
8. Practical points

Quantile crossing
The quantile of 0.9 must never be below the quantile of 0.8, but separate fits do not know that. With a continuous predictor, the fitted lines can cross, usually at extreme values of the predictor, and then give an impossible prediction: a 90th percentile lower than the 80th. Crossing signals that the linear model is wrong for that part of the data, or that the extrapolation goes too far.


Code
fit_ends <- rq(f, tau = c(0.01, 0.99), data = homes)
all_taus <- c(0.01, taus, 0.99)
B <- cbind(coef(fit_ends)[, 1], coef(fits_path), coef(fit_ends)[, 2])
all_cells <- expand.grid(type = levels(homes$type), new = levels(homes$new), london = levels(homes$london))
pred_all  <- model.matrix(~ type + new + london, all_cells) %*% B      # one row per kind of home, one column per tau
crossings <- sum(apply(pred_all, 1, function(x) any(diff(x) < 0)))


I checked all 16 combinations of type, new and London at 21 quantiles from 0.01 to 0.99: 0 of them have crossing quantiles. Crossing here is unlikely, because the predictors are categorical and every combination has many sales. If it does happen, the usual remedies are to fit a simpler model, to restrict predictions to the range of the data, or to rearrange: sort the predicted quantiles of each case into increasing order, which can only improve the estimates (Chernozhukov et al., 2010). In R, sort() on the row of predictions does it.


A log outcome, and back-transformation
Prices are often analysed on the log scale: then the coefficients are percentages and the skew is much smaller. For quantiles the log scale has a special property. Quantiles commute with monotone transformations; means do not:
\[Q_\tau\bigl(\log y\bigr) = \log Q_\tau(y) \qquad\text{but}\qquad E\bigl(\log y\bigr) \ne \log E(y)\]
The median of the logs is the log of the median. The mean of the logs is the log of the geometric mean, which is smaller than the mean. So a quantile regression of \(\log y\) can be back-transformed with exp() and gives a quantile of the price itself, whereas back-transforming an OLS of \(\log y\) gives the geometric mean (or, with a “smearing” correction, an estimate of the mean that depends on the distribution of the errors).


Code
c(`log of the median` = log(median(homes$k)), `median of the logs` = median(log(homes$k)),
  `log of the mean` = log(mean(homes$k)), `mean of the logs` = mean(log(homes$k)))


 log of the median median of the logs    log of the mean   mean of the logs 
          5.703782           5.703782           5.930437           5.720243 


Code
f_log   <- log(k) ~ type + new + london
log_fit <- rq(f_log, tau = taus, data = homes)
log_ols <- lm(f_log, data = homes)

# the median regression on the log scale, back-transformed, against the median regression on the price
log50   <- rq(f_log, tau = 0.5, data = homes)
back    <- exp(predict(log50, cases))
rbind(`median regression of price` = pred$q50[match(cases$label, pred$label)],
      `median regression of log price, exp()` = back) |> round(0) |> `colnames<-`(cases$label)


                                      Flat, elsewhere Terraced, elsewhere Detached, elsewhere Flat, London Terraced, London Detached, London
median regression of price                        170                 230                 420          480              540              730
median regression of log price, exp()             179                 227                 415          437              555             1014


The two models estimate the same quantile, but one is additive in pounds and the other additive in logs, so they only agree where an additive model is a good description: for a terraced home elsewhere they give £230k and £179k, but for a detached home in London £730k and £1,014k. Back-transforming a quantile is exact for one variable; it is no reason to expect two different models to agree. exp(coef) on the log scale is a ratio: a London home has a median price 2.44 times that elsewhere, that is 144% more. The question changes with the scale: on the pound scale the London premium grows from the bottom to the top of the market; as a percentage it does not, as the chart shows:


Code
lb <- coef(log_fit)[terms, , drop = FALSE]
log_path <- data.frame(tau = rep(taus, each = length(terms)),
                       term = factor(rep(names_short, times = length(taus)), levels = names_short),
                       pc = 100 * (exp(as.vector(lb)) - 1))
log_ols_pc <- data.frame(term = factor(names_short, levels = names_short),
                         pc = 100 * (exp(coef(log_ols)[terms]) - 1))

ggplot(log_path, aes(tau, pc)) +
  geom_hline(data = log_ols_pc, aes(yintercept = pc, colour = "OLS (geometric mean)"), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = "Quantile regression"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "Quantile regression"), size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ term, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Quantile regression` = blue, `OLS (geometric mean)` = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)) +
  labs(title = "The same model on the log scale, as percentage differences",
       x = expression("quantile " * tau), y = "difference in price (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
lp <- function(term, t) 100 * (exp(coef(log_fit)[term, which.min(abs(taus - t))]) - 1)
test_log <- anova(rq(f_log, tau = 0.1, data = homes), log50, rq(f_log, tau = 0.9, data = homes))


On the percentage scale the London premium is 185% at \(\tau\) = 0.1, 144% at the median and 193% at \(\tau\) = 0.9. It is lowest near the middle (144%) and rises towards both ends, so across the middle 80% of the market it varies much less than the £205k to £800k in pounds. Prices in London are higher by a multiple rather than by a fixed sum, and part of the “growing” effect in pounds is just proportions on a skewed outcome. The shape of the curve depends on the scale: a steady rise in pounds becomes a U in percentages. A test of equal slopes on the log scale is still significant (F(10, 221,696) = 106.3, p < .001) but the differences are smaller. A report should say which scale it uses: the pound scale answers “how many pounds more?”, the log scale “how many times more?”.


Median regression resists outliers in y
OLS minimises squared residuals, so a single huge price pulls the line towards it. The median regression minimises absolute residuals: an extreme price costs a little more than a moderate one, but not squared. Only the ordering of the prices around the line matters, not how far away they are, which is why the median regression is a robust method, in the same spirit as robust regression (which also handles outliers in the predictors, which median regression does not). To see it, simulate a data-entry error: 100 random sales are entered with two extra zeros (£250,000 becomes £25,000,000).


Code
set.seed(2026)
dirty <- homes
bad   <- sample(n, 100)
dirty$k[bad] <- dirty$k[bad] * 100

effect <- rbind(
  OLS_clean    = coef(lm(f, homes)),
  OLS_dirty    = coef(lm(f, dirty)),
  median_clean = coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = homes)),
  median_dirty = coef(suppressWarnings(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = dirty))))
round(effect[, c("typeDetached", "londonLondon")], 1)


             typeDetached londonLondon
OLS_clean           247.1        475.9
OLS_dirty           289.7        543.4
median_clean        190.5        310.5
median_dirty        190.2        310.2


With 100 wrong prices out of 73,902 (0.14%), the OLS coefficient for London goes from £476k to £543k, and the one for detached homes from £247k to £290k. The median regression moves from £310k to £310k for London and from £190k to £190k for detached homes. A fully robust method would also resist bad predictors, and quantile regression does not, but for outliers in the outcome it is hard to beat. The same data contain real outliers too (the dearest sale is £25,400k): median regression is not disturbed by them.


Other points

Sample size. The extreme quantiles (\(\tau\) = 0.01 or 0.99) need many observations, since the line is fitted to a few points in the tail. As a rule of thumb, you want at least 10 or so observations in the tail for each parameter.
Dependence. Sales in the same street or town are alike, and the standard errors assume independent rows. With clustered data use a cluster bootstrap (boot.rq()) or see the multilevel page.
Weights and heteroscedasticity. Quantile regression does not need constant variance: unequal spread is the thing it describes. If the aim is a better mean line instead, see weighted least squares and generalised least squares.
Trees instead of lines. The random forest page shows quantile regression forests: the same idea with a flexible, non-linear model in place of a straight one.
Not causal. A London coefficient is a difference between groups of homes that differ in many other ways.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) states the data, the quantiles, the standard error method, the coefficients at the quantiles that matter, the comparison with OLS and the test of equal slopes.


Code
ci_of <- function(model, tau) {
  s <- summary(model, se = "nid")$coefficients
  cbind(est = s[, "Value"], lo = s[, "Value"] - qnorm(.975) * s[, "Std. Error"],
        hi = s[, "Value"] + qnorm(.975) * s[, "Std. Error"])
}
c10 <- ci_of(fit10); c50 <- ci_of(fit50); c90 <- ci_of(fit90)
co  <- cbind(est = coef(fit_ols), confint(fit_ols))
cell <- function(m, term) paste0(f0(m[term, 1]), " [", f0(m[term, 2]), ", ", f0(m[term, 3]), "]")

apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Flat (vs terraced)", "Semi-detached (vs terraced)", "Detached (vs terraced)",
                "New build (vs established)", "London (vs elsewhere)"),
  `τ = .10` = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(c10, t)),
  `τ = .50` = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(c50, t)),
  `τ = .90` = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(c90, t)),
  OLS       = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(co, t)),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)


Method (data analysis):

We analysed 73,902 sales of homes in England and Wales completed between October 2025 and September 2026, from the HM Land Registry Price Paid Data (standard sales of detached, semi-detached, terraced and flat properties; Open Government Licence v3.0). The outcome was the sale price in thousands of pounds. The predictors were the type of home (reference: terraced), whether it was newly built and whether it was in Greater London. Price was strongly right-skewed (median = £300k, mean = £376k), so we estimated linear quantile regressions at τ = .10, .50 and .90, and on a grid from .05 to .95, with the quantreg package (Version 6.1; Koenker, 2005), and compared them with ordinary least squares. Standard errors for the quantile regressions were of the nid (sandwich) type (Hendricks & Koenker, 1992). Equality of the coefficients across τ = .10, .50 and .90 was tested with the Wald-type test of Koenker and Bassett (1982). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

The effects of the predictors differed across the price distribution (Table 1). The London difference was £205k at the 10th percentile, 95% CI [200, 210], £310k at the median, 95% CI [303, 318], and £800k at the 90th percentile, 95% CI [762, 837]; the OLS estimate for the mean was £476k, 95% CI [468, 484]. Detached homes cost £130k, £190k and £410k more than terraced homes at the three quantiles. New builds were £50k dearer than established homes at the 10th percentile, but at the 90th the difference was -£2k, 95% CI [-22, 18]. The coefficients were not equal across the three quantiles, F(10, 221,696) = 419.3, p < .001. On the log scale the percentage London premium varied less (185% at τ = .10, 144% at τ = .50 and 193% at τ = .90), though the slopes still differed, F(10, 221,696) = 106.3, p < .001.

Points to remember:

Say which quantiles you fitted, and why those.
Say that coefficients are conditional quantile differences, and name the units.
Say which standard error method you used (nid, boot, …) and the number of bootstrap samples.
Report the test of equal slopes, but base the conclusion on the size of the differences.
Say whether the outcome is on the original or the log scale.
Show the coefficients against τ: a table of three quantiles cannot show the shape.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
10. Summary



When
The effect of a predictor may differ between the low and high ends of the outcome: skewed outcomes (prices, wages, incomes), or interest in the tails (risk, growth charts)


The model
\(Q_\tau(y \mid x) = x^\top \beta(\tau)\): one linear regression for each quantile \(\tau\)


The loss
Check loss \(\rho_\tau(u) = u(\tau - I(u < 0))\). Median: \(\tau = 0.5\), least absolute deviations


How (R)
quantreg::rq(y ~ x, tau = c(.1, .5, .9), data = d); summary(fit, se = "nid") or se = "boot"


Standard errors
"nid" for large samples; "boot" when in doubt; not "iid" with unequal spread


Equal slopes?
anova(fit10, fit50, fit90) (joint test), joint = FALSE (one predictor at a time)


Reading it
A difference in a conditional quantile, not an effect on the people at the top


Advantages
No normality or constant variance needed; robust to outliers in \(y\); quantiles commute with log and other monotone transformations


Dangers
Crossing quantiles; extreme \(\tau\) with small samples; dependent data; not robust to outliers in \(x\)


Alternatives
Robust regression, WLS and GLS for the mean; quantile forests for non-linear quantiles; unconditional quantile regression (RIF) for effects on the whole market

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Ordinary least squares (OLS) picks coefficients \(\beta\) that minimize the residual sum of squares (RSS): \(\sum(y_i - X_i\beta)^2\). That works fine until predictors are correlated with each other (multicollinearity) or there are many predictors relative to observations — then OLS coefficients become unstable: tiny changes in the data can swing them wildly, and the model overfits.
Regularized regression fixes this by adding a penalty on the size of the coefficients to the loss function, so the optimizer is discouraged from letting any coefficient get too large. Which penalty you choose gives you a different member of the same family:









Method
Penalty added to RSS
glmnet alpha
Effect




Ridge
\(\lambda \sum \beta_j^2\) (L2)
0
Shrinks coefficients toward zero, never exactly zero


Lasso
\(\lambda \sum \lvert\beta_j\rvert\) (L1)
1
Shrinks and can zero coefficients out (variable selection)


Elastic Net
a weighted mix of L1 and L2
0–1
Compromise: some sparsity, handles correlated predictors better than pure lasso



All of these introduce one new tuning parameter, \(\lambda\) (how strong the penalty is), which has to be chosen — that choice is a running theme through this script.
The dataset throughout is the built-in mtcars: predicting mpg (miles per gallon) from the other car characteristics (cylinders, weight, horsepower, etc.), several of which are strongly correlated (e.g. wt and disp) — exactly the setting where ridge/lasso earn their keep over plain lm().


Code
# y is centered; X is standardized inside glmnet for the CV/IC fits (standardize = TRUE);
# the coefficient-path plots and hridge use raw X (standardize = FALSE)
y <- as.matrix(scale(mtcars$mpg, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE))
X <- as.matrix(mtcars[, !names(mtcars) %in% "mpg"])
dim(X)


[1] 32 10


Code

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Ridge regression

Fitting ridge and choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation
glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, ...) — alpha = 0 is what tells glmnet “this is ridge, not lasso.” The function needs a value (or grid) of lambda to try. Rather than guess one, cv.glmnet() performs k-fold cross-validation: it fits ridge on each grid value of \(\lambda\), holds out folds to measure prediction error, and reports which \(\lambda\) generalizes best (lambda.min).


Code
lambdas_to_try <- 10^seq(-3, 5, length.out = 100)

ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambdas_to_try,
                       standardize = TRUE, nfolds = 10)
plot(ridge_cv)









The plot shows cross-validated MSE (y-axis) against \(-\log(\lambda)\) (x-axis, so penalty strength decreases from left to right). Too large a \(\lambda\) underfits (left), too small overfits (right). The two dotted vertical lines mark lambda.min (minimum CV error) and lambda.1se (the largest \(\lambda\) whose CV error is within one standard error of that minimum).


Code
lambda_cv <- ridge_cv$lambda.min
lambda_cv


[1] 2.983647


Code
model_cv <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_cv, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_cv <- predict(model_cv, X)
rsq_ridge_cv <- cor(y, y_hat_cv)^2
rsq_ridge_cv


            s0
[1,] 0.8524086




Choosing \(\lambda\) by information criteria (AIC/BIC) instead
Cross-validation isn’t the only way to pick \(\lambda\). This section computes AIC and BIC directly for every candidate \(\lambda\), as an alternative to CV.
The subtlety: AIC/BIC need a “degrees of freedom” value, and in ridge regression that isn’t just the number of predictors (since coefficients are shrunk, not freely estimated) — it’s the trace of the ridge hat matrix \(H = X(X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\), which continuously decreases from \(p\) (at \(\lambda=0\), same as OLS) toward 0 as \(\lambda \to \infty\).
One caveat: glmnet minimizes \(\frac{1}{2N}\text{RSS} + \frac{\lambda}{2}\sum\beta_j^2\) (and scales \(y\) internally), so its \(\lambda\) is not on the same scale as the \(\lambda\) in \(X^\top X + \lambda I\). The df computed here is therefore an approximation, not the exact effective df of each glmnet fit. The residuals come from the actual glmnet predictions, and BIC uses the usual \(\text{df} \cdot \log(n)\) penalty.


Code
X_scaled <- scale(X)
aic <- bic <- c()

for (lambda in seq(lambdas_to_try)) {
  model <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambdas_to_try[lambda], standardize = TRUE)
  resid <- y - predict(model, X)

  # Ridge hat matrix and its trace = effective degrees of freedom
  ld <- lambdas_to_try[lambda] * diag(ncol(X_scaled))
  H <- X_scaled %*% solve(t(X_scaled) %*% X_scaled + ld) %*% t(X_scaled)
  df <- tr(H)  # tr() comes from the psych package

  aic[lambda] <- nrow(X_scaled) * log(t(resid) %*% resid) + 2 * df
  bic[lambda] <- nrow(X_scaled) * log(t(resid) %*% resid) + df * log(nrow(X_scaled))
}

plot(log(lambdas_to_try), aic, col = "orange", type = "l", ylim = range(c(aic, bic)),
     ylab = "Information Criterion")
lines(log(lambdas_to_try), bic, col = "skyblue3")
legend("bottomright", lwd = 1, col = c("orange", "skyblue3"), legend = c("AIC", "BIC"))









BIC penalizes model complexity (degrees of freedom) more heavily than AIC once you have more than a handful of observations, which is why it typically prefers a larger \(\lambda\) (a simpler, more shrunk model) than AIC does — visible here as the skyblue curve’s minimum (at \(\lambda \approx\) 5.21) sitting to the right of the orange curve’s (at \(\lambda \approx\) 2.48).


Code
lambda_aic <- lambdas_to_try[which.min(aic)]
lambda_bic <- lambdas_to_try[which.min(bic)]
c(lambda_aic = lambda_aic, lambda_bic = lambda_bic)


lambda_aic lambda_bic 
  2.477076   5.214008 


Code
model_aic <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_aic, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_aic <- predict(model_aic, X)
rsq_ridge_aic <- cor(y, y_hat_aic)^2

model_bic <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_bic, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_bic <- predict(model_bic, X)
rsq_ridge_bic <- cor(y, y_hat_bic)^2

c(rsq_ridge_aic = rsq_ridge_aic, rsq_ridge_bic = rsq_ridge_bic)


rsq_ridge_aic rsq_ridge_bic 
    0.8536968     0.8481806 




Visualizing the shrinkage itself
This is the most direct illustration of what ridge actually does. Each line is one predictor’s coefficient, traced across every value of \(\lambda\) tried. The x-axis is \(-\log(\lambda)\), so \(\lambda\) grows from right to left. Follow any single line from right (small \(\lambda\), close to the unpenalized OLS coefficient) to left (large \(\lambda\)): it bends toward zero, but — unlike lasso below — none of the lines ever reaches zero and stays there.


Code
plot(glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambdas_to_try, standardize = FALSE), xvar = "lambda")
legend("bottomright", lwd = 1, col = 1:6, legend = colnames(X), cex = 0.7)

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
section: Heteroscedastic ridge: penalizing each coefficient differently
text:
Heteroscedastic ridge: penalizing each coefficient differently
Plain ridge penalizes every coefficient equally (\(\lambda \sum \beta_j^2\), same \(\lambda\) for every \(j\)). But if some predictors are inherently noisier than others, treating them identically may not be ideal. Heteroscedastic ridge instead gives each coefficient its own penalty weight \(w_j\), derived from that predictor’s own simple (univariate) regression:
\[\text{minimize} \quad \sum(y_i - X_i\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum w_j \beta_j^2\]
Predictors whose univariate slope has a larger standard error get a larger \(w_j\) and are shrunk more. Because \(X\) is not standardized here, these weights largely reflect each predictor’s units (e.g. disp, measured in cubic inches, gets a tiny weight), so standardize \(X\) first if you want \(w_j\) to reflect uncertainty.


Code
# w_j = variance of the coefficient from a simple regression of y on X[,j] alone
weights <- sapply(seq(ncol(X)), function(predictor) {
  uni_model <- lm(y ~ X[, predictor])
  summary(uni_model)$coefficients[2, 2]^2  # squared standard error
})
names(weights) <- colnames(X)
weights


         cyl         disp           hp         drat           wt         qsec           vs           am         gear         carb 
1.039475e-01 2.220137e-05 1.024003e-04 2.270160e+00 3.125940e-01 3.127160e-01 2.664632e+00 3.113184e+00 1.711206e+00 3.232441e-01 




Code
hridge_loss <- function(betas, y, X, lambda, weights) {
  sum((y - X %*% betas)^2) + lambda * sum(weights * betas^2)
}

hridge <- function(y, X, lambda, weights) {
  # Regular ridge gives a sensible starting point for the numerical optimizer
  model_init <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda, standardize = FALSE)
  betas_init <- as.vector(model_init$beta)

  # Pass lambda/weights explicitly so the loss never picks up a global variable;
  # BFGS converges here, while the default Nelder-Mead stops at maxit for 10 parameters
  coef <- optim(betas_init, hridge_loss, y = y, X = X, lambda = lambda,
                weights = weights, method = "BFGS")$par
  fitted <- X %*% coef
  rsq <- cor(y, fitted)^2
  names(coef) <- colnames(X)
  list(coef = coef, fitted = fitted, rsq = rsq)
}

hridge_model <- hridge(y, X, lambda = 0.001, weights = weights)
rsq_hridge_0001 <- hridge_model$rsq
hridge_model$coef


        cyl        disp          hp        drat          wt        qsec          vs          am        gear        carb 
-0.40433235  0.01319901 -0.02206732  0.50014598 -3.64524339  0.58652650  0.39718262  2.31882063  0.40427348 -0.15931827 


Choosing \(\lambda\) here could use the same cross-validation or AIC/BIC strategies shown above for plain ridge — not implemented here, but see momisc::hridge for a fuller implementation.

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Lasso: L1 penalty, sparse coefficients
Switching alpha from 0 to 1 changes the penalty from L2 (\(\sum\beta_j^2\)) to L1 (\(\sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert\)). The geometry of the L1 penalty (a diamond-shaped constraint region vs. ridge’s circular one) means its corners often land exactly on an axis — i.e., some coefficients get shrunk all the way to zero. That makes lasso a built-in variable-selection method, not just a shrinkage method.


Code
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lambdas_to_try, standardize = TRUE, nfolds = 10)
plot(lasso_cv)









Code
lambda_cv_lasso <- lasso_cv$lambda.min
model_cv_lasso <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_cv_lasso, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_cv_lasso <- predict(model_cv_lasso, X)
rsq_lasso_cv <- cor(y, y_hat_cv_lasso)^2
rsq_lasso_cv


            s0
[1,] 0.8424217




Code
res <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lambdas_to_try, standardize = FALSE)
plot(res, xvar = "lambda")
legend("bottomright", lwd = 1, col = 1:6, legend = colnames(X), cex = 0.7)









Compare this plot to ridge’s coefficient path above: here, lines don’t just bend toward zero, they hit zero and stay there as \(\lambda\) grows (moving left on the \(-\log(\lambda)\) axis; the numbers along the top count the non-zero coefficients) — each one dropping out is lasso “deciding” that predictor isn’t worth keeping at that penalty strength.

Comparing R² across methods so far


Code
rsq <- cbind("R-squared" = c(rsq_ridge_cv, rsq_ridge_aic, rsq_ridge_bic,
                              rsq_hridge_0001, rsq_lasso_cv))
rownames(rsq) <- c("ridge cross-validated", "ridge AIC", "ridge BIC",
                    "hridge 0.001", "lasso cross-validated")
print(rsq)


                      R-squared
ridge cross-validated 0.8524086
ridge AIC             0.8536968
ridge BIC             0.8481806
hridge 0.001          0.8679368
lasso cross-validated 0.8424217


These are all in-sample R² (predicting on the same X used to fit), so they’re useful for comparing the methods to each other here, but shouldn’t be read as an estimate of real-world predictive accuracy — that’s what the cross-validation step is doing internally when picking \(\lambda\), just not reported as a final held-out number here.

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
section: Elastic net: mixing L1 and L2
text:
Elastic net: mixing L1 and L2
Elastic net adds both penalties at once, weighted by alpha between 0 (pure ridge) and 1 (pure lasso). In glmnet’s parameterization the penalty is:
\[\lambda \left[ \alpha \sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\sum\beta_j^2 \right]\]
It’s useful when you want lasso’s variable-selection behavior but have groups of correlated predictors — pure lasso tends to arbitrarily pick just one predictor out of a correlated group and zero out the rest, while elastic net’s ridge component lets correlated predictors share the credit more smoothly.
Here, caret::train() searches over both alpha and lambda simultaneously (method = "glmnet"), using repeated cross-validation to score each combination.
Note: building the data with cbind(y, X) would not work. scale() returns an unnamed column, so the first column is named "" (V1 once coerced to a data frame), and mpg ~ . fails with “object ‘mpg’ not found”. Naming the column explicitly avoids this:


Code
library(caret)
train_control <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, repeats = 5,
                               search = "random", verboseIter = FALSE)

data_enet <- data.frame(mpg = as.vector(y), X)
elastic_net_model <- train(mpg ~ ., data = data_enet, method = "glmnet",
                            preProcess = c("center", "scale"), tuneLength = 25,
                            trControl = train_control)




Code
elastic_net_model$bestTune


       alpha   lambda
1 0.06072057 1.166075


Code
y_hat_enet <- predict(elastic_net_model, X)
rsq_enet <- cor(y, y_hat_enet)^2
rsq_enet


          [,1]
[1,] 0.8579053

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Summary

All four methods (ridge, heteroscedastic ridge, lasso, elastic net) are OLS plus a penalty on coefficient size; they differ only in which penalty.
Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero — good for multicollinearity, keeps every predictor in the model.
Heteroscedastic ridge lets each predictor be penalized by its own confidence (via per-coefficient weights) instead of one blanket penalty.
Lasso (L1) shrinks and zeroes out coefficients — a built-in feature selector, at the cost of being less stable when predictors are correlated.
Elastic net mixes both, tunable via alpha, and is often the practical default when you’re not sure which of ridge or lasso suits your data.
In every case, the real modeling decision isn’t “ridge vs. lasso” alone — it’s how you choose \(\lambda\) (cross-validation vs. information criteria), since that controls the whole bias/variance trade-off.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
An employer hires customer-service advisers. Every applicant takes a reasoning test, and only those above a cut score are hired. A year later each new adviser’s supervisor rates their job performance. The employer wants to know: how well does the test predict performance? That number, the correlation between test scores and performance, is the test’s validity coefficient.
The obvious answer is to correlate the test scores of the hires with their ratings. That correlation is almost always too low, for two reasons:

Range restriction. Performance ratings exist only for the people who were hired, and they all scored above the cut. Among them the test scores vary much less than among all applicants, and a correlation computed on a narrow range of scores is smaller. But the test is used to choose among applicants, so the validity that matters is the one among applicants.
An unreliable criterion. Supervisors disagree. Part of each rating is the supervisor’s personal view, not the adviser’s performance, and that noise lowers the correlation with anything.

So we need to be clear about which validity we mean:










Validity
Test
Performance
People
Used for




Observed
observed scores
one supervisor’s ratings
the hires
what the data give


Operational
observed scores
true performance
all applicants
decisions about using the test


Construct-level
true ability
true performance
all applicants
theory: how strongly the ability itself matters



The operational validity is the one for practical decisions: the test is used as it is, with its measurement error, on applicants, to predict their real performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998). As in other pages of this site, we simulate the applicant pool, so we know every true value and can check each correction against it.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side
library(mvtnorm)    # pmvnorm(): areas of the bivariate normal distribution (section 6)

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility

Among them the test scores vary much less than among all applicants, and a correlation computed on a narrow range of scores is smaller. But the test is used to choose among applicants, so the validity that matters is the one among applicants.
An unreliable criterion. Supervisors disagree. Part of each rating is the supervisor’s personal view, not the adviser’s performance, and that noise lowers the correlation with anything.

So we need to be clear about which validity we mean:

The operational validity is the one for practical decisions: the test is used as it is, with its measurement error, on applicants, to predict their real performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998). As in other pages of this site, we simulate the applicant pool, so we know every true value and can check each correction against it.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side
library(mvtnorm)    # pmvnorm(): areas of the bivariate normal distribution (section 6)

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
1. Simulate the applicant pool
The true values, for the whole applicant pool:

Construct-level validity \(\rho = 0.60\): the correlation between true reasoning ability and true job performance.
Test reliability \(r_{xx} = 0.85\): 85% of the variance of the test scores is true ability, 15% measurement error.
Rating reliability \(r_{yy} = 0.52\): the reliability of a single supervisor’s rating, the typical value found for supervisory ratings of job performance (Viswesvaran et al., 1996).
Selection ratio 30%: the top 30% of applicants on the test are hired.

From these the true operational validity is \(\rho \sqrt{r_{xx}} = 0.60 \times \sqrt{0.85} = 0.553\): measurement error in the test lowers the correlation by the square root of its reliability.


Code
rho <- 0.60; rxx <- 0.85; ryy <- 0.52
truth <- c(construct = rho, operational = rho * sqrt(rxx))

simulate_pool <- function(n) {
  ability     <- rnorm(n)                                        # true reasoning ability
  performance <- rho * ability + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)      # true job performance
  test_error  <- rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 / rxx - 1))                # so that reliability = rxx
  e1 <- rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 / ryy - 1))                         # supervisor 1's personal view
  e2 <- rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 / ryy - 1))                         # supervisor 2's personal view
  data.frame(ability, performance, test_error, e1,
             test    = 50 + 10 * sqrt(rxx) * (ability + test_error),     # test score: mean 50, SD 10
             rating1 = 50 + 10 * sqrt(ryy) * (performance + e1),         # rating by supervisor 1
             rating2 = 50 + 10 * sqrt(ryy) * (performance + e2))         # rating by supervisor 2
}

set.seed(65)
pool <- simulate_pool(5000)                     # five years of applicants
cut_score <- quantile(pool$test, 0.70)          # the top 30% are hired
pool$hired <- pool$test >= cut_score
hires <- pool[pool$hired, ]
c(applicants = nrow(pool), hired = nrow(hires), cut_score = unname(round(cut_score, 1)))


applicants      hired  cut_score 
    5000.0     1500.0       55.8 


Every applicant has a test score, but in real life only the 1,500 hires get performance ratings. Each hire is rated by two supervisors (in practice, often only a subsample is), which tells us how reliable the ratings are. The ratings of the rejected applicants exist only because this is a simulation.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
2. What the employer sees


Code
r_pool  <- cor(pool$test, pool$rating1)
r_hires <- cor(hires$test, hires$rating1)
ggplot(pool, aes(test, rating1)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(pool, !hired), colour = "#95A5A6", alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  geom_point(data = hires, colour = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cut_score, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(data = hires, method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#E74C3C") +
  annotate("text", x = cut_score + 1, y = 18, hjust = 0, size = 3.5,
           label = sprintf("hired (blue): r = %.2f", r_hires)) +
  annotate("text", x = cut_score - 1, y = 18, hjust = 1, size = 3.5,
           label = sprintf("all applicants: r = %.2f", r_pool)) +
  labs(title = "Ratings exist only for the hires (blue).\nThe grey ratings are never seen in real life",
       x = "test score", y = "performance rating (supervisor 1)")











Code
data.frame(group = c("all applicants", "hires"),
           n = c(nrow(pool), nrow(hires)),
           sd_test = round(c(sd(pool$test), sd(hires$test)), 2),
           r_test_rating = round(c(r_pool, r_hires), 3))


           group    n sd_test r_test_rating
1 all applicants 5000   10.16         0.406
2          hires 1500    5.24         0.215


Among all applicants the test correlates 0.41 with a supervisor’s rating; among the hires only 0.22. The test scores of the hires vary about half as much (SD 5.2 against 10.2). Over such a narrow range, the noise in the ratings swamps the trend. The test did not get worse; we are looking at the slice of applicants where it has least to do.
And the true operational validity is higher still: 0.553. The two corrections below recover it.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
3. Correction 1: the unreliable ratings

How reliable are the ratings?
When two supervisors rate the same advisers, the correlation between their ratings is the interrater reliability of one supervisor’s rating:


Code
ryy_hires <- cor(hires$rating1, hires$rating2)
ryy_hires


[1] 0.437224


It is 0.44 among the hires, lower than the 0.52 that holds for all applicants. The supervisors are no worse; the true performance of the hires varies less (it was partly selected through the test), so the same amount of rating noise is a larger share of the total.


The correction for attenuation
Spearman’s (1904) formula removes the effect of measurement error in the criterion:
\[r_{c} = \frac{r_{xy}}{\sqrt{r_{yy}}}\]
We correct for the unreliability of the ratings only. The unreliability of the test stays in, because the test will always be used with its measurement error: that is what “operational” means. Correcting for it too would describe a perfect test that does not exist.


Code
r_obs <- r_hires
r_crit <- r_obs / sqrt(ryy_hires)
c(observed = r_obs, corrected_for_ratings = r_crit)


             observed corrected_for_ratings 
            0.2151800             0.3254243 


\[r_c = \frac{0.215}{\sqrt{0.437}} = 0.325\]
This is the validity among the hires, as if their performance had been measured without error. It is still range-restricted.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
4. Correction 2: range restriction

Thorndike’s Case II
When people were selected directly on the test, the validity in the applicant pool follows from the validity among the hires and from how much the selection narrowed the test scores (Thorndike, 1949). Write \(u\) for the ratio of the test’s standard deviation among the hires (\(s\)) to that among all applicants (\(S\)), and \(U = 1/u\):
\[u = \frac{s}{S}, \qquad R = \frac{r\,U}{\sqrt{1 + r^2\,(U^2 - 1)}}\]
where \(r\) is the restricted correlation and \(R\) the corrected one. \(S\) is easy to get: every applicant took the test, so their scores are on file even if they were not hired.


Code
case_ii <- function(r, u) {                    # Thorndike's Case II: direct selection on the test
  U <- 1 / u
  r * U / sqrt(1 + r^2 * (U^2 - 1))
}
u <- sd(hires$test) / sd(pool$test)
r_op <- case_ii(r_crit, u)
c(u = u, operational_validity = r_op, truth = unname(truth["operational"]))


                   u operational_validity                truth 
           0.5153647            0.5553490            0.5531727 


\[u = \frac{5.24}{10.16} = 0.515, \qquad R = \frac{0.325 \times 1.940}{\sqrt{1 + 0.325^2 (1.940^2 - 1)}} = 0.555\]
The estimate of the operational validity, 0.555, is close to the true 0.553. The observed 0.22 understated it by about 61%.
Case II assumes that the relationship is linear with the same spread at every test score, and that selection was made on the test itself. Both are true here; section “Indirect range restriction” shows what happens when the second is not.


The order of the corrections
Each correction must use a reliability from the same group as the correlation it corrects. Our rating reliability comes from the hires, so it goes with the hires’ correlation: correct for the ratings first, then for range restriction. The other way round would need the rating reliability among all applicants, which is never available, because the rejected applicants were never rated.


Code
data.frame(
  order = c("ratings first (hires' reliability), then range restriction",
            "range restriction first, then ratings with the hires' reliability (wrong)",
            "range restriction first, then ratings with the applicants' reliability"),
  estimate = round(c(r_op,
                     case_ii(r_obs, u) / sqrt(ryy_hires),
                     case_ii(r_obs, u) / sqrt(cor(pool$rating1, pool$rating2))), 3))


                                                                      order estimate
1                ratings first (hires' reliability), then range restriction    0.555
2 range restriction first, then ratings with the hires' reliability (wrong)    0.595
3    range restriction first, then ratings with the applicants' reliability    0.542


The wrong mix over-corrects to 0.595. The third line gives practically the same answer as the first, but needs the applicants’ rating reliability, which we have only because this is a simulation.


Construct-level validity
For theory, how strongly reasoning ability itself relates to performance, also remove the measurement error of the test. Use the test’s reliability among applicants, because by now the correlation describes the applicants:
\[\rho = \frac{R}{\sqrt{r_{xx}}}\]


Code
r_con <- r_op / sqrt(rxx)
c(construct_level = r_con, truth = unname(truth["construct"]))


construct_level           truth 
      0.6023606       0.6000000 


In the simulation we know every applicant’s true scores and errors, so we can check this directly. The rwf package’s compute_dissatenuation() takes the true scores and errors of two variables, computes the observed correlation and both reliabilities, and corrects for both:


Code
rwf_construct <- compute_dissatenuation(variable1 = pool$ability, error1 = pool$test_error,
                                        variable2 = pool$performance, error2 = pool$e1)
rwf_construct


[1] 0.6089731


It gives 0.609, close to both our estimate (0.602) and the truth (0.60); the small differences are sampling error. In real data the true scores are unknown, and the reliabilities come from a test manual, an internal-consistency estimate or a second rater, as above.


All the steps at once


Code
steps <- data.frame(
  step = factor(c("observed\n(hires)", "+ ratings\ncorrected", "+ range\nrestriction", "+ test\nreliability"),
                levels = c("observed\n(hires)", "+ ratings\ncorrected", "+ range\nrestriction", "+ test\nreliability")),
  value = c(r_obs, r_crit, r_op, r_con))
ggplot(steps, aes(step, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0082c8", width = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = truth, linetype = "dashed", colour = c("#8E44AD", "#E74C3C")) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = truth + 0.025, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = c("#8E44AD", "#E74C3C"),
           label = c("true construct-level validity", "true operational validity")) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0.03, label = sprintf("%.3f", value)), size = 3.5, colour = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.7)) +
  labs(title = "From the observed to the operational and construct-level validity",
       x = NULL, y = "validity coefficient")











Indirect range restriction
Selection is rarely made on the test that is being validated. More often a new test is tried out on staff who were hired with something else: an interview, an older test, a mix of criteria. If that something correlates with the new test, the new test’s range is restricted indirectly. The test scores still look narrower among the staff, but Case II, which assumes direct selection on this test, then under-corrects (Hunter et al., 2006).
Hunter, Schmidt and Le’s correction (often called Case IV) assumes that the selection worked through the true ability that the test measures:

Turn the applicant reliability of the test into its reliability among the hires: \(r_{xx,i} = 1 - (1 - r_{xx,a}) / u_X^2\).
Correct the hires’ correlation for both unreliabilities, with the hires’ reliabilities: \(\rho_i = r / \sqrt{r_{xx,i}\,r_{yy,i}}\).
Get the range restriction on true scores: \(u_T = \sqrt{\dfrac{u_X^2 - (1 - r_{xx,a})}{r_{xx,a}}}\).
Apply the Case II formula with \(u_T\); this gives the construct-level validity among applicants.
Multiply by \(\sqrt{r_{xx,a}}\) to get the operational validity.

A second employer validates our test on advisers who were hired with an older test of the same ability (one that correlates 0.90 with true ability), again the top 30%:


Code
set.seed(7)
pool2 <- simulate_pool(20000)
pool2$old_test <- 0.9 * pool2$ability + sqrt(1 - 0.9^2) * rnorm(20000)   # what the hiring was based on
staff <- pool2[pool2$old_test >= quantile(pool2$old_test, 0.70), ]

r2   <- cor(staff$test, staff$rating1)
ry2  <- cor(staff$rating1, staff$rating2)
u2   <- sd(staff$test) / sd(pool2$test)
rxx_i <- 1 - (1 - rxx) / u2^2                       # step 1
rho_i <- r2 / sqrt(rxx_i * ry2)                     # step 2
u_t   <- sqrt((u2^2 - (1 - rxx)) / rxx)             # step 3
case_iv <- case_ii(rho_i, u_t) * sqrt(rxx)          # steps 4 and 5
round(c(observed = r2, ratings_corrected_only = r2 / sqrt(ry2), case_ii = case_ii(r2 / sqrt(ry2), u2),
        case_iv = case_iv, truth = cor(pool2$test, pool2$performance)), 3)


              observed ratings_corrected_only                case_ii                case_iv                  truth 
                 0.247                  0.365                  0.489                  0.564                  0.555 


Case II moves the estimate in the right direction but stops at 0.49; Case IV reaches 0.56, close to the truth. When you cannot tell whether selection was direct or indirect, Case II is the cautious choice: if the selection was in fact indirect, it errs on the low side. Corrections are only as good as their inputs, though, and a recent re-analysis argues that many published validities were over-corrected because the range restriction values used were too large (Sackett et al., 2022). Use the actual applicant standard deviation of your own test whenever you have it.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
5. Corrected coefficients are noisier
A validation study of 1,500 hires is rare. With a more typical 200 hires, how much do the observed and corrected validities vary from study to study? We repeat the whole study 2,000 times: 667 applicants, the top 200 hired, two supervisors rating each:


Code
set.seed(11)
one_study <- function() {
  p <- simulate_pool(667)
  h <- p[p$test >= quantile(p$test, 0.70), ]
  r <- cor(h$test, h$rating1)
  c(observed = r,
    p_value = cor.test(h$test, h$rating1)$p.value,
    operational = case_ii(r / sqrt(cor(h$rating1, h$rating2)), sd(h$test) / sd(p$test)))
}
studies <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(2000, one_study())))
round(data.frame(mean = sapply(studies[c("observed", "operational")], mean),
                 median = sapply(studies[c("observed", "operational")], median),
                 sd = sapply(studies[c("observed", "operational")], sd)), 3)


             mean median    sd
observed    0.217  0.220 0.070
operational 0.538  0.552 0.138


Code
mean(studies$p_value > 0.05)    # share of studies that find no significant validity


[1] 0.137




Code
long <- rbind(data.frame(validity = "observed (hires)", value = studies$observed),
              data.frame(validity = "corrected (operational)", value = studies$operational))
long$validity <- factor(long$validity, levels = c("observed (hires)", "corrected (operational)"))
ggplot(long, aes(value, fill = validity)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45, colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = truth["operational"], linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = truth["operational"] + 0.01, y = 4.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.3, label = "true operational\nvalidity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#0082c8")) +
  labs(title = "2,000 validation studies with 200 hires each", x = "validity coefficient", y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










The corrected values are centred close to the truth (median 0.552), but they spread twice as widely (SD 0.138 against 0.070). A correction removes bias, not uncertainty: it multiplies the sampling error along with the coefficient.
14% of these studies would have found no significant validity at .05, for a test whose operational validity is 0.55. A small validation study that “finds nothing” is weak evidence that the test does not work.
To give a confidence interval for a corrected validity, compute the interval of the observed correlation and pass both limits through the same corrections (section 8).

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
section: 6. What validity is worth in practice
text:
6. What validity is worth in practice
A correlation of 0.55 sounds modest. Three classic tools translate it into things a manager understands.

Expectancy chart
Split the applicants into five equal bands by test score, and show the chance of being a good performer (here: true performance above the applicants’ median) in each band. With the estimated operational validity, the bivariate normal distribution predicts this chance for each band:
\[P(\text{good} \mid \text{band}) = \frac{P(x_{low} < X < x_{high},\; Y > y_c)}{P(x_{low} < X < x_{high})}\]


Code
upper_tail <- function(a, b, r) {               # P(X > a, Y > b) for a standard bivariate normal
  if (a == -Inf) return(pnorm(b, lower.tail = FALSE))   # no lower limit on X
  if (a == Inf) return(0)                                 # nobody is above +infinity
  as.numeric(pmvnorm(upper = c(-a, -b), corr = matrix(c(1, r, r, 1), 2), algorithm = TVPACK()))
}
edges <- qnorm(seq(0, 1, by = 0.2))             # five bands of 20% of applicants each
model <- sapply(1:5, function(k) (upper_tail(edges[k], 0, r_op) - upper_tail(edges[k + 1], 0, r_op)) / 0.2)

pool$band <- cut(pool$test, quantile(pool$test, seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)), include.lowest = TRUE,
                 labels = c("lowest 20%", "20-40%", "40-60%", "60-80%", "top 20%"))
pool$good <- pool$performance > median(pool$performance)
chart <- data.frame(band = levels(pool$band), simulated = as.numeric(tapply(pool$good, pool$band, mean)), model = model)
chart$band <- factor(chart$band, levels = chart$band)
round(chart[, -1], 3)


  simulated model
1     0.201 0.186
2     0.371 0.362
3     0.487 0.500
4     0.626 0.638
5     0.815 0.814


Code
ggplot(chart, aes(band, simulated)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0082c8", width = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = model), colour = "#E74C3C", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0.04, label = scales::percent(simulated, accuracy = 1)), size = 3.5, colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Chance of being a good performer, by test-score band",
       subtitle = "bars: simulated applicants; red points: predicted from the corrected validity",
       x = "test-score band among applicants", y = "good performers")









Applicants in the top fifth of test scores are good performers 82% of the time, those in the bottom fifth 20%. Without the test, it would be 50% everywhere.


Taylor-Russell: the success ratio
Taylor and Russell (1939) asked: if we hire the top fraction of applicants (the selection ratio, SR) and a share of applicants would succeed anyway (the base rate), what share of those hired will succeed? With a cut \(x_c\) on the test and a success threshold \(y_c\) on performance, both on the standard normal scale:
\[\text{success ratio} = P(Y > y_c \mid X > x_c) = \frac{P(X > x_c,\; Y > y_c)}{\text{SR}}, \qquad x_c = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \text{SR}),\; y_c = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \text{base rate})\]


Code
success_ratio <- function(r, sr, base_rate) upper_tail(qnorm(1 - sr), qnorm(1 - base_rate), r) / sr
validities <- c(0, 0.2, 0.4, round(r_op, 2))
sr_values  <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)
tr <- outer(validities, sr_values, Vectorize(function(r, sr) success_ratio(r, sr, base_rate = 0.5)))
dimnames(tr) <- list(validity = validities, selection_ratio = sr_values)
round(tr, 2)


        selection_ratio
validity  0.1  0.3  0.5  0.7  0.9
    0    0.50 0.50 0.50 0.50 0.50
    0.2  0.64 0.59 0.56 0.54 0.52
    0.4  0.77 0.69 0.63 0.58 0.53
    0.56 0.87 0.77 0.69 0.62 0.54


Read a row as one test, a column as one hiring situation. With no validity (first row) the success ratio is the base rate, 50%, whatever the selection ratio. With our test (last row) and the employer’s selection ratio of 30%, 77% of hires succeed. A test pays off most when the selection ratio is low: when there are many applicants for each job.


Code
grid_sr <- seq(0.05, 1, by = 0.01)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.2, 0.4, round(r_op, 2)), function(r)
  data.frame(sr = grid_sr, success = sapply(grid_sr, function(s) success_ratio(r, s, 0.5)),
             validity = sprintf("validity %.2f", r))))
ggplot(curves, aes(sr, success, colour = validity)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#f39c12", "#0082c8")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.45, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Share of hires who succeed (base rate 50%)",
       x = "selection ratio (share of applicants hired)", y = "success ratio", colour = NULL)











Utility: what the test is worth in money
The Brogden-Cronbach-Gleser model (Brogden, 1949; Cronbach & Gleser, 1965) puts a money value on the gain from hiring with the test instead of at random:
\[\Delta U = N_s \cdot T \cdot r_{xy} \cdot SD_y \cdot \bar z_x \; - \; N \cdot C\]

\(N_s\): people hired per year; \(N = N_s / \text{SR}\): applicants tested.
\(T\): average years a hire stays.
\(r_{xy}\): the operational validity.
\(SD_y\): the standard deviation of performance in money per year: how much more a good adviser (one SD above average) is worth than an average one. A common rough estimate is 40% of the salary (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998).
\(\bar z_x\): the average test score of those hired, in standard units. For the top SR of a normal distribution it is \(\bar z_x = \phi(z_c) / \text{SR}\), the height of the normal curve at the cut divided by the selection ratio.
\(C\): the cost of testing one applicant.



Code
utility <- function(r, sr, n_hired = 100, years = 3, sd_y = 12000, cost = 40) {
  z_bar <- dnorm(qnorm(1 - sr)) / sr                  # average standard score of those hired
  n_hired * years * r * sd_y * z_bar - (n_hired / sr) * cost
}
z_bar_30 <- dnorm(qnorm(0.7)) / 0.3
c(z_bar = z_bar_30, utility_corrected = utility(r_op, 0.3), utility_observed = utility(r_obs, 0.3))


            z_bar utility_corrected  utility_observed 
     1.158975e+00      2.303756e+06      8.844648e+05 


With 100 hires a year who stay 3 years, an \(SD_y\) of €12,000 (40% of a €30,000 salary), €40 per test and a selection ratio of 30% (\(\bar z_x\) = 1.16), the test is worth about €2,304,000 for each year’s intake, or about €7,680 per hire per year. With the uncorrected validity the same test would look worth only €884,000, 62% less: using observed validities makes good tests look much less useful than they are.


Code
u_curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(r_obs, r_op), function(r)
  data.frame(sr = grid_sr[grid_sr < 1], gain = sapply(grid_sr[grid_sr < 1], function(s) utility(r, s)) / 1e6,
             validity = sprintf("%s validity %.2f", ifelse(r == r_op, "operational", "observed"), r))))
ggplot(u_curves, aes(sr, gain, colour = validity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#0082c8")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Gain from 100 hires a year, over 3 years",
       x = "selection ratio", y = "gain (million euros)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Treat these numbers as rough and optimistic. They ignore that some offers are refused, that money later is worth less than money now, and taxes and variable costs; \(SD_y\) is itself only an estimate (Cascio & Aguinis, 2019). Even after heavy discounts, a valid test used with a low selection ratio usually pays for itself many times over.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
7. Adverse impact
A test can be valid and still select members of one group at a lower rate than another. When groups differ on average on what the test measures, any cut score turns that difference into different selection rates. The common screen is the four-fifths rule from the United States’ Uniform Guidelines (1978): if a group’s selection rate is below 80% of the rate of the group selected most often, that is taken as evidence of adverse impact:
\[\text{impact ratio} = \frac{\text{selection rate of the group selected less often}}{\text{selection rate of the group selected most often}} < 0.80\]
Suppose 30% of the applicants belong to group B, whose mean on the test is half a standard deviation below group A’s (a difference of \(d = 0.5\)), and the employer keeps the cut that hires the top 30% overall:


Code
set.seed(3)
n_a <- 3500; n_b <- 1500
applicants <- data.frame(group = rep(c("A", "B"), c(n_a, n_b)),
                         test = c(rnorm(n_a, 50, 10), rnorm(n_b, 45, 10)))   # group B: 0.5 SD lower
cut_ab <- quantile(applicants$test, 0.70)
applicants$hired <- applicants$test >= cut_ab
rates <- aggregate(hired ~ group, applicants, function(h) c(applicants = length(h), hired = sum(h), rate = mean(h)))
rates <- data.frame(group = rates$group, rates$hired)
rates


  group applicants hired      rate
1     A       3500  1214 0.3468571
2     B       1500   286 0.1906667


Code
impact_ratio <- rates$rate[rates$group == "B"] / rates$rate[rates$group == "A"]
impact_ratio


[1] 0.549698


Code
prop.test(rates$hired, rates$applicants)$p.value          # are the two selection rates different?


[1] 3.394971e-28


Group A is hired at 35%, group B at 19%: an impact ratio of 0.55, well below 0.80. The difference is also statistically significant; with small numbers of applicants, the four-fifths rule and a significance test can disagree, and both are usually reported.
How the impact depends on the cut score and the size of the group difference, computed from the normal distribution:


Code
impact_curve <- function(d, sr, share_b = 0.3) {
  overall <- function(cut) (1 - share_b) * (1 - pnorm(cut)) + share_b * (1 - pnorm(cut + d)) - sr
  cut <- uniroot(overall, c(-6, 6))$root               # the cut that hires sr of all applicants
  (1 - pnorm(cut + d)) / (1 - pnorm(cut))
}
ic <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8), function(d)
  data.frame(sr = grid_sr[grid_sr < 1], ratio = sapply(grid_sr[grid_sr < 1], function(s) impact_curve(d, s)),
             difference = sprintf("d = %.1f", d))))
ggplot(ic, aes(sr, ratio, colour = difference)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.07, y = 0.83, hjust = 0, size = 3.3, label = "four-fifths line") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#f39c12", "#E74C3C")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Impact ratio by selection ratio and group difference",
       x = "selection ratio (share of all applicants hired)", y = "impact ratio (B / A)", colour = NULL)









Code
# the selection ratio below which each difference fails the four-fifths rule
crossing <- sapply(c(0.2, 0.5), function(d) uniroot(function(s) impact_curve(d, s) - 0.8, c(0.05, 0.99))$root)
round(crossing, 2)


[1] 0.34 0.76



The stricter the cut (the lower the selection ratio), the lower the impact ratio. The same test can pass the four-fifths rule at one cut and fail it at another.
Even a small difference (\(d = 0.2\)) falls below 0.80 when fewer than about 34% of applicants are hired. With \(d = 0.5\), the rule is met only if more than about 76% are hired.

Adverse impact is not the same as an unfair test. If the test predicts performance equally well in both groups (the same regression line), the selection rates reflect a real difference in what the test measures. Whether it does is a separate analysis: differential prediction (comparing the groups’ regression lines) and measurement invariance, as in the Measurement Invariance tutorial. Ways to reduce impact while keeping validity include combining the test with other valid predictors on which the groups differ less. The legal rules differ between countries; the four-fifths rule is a screen, not a verdict.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A validation report (APA 7th edition) should give the design and samples, the observed validity with its uncertainty, every correction with the values used and their sources, and the corrected validities. We collect the numbers from the R objects, and get the confidence interval of the corrected validity by correcting both limits of the observed interval:


Code
n_h <- nrow(hires)
ci_obs <- tanh(atanh(r_obs) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n_h - 3))     # Fisher z interval
correct_op <- function(r) case_ii(r / sqrt(ryy_hires), u)                   # the same two corrections
ci_op  <- correct_op(ci_obs)
ci_con <- ci_op / sqrt(rxx)
p_obs  <- cor.test(hires$test, hires$rating1)$p.value

nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))


Method (data analysis):

All 5,000 applicants completed the reasoning test; the 1,500 with the highest scores (selection ratio = .30) were hired. After one year, each hire was rated by two supervisors. The criterion was the rating of the first supervisor; the correlation between the two supervisors’ ratings served as the reliability of a single rating (ryy = .44). Validity was corrected for criterion unreliability using this estimate and then for direct range restriction on the test (Thorndike’s Case II), with the ratio of the test’s standard deviation among hires to that among all applicants (u = .52). The resulting operational validity was further corrected for test unreliability (rxx = .85 among applicants) to estimate construct-level validity. Confidence limits were corrected in the same way. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

Among hires, test scores correlated with supervisor ratings, r(1498) = .22, 95% CI [.17, .26], p < .001. Corrected for criterion unreliability and range restriction, the operational validity of the test was .56, 95% CI [.45, .64]. Further corrected for test unreliability, the construct-level correlation between reasoning ability and job performance was .60, 95% CI [.49, .70]. At a selection ratio of .30 and a base rate of .50, this operational validity implies that 77% of those hired would be successful, compared with 50% under random selection.

Note. N = 5,000 applicants, of whom 1,500 were hired. ryy = interrater reliability of one supervisor’s rating among hires; u = SD of test scores among hires / SD among applicants; rxx = test reliability among applicants. Confidence limits were corrected in the same way as the coefficients.
Points to remember:

Report the observed validity with its sample size and interval, then each corrected value: never only the corrected one.
Give every value used in a correction (\(r_{yy}\), \(u\), \(r_{xx}\)), in which group it was estimated, and where it came from.
Say which range restriction correction you used (direct or indirect), and why.
Correct the criterion only for operational validity; correct the test too only for construct-level claims.
Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("mvtnorm") in R give the exact references.

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
9. Summary







Observed validity
Correlation of test and ratings among hires: too low, because of range restriction and unreliable ratings


Operational validity
Observed test, true performance, all applicants: the one for decisions


Criterion unreliability
\(r / \sqrt{r_{yy}}\), with the rating reliability from the same group as \(r\) (usually the hires)


Direct range restriction
Case II: \(R = rU / \sqrt{1 + r^2(U^2 - 1)}\), \(U = S/s\)


Order
Ratings first (with the hires’ reliability), then range restriction


Indirect range restriction
Selection on something else: Case II under-corrects; use the true-score correction (Case IV)


Construct-level validity
Also divide by \(\sqrt{r_{xx}}\) (applicants’ reliability); for theory, not for decisions


Uncertainty
Corrections multiply the sampling error; correct the confidence limits too


Practical value
Expectancy charts, Taylor-Russell success ratios, utility \(\Delta U = N_s T r SD_y \bar z_x - NC\)


Adverse impact
Impact ratio below 0.80 (four-fifths rule); worse at strict cut scores; not the same as test bias


R
cor(), the formulas above, mvtnorm::pmvnorm(); rwf::compute_dissatenuation() for checks with simulated true scores
