title: Βαθμολόγηση Thurstonian IRT — Θεωρία
text:
Εξήγηση

Το μοντέλο Thurstonian IRT
Το Thurstonian Item Response Theory (TIRT) είναι ένα ψυχομετρικό μοντέλο για ερωτηματολόγια αναγκαστικής επιλογής (forced-choice), στα οποία ο εξεταζόμενος δεν βαθμολογεί κάθε πρόταση ανεξάρτητα, αλλά επιλέγει μεταξύ ζευγών ή ομάδων προτάσεων. Κάθε ζεύγος παράγει μια δυαδική απάντηση \(y \in \{0, 1\}\), ανάλογα με ποια πρόταση προτιμήθηκε.

Δομή του μοντέλου
Έστω:

\(\boldsymbol{\eta} = (\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_K)^\top\) : το διάνυσμα των \(K\) λανθανουσών ιδιοτήτων (latent traits) του εξεταζόμενου
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) : ο πίνακας παραμέτρων φόρτισης (\(N \times K\)), όπου \(\lambda_{ik}\) εκφράζει πόσο ισχυρά σχετίζεται το \(i\)-οστό ζεύγος με την \(k\)-οστή ιδιότητα
\(\tau_i\) : το κατώφλι (threshold) του \(i\)-οστού ζεύγους — αντιστοιχεί στη δυσκολία της επιλογής
\(\theta_i\) : η υπολειπόμενη διακύμανση (residual variance) του \(i\)-οστού ζεύγους
\(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) : ο πίνακας διακύμανσης-συνδιακύμανσης (\(K \times K\)) των λανθανουσών ιδιοτήτων



Μοντέλο πιθανότητας απάντησης (probit link)
Για κάθε δυαδική απάντηση \(y_i\), η πιθανότητα να επιλεγεί η πρώτη επιλογή (\(y_i = 1\)) δίνεται από:
\[P(y_i = 1 \mid \boldsymbol{\eta}) = \Phi(z_i)\]
όπου \(\Phi(\cdot)\) είναι η τυπική κανονική αθροιστική κατανομή (CDF) και
\[z_i = \frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\eta} - \tau_i}{\sqrt{\theta_i}}\]
Ο αριθμητής \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\eta} - \tau_i\) εκφράζει πόσο «εύκολο» είναι να επιλεγεί η πρώτη επιλογή για έναν εξεταζόμενο με ιδιότητες \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\). Η διαίρεση με \(\sqrt{\theta_i}\) κανονικοποιεί ώστε να ληφθεί υπόψη η μοναδικότητα του ζεύγους.




Εκτίμηση MAP (Maximum A Posteriori)
Ο στόχος είναι να βρούμε το διάνυσμα \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*\) που μεγιστοποιεί την εκ των υστέρων πιθανότητα (posterior probability) δεδομένου του παρατηρηθέντος μοτίβου απαντήσεων \(\mathbf{y}\).

Λογαριθμική πιθανοφάνεια (log-likelihood)
Υποθέτουμε, ως απλουστευτική παραδοχή, υπό συνθήκη ανεξαρτησία των δυαδικών απαντήσεων δεδομένου \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\)· η παραδοχή ισχύει ακριβώς για ζεύγη, ενώ για ομάδες 3 ή περισσότερων προτάσεων αγνοεί τις συσχετίσεις των σφαλμάτων εντός ομάδας, με αμελητέα επίδραση στις εκτιμήσεις (Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2011· Maydeu-Olivares & Brown, 2010). Τότε:
\[\ell(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ y_i \log \Phi(z_i) + (1 - y_i) \log\bigl(1 - \Phi(z_i)\bigr) \right]\]


Λογαριθμική εκ των προτέρων κατανομή (log-prior)
Υποθέτουμε πολυμεταβλητή κανονική εκ των προτέρων κατανομή για τις λανθάνουσες ιδιότητες:
\[\boldsymbol{\eta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\, \boldsymbol{\Psi})\]
\[\log p(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\frac{1}{2}\, \boldsymbol{\eta}^\top \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\eta} + \text{const}\]


Αντικειμενική συνάρτηση
Η εκτίμηση MAP ισοδυναμεί με ελαχιστοποίηση του αρνητικού λογαρίθμου της εκ των υστέρων κατανομής:
\[Q(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\ell(\boldsymbol{\eta}) - \log p(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\sum_{i} \left[ y_i \log \Phi(z_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\Phi(z_i)) \right] + \frac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\eta}^\top \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\eta}\]


Κλίση (gradient) για τον αλγόριθμο BFGS
Ο αναλυτικός υπολογισμός της κλίσης επιταχύνει σημαντικά τη βελτιστοποίηση. Ορίζουμε:
\[w_i = \frac{(y_i - \Phi(z_i))\,\phi(z_i)}{\Phi(z_i)\,(1-\Phi(z_i))\,\sqrt{\theta_i}}\]
όπου \(\phi(\cdot)\) είναι η τυπική κανονική πυκνότητα (PDF). Τότε η κλίση της \(Q\) ως προς \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) είναι:
\[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\, Q(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{obs}}^\top \mathbf{w} + \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\eta}\]
όπου \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{obs}}\) περιέχει μόνο τις γραμμές του \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) για τις μη ελλείπουσες απαντήσεις (οι ελλείπουσες απλώς παραλείπονται από την πιθανοφάνεια).
Ο πρώτος όρος \(-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{obs}}^\top \mathbf{w}\) αντιστοιχεί στη συνεισφορά των παρατηρηθέντων απαντήσεων και το δεύτερο \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\eta}\) στην «έλξη» της εκ των προτέρων κατανομής προς το μηδέν.


Αναστροφή πίνακα (Gauss-Jordan)
Η αναστροφή του \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) υλοποιείται χειροκίνητα με απαλοιφή Gauss-Jordan με μερική οδήγηση (partial pivoting) (συνάρτηση compute_solve()), αντί της solve() της βασικής R:
\[[\boldsymbol{\Psi} \mid \mathbf{I}] \xrightarrow{\text{Gauss-Jordan}} [\mathbf{I} \mid \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}]\]
Η μέθοδος υλοποιείται στις συναρτήσεις score_tirt() / score_tirt_pattern() του πακέτου rwf (εκτίμηση με stats::optim(method = "BFGS")).

title: Βαθμολόγηση Thurstonian IRT — Θεωρία
text:
Απλή Εξήγηση

Τι μετράμε;
Φανταστείτε ένα ψυχολογικό τεστ που δεν σας ζητά να βαθμολογήσετε κάθε πρόταση χωριστά («πόσο με εκφράζει αυτό;»), αλλά σας παρουσιάζει ζεύγη προτάσεων και σας ρωτά: «Ποια από τις δύο σε περιγράφει καλύτερα;»
Για παράδειγμα:

(Α) Μου αρέσει να εργάζομαι με ανθρώπους. (Β) Μου αρέσει να αναλύω δεδομένα.

Επιλέγετε ένα από τα δύο — αυτή είναι η αναγκαστική επιλογή. Το τεστ περιέχει δεκάδες τέτοια ζεύγη, και από το σύνολο των απαντήσεών σας θέλουμε να υπολογίσουμε πόσο ψηλά σκοράρετε σε κάθε χαρακτηριστικό (π.χ. κοινωνικότητα, αναλυτική σκέψη, κ.ο.κ.).



Πώς λειτουργεί η βαθμολόγηση;

Βήμα 1 — Τι ξέρουμε εκ των προτέρων
Ξεκινάμε με την παραδοχή ότι οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι είναι κοντά στον μέσο όρο για κάθε χαρακτηριστικό. Αυτό σημαίνει ότι, για να αποδώσουμε ακραίο σκορ, χρειαζόμαστε ισχυρές και συνεπείς ενδείξεις από το μοτίβο των επιλογών.


Βήμα 2 — Τι μας λένε οι απαντήσεις
Κάθε ζεύγος ερωτήσεων «φορτίζει» σε ένα ή περισσότερα χαρακτηριστικά. Για παράδειγμα, αν επιλέξετε «Μου αρέσει να εργάζομαι με ανθρώπους», αυτό αυξάνει το σκορ σας στην κοινωνικότητα. Αν επιλέξετε την άλλη, το μειώνει.
Η «δυσκολία» κάθε ζεύγους (threshold) καθορίζει πόσο σπάνια ή συνηθισμένη είναι η μία επιλογή έναντι της άλλης στον γενικό πληθυσμό.


Βήμα 3 — Εύρεση του «καλύτερου» σκορ
Ο αλγόριθμος δοκιμάζει διαφορετικούς συνδυασμούς σκορ για κάθε χαρακτηριστικό και ρωτά:

«Ποιος συνδυασμός σκορ είναι ο πιο πιθανός, λαμβάνοντας υπόψη τόσο τις απαντήσεις του εξεταζόμενου όσο και το ότι οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι βρίσκονται κοντά στον μέσο όρο;»

Αυτό γίνεται με έναν αλγόριθμο βελτιστοποίησης (BFGS) που «ανεβαίνει» στη βουνοκορφή της πιθανότητας — δηλαδή βρίσκει το σκορ που κάνει τις απαντήσεις πιο λογικές.


Βήμα 4 — Ισορροπία μεταξύ δεδομένων και εκ των προτέρων γνώσης
Το τελικό σκορ δεν βασίζεται μόνο στις απαντήσεις, αλλά και στη γνώση μας για τον πληθυσμό. Αν οι απαντήσεις ενός ατόμου είναι αντιφατικές ή ελλιπείς, το σκορ «τραβιέται» προς τον μέσο όρο — αυτό ονομάζεται συρρίκνωση (shrinkage) και αποτρέπει ακραίες εκτιμήσεις όταν τα δεδομένα δεν είναι αρκετά.




Σύνοψη σε μια εικόνα







Τεχνικός όρος
Απλά λόγια




Λανθάνουσα ιδιότητα (\(\eta\))
Το πραγματικό σκορ που θέλουμε να μετρήσουμε


Φόρτιση (\(\lambda\))
Πόσο «μαρτυράει» κάθε ζεύγος για κάθε χαρακτηριστικό


Κατώφλι (\(\tau\))
Πόσο «δύσκολο» είναι να επιλεγεί η μία πλευρά


Υπολειπόμενη διακύμανση (\(\theta\))
Πόσο «θορυβώδης» είναι η απάντηση


Πίνακας \(\Psi\)
Πώς σχετίζονται μεταξύ τους τα χαρακτηριστικά


MAP εκτίμηση
Το πιο πιθανό σκορ δεδομένων των απαντήσεων


BFGS
Ο αλγόριθμος αναζήτησης που βρίσκει το βέλτιστο σκορ




Βιβλιογραφία: Brown & Maydeu-Olivares (2011). Item response modeling of forced-choice questionnaires. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 71(3), 460–502.
Maydeu-Olivares & Brown (2010). Item response modeling of paired comparison and ranking data. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 45(6), 935–974.

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
text:
Every year, many students in New York City sit the SAT, the US college-entrance test. It has three sections: reading, mathematics and writing. The city publishes, for each high school, the average score of its students in each section, and the number of students who sat the test.
This page asks: how closely do a school’s average reading score and its average writing score go together? A regression of the writing average on the reading average gives a slope and a line.
There is a catch. The schools are very different in size. One school averages the scores of 6 students, another the scores of 1,277. An average of 6 students is far less reliable than an average of 1,277: it jumps around more from one year to the next. So the points on the chart are not equally precise, and ordinary regression treats them as if they were. This is called heteroscedasticity: the spread of the errors is not the same for every row.
Weighted least squares (WLS) fixes this by giving the precise rows more say than the imprecise ones. It is a special case of generalized least squares (see EXAMPLE_GENERALIZED_LEAST_SQUARES.Rmd), where the errors have unequal variances but no correlation between them. Ordinary multiple regression is explained in the hierarchical regression example; here we only look at what changes.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(lmtest)     # bptest(): Breusch–Pagan test; coeftest(): tests with a chosen covariance matrix
library(sandwich)   # vcovHC(): heteroscedasticity-consistent ("sandwich") covariance matrices

# one colour per model, the same in every chart
model_colours <- c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "WLS, weights = n" = "#eb6834", "WLS, estimated weights" = "#1baf7a")

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
text:
1. The data
NYC Open Data, the city’s open-data portal, publishes the 2012 SAT Results: one row per high school, free and with no login. We read it straight from the portal’s CSV address.


Code
t0  <- Sys.time()
url <- "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/f9bf-2cp4.csv?$limit=1000"
raw <- read.csv(url)
seconds <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs"))
str(raw)


'data.frame':   478 obs. of  6 variables:
 $ dbn                           : chr  "01M292" "01M448" "01M450" "01M458" ...
 $ school_name                   : chr  "HENRY STREET SCHOOL FOR INTERNATIONAL STUDIES" "UNIVERSITY NEIGHBORHOOD HIGH SCHOOL" "EAST SIDE COMMUNITY SCHOOL" "FORSYTH SATELLITE ACADEMY" ...
 $ num_of_sat_test_takers        : chr  "29" "91" "70" "7" ...
 $ sat_critical_reading_avg_score: chr  "355" "383" "377" "414" ...
 $ sat_math_avg_score            : chr  "404" "423" "402" "401" ...
 $ sat_writing_avg_score         : chr  "363" "366" "370" "359" ...


The columns are the school code (dbn) and name, the number of students who took the SAT, and the average score in reading, mathematics and writing. The portal’s description says only “mean SAT scores” for the seniors of 2012 and gives no unit; the scores in the file run from 279 to 735, which fits the usual SAT scale of 200 to 800 points per section, but the file does not state it. The download took 6.3 seconds.
Some schools have the letter s instead of numbers. The file does not say why; it is most likely a rule that hides the results of very small groups. We cannot use these rows, so we drop them:


Code
sat <- data.frame(school = raw$school_name,
                  n      = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$num_of_sat_test_takers)),
                  read   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$sat_critical_reading_avg_score)),
                  math   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$sat_math_avg_score)),
                  write  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$sat_writing_avg_score)))
n_hidden <- sum(!complete.cases(sat))
sat <- sat[complete.cases(sat), ]
nrow(sat)


[1] 421


Code
summary(sat[, c("n", "read", "write")])


       n               read           write    
 Min.   :   6.0   Min.   :279.0   Min.   :286  
 1st Qu.:  41.0   1st Qu.:368.0   1st Qu.:360  
 Median :  62.0   Median :391.0   Median :381  
 Mean   : 110.3   Mean   :400.9   Mean   :394  
 3rd Qu.:  95.0   3rd Qu.:416.0   3rd Qu.:411  
 Max.   :1277.0   Max.   :679.0   Max.   :682  


That leaves 421 schools, after dropping 57 with hidden results. The smallest school in the file has 6 test takers, the largest 1,277, and half of the schools have fewer than 62. In all, the schools stand for 46,445 students. Each row is a mean, and the means rest on very different numbers of students.

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
ols <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat)

ggplot(sat, aes(read, write)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.45, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6, breaks = c(50, 250, 1000), name = "test takers") +
  labs(title = "Writing against reading: school averages",
       x = "average reading score", y = "average writing score") +
  theme_bw()









The schools lie close to a straight line. The size of each point is the number of students. The big points hug the line, and the small ones scatter more around it. The residuals show it more clearly:


Code
sat$fitted <- fitted(ols)
sat$resid  <- resid(ols)

ggplot(sat, aes(n, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  labs(title = "OLS residuals fan out in the small schools",
       x = "test takers (log scale)", y = "residual (points)") +
  theme_bw()









A funnel: wide on the left, where the schools are small, and narrow on the right. The usual first check is a plot of the residuals against the fitted values, and it is worth doing. But here the fitted values do not drive the spread: the number of students does, so the plot against n shows it best. In general, plot the residuals against the fitted values, against each predictor and against anything that could change the precision of a row.


Code
bands <- cut(sat$n, c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, Inf),
             labels = c("under 25", "25–50", "51–100", "101–200", "over 200"))
spread <- tapply(sat$resid, bands, sd)


The standard deviation of the residuals falls from 22.5 points in the schools with fewer than 25 test takers to 9.1 points in the schools with more than 200.

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: ordinary least squares
\[\text{write}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \,\text{read}_i + \varepsilon_i\]
Ordinary least squares (OLS) finds the \(\beta\)’s that minimise the sum of squared residuals, \(\sum_i e_i^2\). Every row counts the same. It assumes homoscedasticity: all errors have the same variance, \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\).


Step 2: what goes wrong when the variances differ
Suppose instead that \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma_i^2\) differs from row to row. Then OLS is affected in two ways:

The estimates stay unbiased. On average, over many samples, \(\hat\beta\) is still \(\beta\), as long as the mean model is right.
The standard errors are wrong. The usual formula, \(\hat\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\), assumes one common \(\sigma^2\). With unequal variances, the t tests, p values and confidence intervals can be too narrow or too wide, and there is no way to tell which from the output.
OLS is no longer the best. It is not the linear unbiased estimator with the smallest variance (the Gauss–Markov theorem needs equal variances). There is a more precise one, WLS.



Step 3: weighted least squares
WLS minimises a weighted sum of squares:
\[\sum_i w_i\, e_i^2 \qquad \text{with} \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i)}\]
A row with a large variance has a small weight, so it pulls the line less. In matrix form, with \(W\) a diagonal matrix of the weights:
\[\hat\beta_{WLS} = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W y\]
Only the ratios of the weights matter. Multiplying all weights by 10 changes nothing in the estimates, and the standard errors are rescaled by the residual standard error. The weights are not parameters to estimate in the usual way: they must come from somewhere. There are two cases.


Step 4a: known weights, when each row is a mean
If row \(i\) is the mean of \(n_i\) people, and the people vary around the line with variance \(\sigma^2\), then the mean has variance
\[\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n_i} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad w_i = n_i\]
The weight is the number of people. This is the textbook case of known weights, and in R it is lm(y ~ x, weights = n).
It assumes that the variance comes only from averaging people. If schools also differ from each other for other reasons, for example in how well they teach, that adds a constant \(\tau^2\) that does not shrink with \(n_i\):
\[\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \tau^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{n_i}\]
Then giving a school of 1,000 students 1,000 times the weight of a school of one student is too much. We will see which of the two holds in these data.


Step 4b: estimated weights (feasible WLS)
Often the variances are not known, and we must model them from the residuals:

Fit OLS and keep the residuals \(e_i\).
Model the variance: regress \(e_i^2\) (or \(\log e_i^2\)) on the variables that could change it. Here, on \(1/n_i\).
Turn the fitted variances into weights, \(w_i = 1 / \widehat{\text{Var}}_i\).
Refit by WLS.

This is feasible WLS (or feasible generalized least squares). It is not exact, because the weights are themselves estimates, and the standard errors from lm() do not take that uncertainty into account. With a few hundred rows and a simple variance model, this matters little.


Step 5: the other way out, keep OLS and fix the standard errors
OLS is still unbiased. So an alternative is to keep the OLS estimates and replace only the wrong standard errors with heteroscedasticity-consistent ones, also called robust or sandwich standard errors. The covariance matrix of \(\hat\beta\) is built as a sandwich:
\[\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat\beta) = (X^\top X)^{-1} \Big( \sum_i e_i^2\, x_i x_i^\top \Big) (X^\top X)^{-1}\]
The squared residual \(e_i^2\) stands in for the unknown variance of each row, so no model for the variance is needed (White, 1980). The version called HC3 (MacKinnon & White, 1985; type = "HC3" in vcovHC()) is the safest for samples of this size (Long & Ervin, 2000).









WLS
OLS with sandwich standard errors




Estimates
Change (they are weighted)
The same as OLS


Needs
A good model for the variances
Nothing about the variances


Efficiency
Better, if the variance model is right
Not improved: OLS stays inefficient


If the variance model is wrong
Estimates still unbiased, but the usual standard errors are wrong (use sandwich with WLS too)
Not applicable


Makes sense when
The weights are known or well understood, as with group means
The variance pattern is unknown, or you care only about valid inference

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
section: 4. Fitting the model and reading the output
text:
4. Fitting the model and reading the output

Is there heteroscedasticity? The Breusch–Pagan test
The Breusch–Pagan test (Breusch & Pagan, 1979) regresses the squared residuals on a set of variables. The null hypothesis is homoscedasticity. bptest() from lmtest uses the Koenker version, which does not need normal errors. By default it uses the predictors of the model, here the reading score:


Code
bp_read <- bptest(ols)
bp_read



    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  ols
BP = 0.898, df = 1, p-value = 0.3433


With the reading score as the only suspect, the test does not find a problem, \(\chi^2\)(1) = 0.90, p = .343. But the test only looks for variance that is linked to the variables we give it. The funnel is linked to the number of students, so we give it 1/n, the variable that the formula of step 4a points to:


Code
bp_n <- bptest(ols, ~ I(1/n), data = sat)
bp_n



    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  ols
BP = 102.3, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16


Now it is clear, \(\chi^2\)(1) = 102.3, p < .001. A non-significant test does not prove homoscedasticity: it means that this pattern was not found. Always look at the plots, and choose the variables for the test by thinking about where the variance comes from.


The OLS fit


Code
summary(ols)



Call:
lm(formula = write ~ read, data = sat)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-63.292  -7.206   0.851   8.866  44.999 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -7.52321    4.93528  -1.524    0.128    
read         1.00164    0.01219  82.166   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 14.19 on 419 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9416,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9414 
F-statistic:  6751 on 1 and 419 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The slope is 1.002 points of writing for each point of reading, with a standard error of 0.012. The slope is close to 1: a school with 10 points more in reading has about 10 points more in writing. \(R^2\) = .942, which is very high, as expected for averages of the same students.


WLS with known weights: weights = n
lm() takes the weights in its weights argument:


Code
wls_n <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat, weights = n)
summary(wls_n)



Call:
lm(formula = write ~ read, data = sat, weights = n)

Weighted Residuals:

-369.59  -75.02   -7.79   60.09  420.08 

Coefficients:

(Intercept) -24.036681   2.891675  -8.312 1.32e-15 ***
read          1.046313   0.006557 159.563  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 106 on 419 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9838,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9838 
F-statistic: 2.546e+04 on 1 and 419 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The slope is now 1.046 and the intercept -24.0, against -7.5 with OLS. In the output, “Weighted Residuals” are \(\sqrt{w_i}\,e_i\), and the residual standard error is in those units, which is why it is 106.0 and not comparable to OLS’s 14.2 points. It is the estimate of \(\sigma\), the standard deviation of one student, under this model.
Do the weights \(w = n\) do their job? After weighting, the residuals \(\sqrt{n_i}\,e_i\) should have the same spread for all schools. We check this in section 6, but we can already see a warning in the variance model of the next step.


WLS with estimated weights
We follow the four steps of section 3. We regress the squared OLS residuals on \(1/n\):
\[e_i^2 = \tau^2 + \sigma^2 \,\frac{1}{n_i} + \text{error}\]


Code
variance_model <- lm(resid^2 ~ I(1/n), data = sat)
tau2   <- coef(variance_model)[[1]]
sigma2 <- coef(variance_model)[[2]]
c(tau2 = tau2, sigma2 = sigma2)


      tau2     sigma2 
  29.48956 7121.57004 


The intercept is \(\hat\tau^2\) = 29.5, a standard deviation of 5.4 points that every school has whatever its size. The slope is \(\hat\sigma^2\) = 7,122, a standard deviation of 84.4 points for one student. So a school of 10 students has a standard error of about 27.2 points, and a school of 1,000, 6.1: the floor \(\tau\) dominates for the big ones. This picture shows it, with the pure \(\sigma^2/n\) curve of known weights for comparison:


Code
sigma2_only <- sum(sat$resid^2 / sat$n) / sum(1 / sat$n^2)   # least squares for e^2 = sigma^2 / n, no floor
grid <- data.frame(n = exp(seq(log(min(sat$n)), log(max(sat$n)), length.out = 200)))
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(n = grid$n, sd = sqrt(tau2 + sigma2 / grid$n),  model = "floor + σ²/n"),
  data.frame(n = grid$n, sd = sqrt(sigma2_only / grid$n),    model = "σ²/n only (weights = n)"))

ggplot(sat, aes(n)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = abs(resid)), alpha = 0.35, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(y = sd, colour = model), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("floor + σ²/n" = "#1baf7a", "σ²/n only (weights = n)" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 70)) +
  labs(title = "How the typical error shrinks with school size",
       subtitle = "Points: absolute OLS residuals. Lines: the standard deviation each model expects",
       x = "test takers (log scale)", y = "points") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The pure \(\sigma^2/n\) curve keeps falling, and goes under the points for the biggest schools. The curve with a floor flattens, as the data do. Now we turn the fitted variances into weights and refit:


Code
sat$w <- 1 / fitted(variance_model)
wls_est <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat, weights = w)
summary(wls_est)



Call:
lm(formula = write ~ read, data = sat, weights = w)

Weighted Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-2.9155 -0.7596 -0.0614  0.5882  4.2261 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -18.82137    3.47691  -5.413 1.04e-07 ***
read          1.03322    0.00822 125.697  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.033 on 419 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9742,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9741 
F-statistic: 1.58e+04 on 1 and 419 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The fitted variances are all positive here (35.1 to 1,216.4), which is not guaranteed for a regression of \(e^2\). If some were negative, or near zero, the weights would be nonsense. A safer way is to model the logarithm of the squared residuals, which can never give a negative variance:


Code
log_model <- lm(log(resid^2) ~ log(n), data = sat)
wls_log   <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat, weights = 1 / exp(fitted(log_model)))
c(log_n_slope = unname(coef(log_model)[2]))


log_n_slope 
 -0.4573301 


The variance goes with \(n^{-0.46}\): a pure \(\sigma^2/n\) would give \(-1\), and no dependence on the number of students would give 0. The data lie in between, as the floor suggested. The log version gives a slope of 1.028, almost the same as 1.033 from the first one. The two ways of modelling the variance agree. (One could also repeat the cycle, fitting again to the new residuals until nothing changes. One round is usually enough.)


The three lines


Code
line_data <- data.frame(read = seq(min(sat$read), max(sat$read), length.out = 100))
lines_all <- rbind(
  data.frame(read = line_data$read, write = predict(ols,     line_data), model = "OLS"),
  data.frame(read = line_data$read, write = predict(wls_n,   line_data), model = "WLS, weights = n"),
  data.frame(read = line_data$read, write = predict(wls_est, line_data), model = "WLS, estimated weights"))
lines_all$model <- factor(lines_all$model, levels = names(model_colours))

ggplot(sat, aes(read, write)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey70", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = lines_all, aes(colour = model), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Three fitted lines through the same schools",
       x = "average reading score", y = "average writing score") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The lines are close in the middle and part ways at the ends.

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
section: 5. OLS against WLS, and the sandwich alternative
text:
5. OLS against WLS, and the sandwich alternative
We put the estimates and the standard errors of the three fits side by side. For each fit, the standard errors are given in two ways: the usual ones from lm(), and the sandwich ones (HC3):


Code
fits <- list("OLS" = ols, "WLS, weights = n" = wls_n, "WLS, estimated weights" = wls_est)

compare <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
  fit <- fits[[m]]
  usual  <- coef(summary(fit))
  robust <- coeftest(fit, vcov = vcovHC(fit, type = "HC3"))
  data.frame(model = m, term = rownames(usual),
             estimate = usual[, "Estimate"],
             se_usual = usual[, "Std. Error"],
             se_hc3   = robust[, "Std. Error"],
             row.names = NULL)
}))
compare[, 3:5] <- round(compare[, 3:5], 3)
compare


                   model        term estimate se_usual se_hc3
1                    OLS (Intercept)   -7.523    4.935  5.553
2                    OLS        read    1.002    0.012  0.014
3       WLS, weights = n (Intercept)  -24.037    2.892  4.704
4       WLS, weights = n        read    1.046    0.007  0.011
5 WLS, estimated weights (Intercept)  -18.821    3.477  4.538
6 WLS, estimated weights        read    1.033    0.008  0.011




Code
get <- function(m, term, col) compare[compare$model == m & compare$term == term, col]
ratio_ols <- get("OLS", "read", "se_hc3") / get("OLS", "read", "se_usual")


What the table says:

The OLS standard errors were wrong. With sandwich errors, the standard error of the OLS slope is 0.014 instead of 0.012, 1.17 times as large. The usual output was too optimistic here, and the confidence interval is wider than the one lm() printed. The slope is still very significant, so the conclusion is the same, but with another dataset it might not be. The direction of the error is not fixed: in the simulation below the usual standard error is, on the contrary, too large.
The estimates move. The slope is 1.002 with OLS, 1.046 with weights \(n\) and 1.033 with estimated weights. The intercept goes from -7.5 to -24.0 and -18.8. If the model were exactly right, all three would estimate the same thing and differ only by chance. The intercept of the estimated-weights fit is 11.3 points away from the OLS one, which is 2.0 times the sandwich standard error of the OLS intercept. This is not a formal test, but it hints that the straight line fits the small schools and the big schools a little differently. The file cannot tell us why, and the large schools may differ from the small ones in more than size. Weighting changes which schools the line follows, so the two answers are answers to slightly different questions (Solon et al., 2015).
WLS is more precise, when compared fairly. Compare the sandwich errors, which are valid for every fit: the slope has 0.014 for OLS, 0.011 with weights \(n\) and 0.011 with estimated weights. That is the gain that the weights are meant to bring. The simulation below shows a clearer gain, when the variance model is exactly right.
The usual WLS errors are too small here. For WLS with \(w = n\) the usual and the sandwich errors differ (0.007 against 0.011), which says that the weights \(n\) do not describe the variance well. With the estimated weights the gap is smaller but still there (0.008 against 0.011): even this variance model is not perfect, and the variance may depend on more than the number of students. When in doubt, use WLS and sandwich errors: the weights buy precision, and the sandwich protects against a wrong variance model.


Proof by simulation: unbiased, but with wrong errors
To see the claims of step 2 at work, we generate 2,000 new data sets that follow the variance model we found, with a known slope, and fit both models to each:


Code
set.seed(2025)
reps   <- 2000
true_b <- c(0, 1)
X      <- cbind(1, sat$read)
sd_i   <- sqrt(tau2 + sigma2 / sat$n)              # the standard deviation of each school
wt     <- 1 / sd_i^2                               # the ideal weights: 1 / variance
XtX_inv   <- solve(crossprod(X))
XtWX_inv  <- solve(crossprod(X, X * wt))

sim <- t(replicate(reps, {
  y   <- drop(X %*% true_b) + rnorm(nrow(X), 0, sd_i)
  b_o <- XtX_inv %*% crossprod(X, y)
  e_o <- y - X %*% b_o
  b_w <- XtWX_inv %*% crossprod(X, wt * y)
  c(ols = b_o[2], wls = b_w[2],
    se_ols_usual = sqrt(sum(e_o^2) / (nrow(X) - 2) * XtX_inv[2, 2]))
}))
colMeans(sim)


         ols          wls se_ols_usual 
  0.99964236   0.99989103   0.01213058 


Code
apply(sim, 2, sd)


         ols          wls se_ols_usual 
0.0101162999 0.0080339089 0.0005981061 


The true slope is 1.

Unbiased: the average OLS slope is 1.000 and the average WLS slope 1.000. Both hit the target.
Inefficient: the slope of OLS varies from sample to sample with a standard deviation of 0.010, that of WLS with 0.008. WLS is 1.26 times as precise.
Wrong standard errors: the OLS standard error that lm() prints averages 0.012, while the true spread is 0.010.



Code
sim_long <- data.frame(slope = c(sim[, "ols"], sim[, "wls"]),
                       model = rep(c("OLS", "WLS"), each = reps))

ggplot(sim_long, aes(slope, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "WLS" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "WLS" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "2,000 simulated slopes, OLS and WLS",
       subtitle = "Both centre on the true slope (dashed line); WLS is narrower",
       x = "estimated slope", y = "density") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
text:
6. Checking the model after weighting
After weighting, what should be flat is not the raw residual but the weighted (or standardised) one. For a fit with weights, \(\sqrt{w_i}\,e_i\) should have the same spread for all rows. rstandard() divides further by the estimated \(\sigma\) and by a leverage term, and understands weights.


Code
check <- rbind(
  data.frame(n = sat$n, fitted = fitted(ols),     r = rstandard(ols),     model = "OLS"),
  data.frame(n = sat$n, fitted = fitted(wls_n),   r = rstandard(wls_n),   model = "WLS, weights = n"),
  data.frame(n = sat$n, fitted = fitted(wls_est), r = rstandard(wls_est), model = "WLS, estimated weights"))
check$model <- factor(check$model, levels = names(model_colours))

ggplot(check, aes(n, r, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 100, 1000)) +
  labs(title = "Standardised residuals against school size",
       x = "test takers (log scale)", y = "standardised residual") +
  theme_bw()









Left, OLS still has the funnel. In the middle, the weights \(n\) turn it round: now the big schools scatter more than the small ones, an overcorrection, which is what the floor \(\tau^2\) explained. Right, the estimated weights give a much more even band. A table shows the same by size of school:


Code
sd_by_band <- sapply(list("OLS" = ols, "WLS, weights = n" = wls_n, "WLS, estimated weights" = wls_est),
                     function(m) tapply(rstandard(m), bands, sd))
knitr::kable(round(sd_by_band, 2), format = "pipe")






OLS
WLS, weights = n
WLS, estimated weights




under 25
1.59

0.84

0.83
0.97
1.02

0.72

0.65

The standard deviation of the standardised residuals should be near 1 in every row. For OLS it falls from 1.59 to 0.65, with weights \(n\) it rises from 0.72 to 1.46, and with estimated weights it stays between 0.84 and 1.10.
Other checks work as for any regression:

Linearity: plot the standardised residuals against the predictor, and check there is no curve (see EXAMPLE_POLYNOMIAL_REGRESSION.Rmd).
Outliers and influence: a few schools have large standardised residuals. cooks.distance() and hatvalues() work with weights too. If outliers are the main worry, see EXAMPLE_ROBUST_REGRESSION.Rmd.
Normality: it matters little with 421 rows, thanks to the central limit theorem.
Run the Breusch–Pagan test again, on the standardised residuals. The same test that found the problem should now find less of it. The test is simple enough to do by hand (Koenker’s version): regress the squared standardised residuals on \(1/n\), and take the number of rows times \(R^2\), which follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution with 1 degree of freedom. We do it by hand because bptest() on a weighted fit gave, for the weights \(n\), a statistic larger than the number of rows, which this version of the test cannot produce, so we do not rely on it here.



Code
bp_by_hand <- function(fit) {
  aux  <- lm(rstandard(fit)^2 ~ I(1/sat$n))
  stat <- nobs(aux) * summary(aux)$r.squared
  c(statistic = stat, p = pchisq(stat, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
bp_after <- rbind("OLS" = bp_by_hand(ols), "WLS, weights = n" = bp_by_hand(wls_n),
                  "WLS, estimated weights" = bp_by_hand(wls_est))
round(bp_after, 3)


                       statistic     p
OLS                      101.831 0.000
WLS, weights = n           5.869 0.015
WLS, estimated weights     0.265 0.607


Against \(1/n\), the statistic is 101.8 for OLS (p < .001), 5.9 with weights \(n\) (p = .015) and 0.3 with the estimated weights (p = .607). The by-hand version for OLS matches bptest()’s 102.3, as it should.

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

Variance weights, frequency weights and survey weights are different things
Many programs have one box called “weights”, and people put in three different things. They give the same estimates, but different standard errors:









Kind
What a weight of \(w_i\) means
Use when
Standard errors




Variance (precision) weights
The row has variance \(\sigma^2 / w_i\)
Rows are means of \(n_i\) people, or measurements of known precision
This page: lm(weights = )


Frequency weights
The row stands for \(w_i\) identical cases
A table of counts instead of a long data set
The sample size is \(\sum w_i\), not the number of rows


Survey (sampling) weights
The row stands for \(w_i\) people in the population, because it was sampled with probability \(1/w_i\)
A complex survey, to estimate for the population
Need the survey design: survey::svyglm()



lm(weights = ) always treats the weights as variance weights. Here is what happens if you wrongly think of the \(n\) as a frequency, that is, if you take each school to be \(n_i\) separate identical students:


Code
df_rows <- df.residual(wls_n)               # the number of schools, minus 2
df_freq <- sum(sat$n) - 2                   # the number of students, minus 2
se_variance  <- summary(wls_n)$coefficients["read", 2]
se_frequency <- se_variance * sqrt(df_rows / df_freq)


The slope would have a standard error of 0.0006 instead of 0.0066, which is 10.5 times too small. The schools are 421 pieces of information, not 46,445. A frequency weight multiplies the information, a variance weight only redistributes it. If your weights are survey weights, do not use lm(weights = ) for inference at all: the errors need the design of the survey, or at least sandwich errors, and the survey weights are there to make the estimate represent the population, not to make it more precise.


Weighting changes the question
OLS answers “what is the line through the schools?”, WLS answers “what is the line, in which the schools with more information count more?”. If the straight line is exactly right, the two agree and the weights only add precision. If the two lines differ a lot, as with the intercepts of section 5, the model is probably wrong somewhere, and the weights should not hide it. Find the reason, rather than choose the line you prefer.


The caveats of these data

Averages of averages. These are school means, not students. A line through schools says how the school averages go together, which may not be how a student’s writing goes with their reading (the ecological fallacy).
The same students sit all three sections, so the high correlation between reading and writing is partly built in.
Only students who took the SAT, and in 2012 only. The schools with hidden results are not in the data.
The file does not state the scale of the scores or why some are hidden, as noted in section 1.



Other warnings

Wrong weights can mislead. If the weights follow a wrong idea of the variance, for example the pure \(\sigma^2 / n\) here, the standard errors of the usual output are wrong again. Use sandwich errors for safety.
Estimated weights come with uncertainty that lm() ignores. For large samples it does not matter. For small ones, bootstrap the whole procedure, or use nlme::gls() with a varFunc (for example varPower()), which estimates the variance function and the coefficients together by maximum likelihood (see EXAMPLE_GENERALIZED_LEAST_SQUARES.Rmd).
Heteroscedasticity can be the finding. If the spread itself is what interests you, for example if the best students vary more than the weak ones, model it, or use quantile regression, which describes the whole distribution of the outcome rather than one line through its middle.
Transforming the outcome (for example, taking logs) is another remedy when the spread grows with the mean, at the price of changing the meaning of the coefficients.

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the data and the unit of analysis, the test that showed the heteroscedasticity, where the weights came from, the estimates with their uncertainty, and what the robust standard errors say. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
ci_est  <- confint(wls_est)
rob_est <- coeftest(wls_est, vcov = vcovHC(wls_est, type = "HC3"))
ci_rob  <- coefci(wls_est, vcov. = vcovHC(wls_est, type = "HC3"))
r2_est  <- summary(wls_est)$r.squared

apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model        = c("OLS", "OLS", "WLS, weights = n", "WLS, weights = n", "WLS, estimated weights", "WLS, estimated weights"),
  Term         = rep(c("Intercept", "Reading"), 3),
  `*b*`        = f3(compare$estimate),
  `SE`         = f3(compare$se_usual),
  `SE (HC3)`   = f3(compare$se_hc3),
  check.names = FALSE)


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 2012 SAT results of 421 New York City high schools (NYC Department of Education, 2013), after removing 57 schools whose results were not published. Each row is a school mean based on between 6 and 1,277 students (M = 110.3, Mdn = 62). We regressed the mean writing score on the mean reading score. Because school means rest on very different numbers of students, we tested for heteroscedasticity with the studentised Breusch–Pagan test (Koenker, 1981), and we compared ordinary least squares (OLS) with weighted least squares (WLS), using weights equal to the number of test takers and weights estimated from a regression of the squared OLS residuals on the reciprocal of the number of test takers. We report heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors (MacKinnon & White, 1985). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the packages lmtest (Zeileis & Hothorn, 2002) and sandwich (Zeileis, 2004).

Results:

The residuals of the OLS model were more spread out in schools with fewer test takers, Breusch–Pagan χ²(1) = 102.3, p < .001 (for the reciprocal of the number of test takers); the standard deviation of the residuals was 22.5 points in schools with fewer than 25 test takers and 9.1 points in schools with more than 200. In the model with estimated weights, each point of reading score went with 1.03 points of writing score, b = 1.033, 95% CI [1.017, 1.049], SE = 0.008, R² = .974. With HC3 standard errors, the 95% CI was [1.011, 1.055]. The OLS slope was 1.002 with a model-based standard error of 0.012, which rose to 0.014 with HC3 standard errors (Table 1). Weights equal to the number of test takers over-corrected: the standardised residuals then grew with school size, from SD = 0.72 to 1.46, because schools also differ by a variance that does not shrink with size, estimated here as SD = 5.4 points.

Points to remember:

Say what the rows are (here, school means) and how many people each one rests on.
Report the test for heteroscedasticity and the variable it was tested against.
Say where the weights came from, and which kind of weights they are (variance weights).
Give robust standard errors, or say why you did not need them.
Show that the weighting worked, with the standardised residuals.
If OLS and WLS disagree, say so and offer an explanation.

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
text:
9. Summary



When
The spread of the errors differs from row to row: means of groups of different size, measurements of known precision, or a spread that grows with a predictor


The problem
OLS stays unbiased, but its standard errors are wrong and it is not the most precise estimator


Spotting it
Residuals against fitted values, against each predictor and against the group size; lmtest::bptest(fit, ~ z, data = d) for the variable \(z\) you suspect


WLS
Minimise \(\sum w_i e_i^2\), with \(w_i = 1 / \text{Var}(\varepsilon_i)\); in R, lm(y ~ x, weights = w)


Known weights
A mean of \(n_i\) people has variance \(\sigma^2 / n_i\), so \(w_i = n_i\), unless there is also a variance that does not shrink with \(n_i\)


Estimated weights
Regress \(e_i^2\) (or \(\log e_i^2\)) on the suspected variables, take \(w_i = 1 / \widehat{\text{Var}}_i\), refit


Alternative
Keep OLS, and use sandwich standard errors: coeftest(fit, vcov = vcovHC(fit, type = "HC3"))


Do not confuse
Variance weights (lm(weights = )) with frequency weights and survey weights


Checking
The standardised residuals, rstandard(), against the variable that drives the variance


Related pages
Generalized least squares, robust regression, quantile regression

title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
1. Theoretical Framework
Generalized Linear Models (GLMs; Nelder & Wedderburn, 1972) extend ordinary least squares regression to outcome variables whose conditional distribution belongs to the exponential family. A GLM is defined by three components:

Random component — the conditional distribution of \(Y | \mathbf{x}\) (e.g., Normal, Binomial, Poisson, Gamma)
Systematic component — a linear predictor \(\eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}\)
Link function \(g(\cdot)\) — a monotone differentiable function relating the conditional mean \(\mu_i = E[Y_i|\mathbf{x}_i]\) to the linear predictor: \(g(\mu_i) = \eta_i\)

The model is estimated via maximum likelihood, and inference relies on asymptotic normality of the MLE. Parameters are tested with Wald statistics (\(z = \hat\beta / \text{SE}\), asymptotically standard normal) or likelihood ratio tests (LRTs, asymptotically \(\chi^2\)).



Family
Usual link
Use case




Gaussian
Identity
Continuous, symmetric outcome


Binomial
Logit
Binary / proportion outcome


Poisson
Log
Non-negative integer counts


Negative Binomial
Log
Overdispersed counts


Gamma
Inverse / Log
Positive skewed continuous



The links are the canonical ones, except the log for the Negative Binomial and Gamma families.

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
2. Gaussian GLM — Insurance Charges

2.1 Data and Rationale
Medical insurance charges are right-skewed and strictly positive. A log transformation induces approximate normality, making a Gaussian GLM with identity link on \(\log(\text{charges})\) appropriate. Alternatively, a Gamma GLM with log link directly models the original scale without requiring a transformation.


Code
p1 <- ggplot(df_insurance, aes(x=charges)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50, fill="#2166ac", colour="white") +
  theme_bw() + labs(title="Raw charges\n(right-skewed)", x="Charges (USD)")

p2 <- ggplot(df_insurance, aes(x=log_charges)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50, fill="#4dac26", colour="white") +
  theme_bw() + labs(title="Log-transformed charges\n(approx. normal)", x="log(Charges)")

plot_multiplot(p1, p2, cols=2)











2.2 Model Specification and Estimation
We fit a full model with all main effects and the theoretically motivated smoker × bmi interaction (smoking amplifies the effect of obesity on health costs).


Code
m_gauss_null <- glm(log_charges ~ 1,
                    family=gaussian(link="identity"),
                    data=df_insurance)

m_gauss_main <- glm(log_charges ~ age + sex + bmi + children + smoker + region,
                    family=gaussian(link="identity"),
                    data=df_insurance)

m_gauss_full <- glm(log_charges ~ age + sex + bmi + children + smoker + region +
                      smoker:bmi,
                    family=gaussian(link="identity"),
                    data=df_insurance)

summary(m_gauss_full)

2.4 Likelihood Ratio Test — Interaction Term
The deviance of a Gaussian model is its residual sum of squares. The \(\chi^2\) statistic is the drop in deviance divided by the residual variance of the larger model: anova() uses it for the p value but prints only the drop.

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
3. Binomial GLM — Graduate Admission

3.1 Data and Rationale
The df_admission dataset contains binary admission decisions (0/1) from a graduate programme alongside GRE score, GPA, and institutional rank. A binomial GLM with logit link — logistic regression — models the log-odds of admission as a linear function of the predictors.
\[\log\frac{P(\text{admit}=1|\mathbf{x})}{1-P(\text{admit}=1|\mathbf{x})} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{gre} + \beta_2\,\text{gpa} + \beta_3\,\text{rank}\]

  theme_bw() + labs(title="GRE by admission", fill=NULL)

title: Generalized Linear Models
section: 4. Poisson and Negative Binomial GLM — Insurance Children
text:
4. Poisson and Negative Binomial GLM — Insurance Children

4.1 Rationale
The number of dependent children is a non-negative integer — a natural candidate for Poisson regression. A key assumption of the Poisson model is equidispersion (\(\text{Var}[Y] = \mu\)). When the variance exceeds the mean (overdispersion), the Negative Binomial GLM provides a robust alternative by introducing a dispersion parameter \(\alpha\) such that \(\text{Var}[Y] = \mu + \alpha\mu^2\).


4.2 Checking for Overdispersion


Code
cat("Mean of children:", round(mean(df_insurance$children), 4), "\n")


Mean of children: 1.0949 


Code
cat("Var  of children:", round(var(df_insurance$children),  4), "\n")


Var  of children: 1.4532 


Code
cat("Dispersion ratio :", round(var(df_insurance$children)/mean(df_insurance$children), 4), "\n")


Dispersion ratio : 1.3272 




Code
ggplot(df_insurance, aes(x=children)) +
  geom_bar(fill="#2166ac", colour="white") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title="Distribution of number of children", x="Children", y="Count")











4.3 Poisson Model


Code
m_pois <- glm(children ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + region,
              family=poisson(link="log"),
              data=df_insurance)
summary(m_pois)

Rule of thumb for overdispersion: the ratio of the residual deviance to its degrees of freedom; values well above 1 suggest overdispersion.

cat("Residual deviance / df:", round(dispersion_ratio, 4), "\n")


Residual deviance / df: 1.4996

4.4 Negative Binomial Model

               data=df_insurance)
summary(m_nb)

    data = df_insurance, init.theta = 2.596859124, link = log)

(Intercept)     -0.184715   0.185935  -0.993    0.320
age              0.003570   0.002235   1.597    0.110
sexmale          0.039297   0.062625   0.628    0.530
bmi              0.002196   0.005389   0.407    0.684
smokeryes        0.025660   0.077409   0.331    0.740
regionnorthwest  0.092149   0.089517   1.029    0.303
regionsoutheast -0.008422   0.091333  -0.092    0.927
regionsouthwest  0.083844   0.089907   0.933    0.351

(Dispersion parameter for Negative Binomial(2.5969) family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 1507.2  on 1337  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 1502.0  on 1330  degrees of freedom
AIC: 3834.6

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 1

              Theta:  2.597 
          Std. Err.:  0.412 

 2 x log-likelihood:  -3816.557 


Code
cat("\nEstimated dispersion parameter (theta):", round(m_nb$theta, 4), "\n")



Estimated dispersion parameter (theta): 2.5969 




4.5 Poisson vs. Negative Binomial — Likelihood Ratio Test
The Negative Binomial model has one more parameter than the Poisson model, \(\alpha\). With \(\alpha = 0\) it is the Poisson model (glm.nb() reports \(\theta = 1/\alpha\)), so the two are nested and a likelihood ratio test can compare them:
\[LR = 2\,(\ell_{\text{NB}} - \ell_{\text{Poisson}})\]
Because \(\alpha\) cannot be negative, the null hypothesis \(\alpha = 0\) lies at the edge of its range. If it is true, the statistic is 0 about half of the time and follows \(\chi^2_1\) otherwise, so the p value is half of the \(\chi^2_1\) tail area (Lawless, 1987).
anova(m_pois, m_nb, test="LRT") does not give this test. It subtracts the two residual deviances, which are measured from different saturated models, and it has 0 degrees of freedom because it does not count \(\alpha\).


Code
lr_nb <- as.numeric(2 * (logLik(m_nb) - logLik(m_pois)))
p_nb  <- pchisq(lr_nb, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE) / 2

cat("AIC Poisson        :", round(AIC(m_pois), 2), "\n")


AIC Poisson        : 3899.8 


Code
cat("AIC Negative Binom :", round(AIC(m_nb),   2), "\n")


AIC Negative Binom : 3834.56 


Code
cat("Log-likelihood Pois:", round(logLik(m_pois), 2), "\n")


Log-likelihood Pois: -1941.9 


Code
cat("Log-likelihood NB  :", round(logLik(m_nb),   2), "\n")


Log-likelihood NB  : -1908.28 


Code
cat("Likelihood ratio   :", round(lr_nb, 2), "\n")


Likelihood ratio   : 67.24 


Code
cat("p value            :", format.pval(p_nb, digits=3, eps=0.001), "\n")


p value            : <0.001 


The test rejects the Poisson model (LR = 67.24, p < .001) and the AIC of the Negative Binomial model is 65.24 lower, so the counts are overdispersed, as the ratio in section 4.3 suggested. The coefficients of the two models are nearly the same; it is the standard errors that change. They are about 19% larger in the Negative Binomial model, because the Poisson model assumes less variance than the data have.

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
6. Model Comparison and Selection

6.1 Information Criteria
AIC penalises model complexity as \(-2\ell + 2k\); BIC uses \(-2\ell + k\ln n\) and imposes a heavier penalty for larger samples, favouring more parsimonious models. Here \(\ell\) is the log-likelihood and \(k\) the number of estimated parameters: the coefficients, plus the residual variance of a Gaussian model or \(\theta\) of a Negative Binomial model.


Code
models <- list(
  "Gaussian — main effects"    = m_gauss_main,
  "Gaussian — + smoker×bmi"    = m_gauss_full,
  "Logistic — admission"       = m_admit_main,
  "Poisson — children"         = m_pois,
  "Neg. Binom — children"      = m_nb,
  "Logistic — Titanic main"    = m_titanic_main,
  "Logistic — Titanic + int."  = m_titanic_int
)

aic_df <- data.frame(
  Model    = names(models),
  k        = sapply(models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  LogLik   = sapply(models, function(m) round(as.numeric(logLik(m)), 2)),
  AIC      = sapply(models, function(m) round(AIC(m), 2)),
  BIC      = sapply(models, function(m) round(BIC(m), 2)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

Model estimates are provided by three main matrices:  1. The lambda matrix representing factor loadings  2. The theta matrix, containing residual (error) variances of the items on the diagonal and residual covariances between items off the diagonal  3. The psi matrix, containing factor variances on the diagonal and factor covariances off the diagonal 
Model estimates from a converged CFA model reproduce a model-implied covariance matrix, Sigma = Lambda × Psi × Lambda’ + Theta. A covariance matrix can also be computed directly from the item responses (the observed, sample covariance matrix). Because of that, we can compare the covariance matrix implied by the model and the covariance matrix computed from item responses. In a good model, these two matrices should have similar values. Fit indices, shown below, quantify model fit. There is conflicting information and several opinions on critical values of fit indices. In our case we consider good model fit to be indicated by:  1. RMSEA < .07  2. CFI > .90 (acceptable; > .95 good)  3. TLI > .90 (acceptable; > .95 good)  4. SRMR < .08  5. GFI > .95

title: Measurement invariance
text:
Testing for invariance
We first fit the model separately in each group, then fit a series of multi-group models with increasing equality constraints; if constraining lambda, nu (intercepts), theta or psi to be equal significantly worsens fit, the measurement is non-invariant at that level.

Separate-group baseline models
Before testing invariance, we fit the model separately to Group1 and Group2 to check that it fits acceptably in each group (separate-group baseline models).


Code
# Model with the first group responses
ft<-lavaan::cfa(bf_model,data=model_data[model_data$group %in% "Group1",])
# Model with the second group responses
st<-lavaan::cfa(bf_model,data=model_data[model_data$group %in% "Group2",])
data.frame(Group1=lavaan::fitMeasures(ft,c("rmsea","cfi","tli","rni","rfi","ifi","srmr","gfi")),
           Group2=lavaan::fitMeasures(st,c("rmsea","cfi","tli","rni","rfi","ifi","srmr","gfi")))

rmsea 0.0000 0.00512
cfi   1.0000 0.99941
tli   1.0012 0.99912
rni   1.0008 0.99941
rfi   0.9978 0.99575
ifi   1.0008 0.99941
srmr  0.0049 0.00749
gfi   1.0000 0.99986




Test for CONFIGURAL INVARIANCE
For configural invariance we specify a model with 2 groups. This procedure estimates separate lambda, theta, psi and nu (item intercept) matrices for each group, with latent means (alpha) fixed to 0. By comparing the two lambda and theta matrices we notice that their values are not identical. The question is whether the differences between these values are statistically significant. In any case, the configural invariance model below displays similar fit indices compared with the separate-group models above. But more importantly, according to fit indices the model fits the data and this suggests configural invariance.

# CONFIGURAL INVARIANCE

lavaan::fitMeasures(bf,c("rmsea","cfi","tli","rni","rfi","ifi","srmr","gfi"))

In order to test if differences between estimated matrices among models are significant, we have to create a series of models for which impose equality constraints for parameters between groups. By imposing constraints we impose the estimator procedure to keep a matrix between groups equal. For instance by imposing an equality constraint on loadings, we force the parameter estimator to produce models that have equal lambda matrices between groups. Finally we compare the unconstrained and constrained models to see if they have any differences. If the constrained model does not fit significantly worse (and ΔCFI ≤ .01; Cheung & Rensvold, 2002), invariance at that level is supported.


Test for WEAK METRIC INVARIANCE
For weak metric invariance we impose a restriction that groups have equal loadings.


Code

lavaan::anova(bf,bf_metric)

bf        48 573054 573528  46.0                                    
bf_metric 54 573045 573471  48.7       2.79     0       6       0.83




Test for STRONG SCALAR INVARIANCE
For strong scalar invariance we impose the restriction that groups have equal loadings and intercepts and then compare the strong scalar invariance model with the weak metric invariance model.

title: MST
text:
Description
This vignette demonstrates Multi-Stage Testing (MST) using the mstR package alongside helper functions from rwf. MST is an adaptive testing methodology that sits between traditional linear tests and fully adaptive Computerised Adaptive Testing (CAT). Instead of selecting items one at a time, MST groups items into modules and selects the next module based on the examinee’s performance on the previous one.
A typical MST design has multiple stages (e.g., stage 1 → stage 2 → stage 3) and multiple panels (parallel test forms). Stage 1 is usually a single routing module; after each stage, the examinee is routed to an easier or harder module in the next stage depending on their provisional ability estimate (θ̂). This balances measurement precision with practical constraints such as content balancing and test security.
Key concepts used throughout this vignette:

Item bank: a pool of items described by IRT parameters (here, the 2-Parameter Logistic model — discrimination a and difficulty b).
Modules: subsets of items from the bank assigned to specific positions in the MST design.
Transition matrix: defines which modules can follow which — routing rules between stages.
Cutoff matrix: θ or raw-score thresholds that determine which module an examinee is routed to next.
θ (theta): the latent ability, scaled here to a standard normal distribution; θ̂ denotes its estimate.

Installation instructions for rwf can be found on the rwf GitHub repository

title: MST
text:
Basic Examples
This section constructs a small 1-2-3 MST design by hand and demonstrates the two core routing functions: startModule and nextModule.
Item bank construction: Six groups of items are generated using genDichoMatrix under the 2PL model. The difficulty priors (bPrior) are shifted so that items in different modules cover different regions of the ability scale — negative difficulties for easy modules and positive difficulties for hard modules.
Module matrix (modules): A 47×6 binary matrix assigning each of the 47 items to one of six modules. Each column is a module; a 1 indicates that item belongs to that module. colSums(modules) confirms the expected module sizes (8, 6, 6, 9, 9, 9).
Transition matrix (trans): A 6×6 binary matrix defining allowed routing paths. Here, module 1 (stage 1) can route to modules 2 or 3 (stage 2); module 2 routes to modules 4 or 5; module 3 routes to modules 5 or 6. Module 5 is reachable from both stage-2 modules, acting as the medium-difficulty path.
startModule: Returns which module to administer first given the item bank, module structure, and transition matrix. The optional fixModule argument (commented out) would force a specific starting module regardless of the design.
thetaEst: Estimates θ from the response pattern x on the first 8 items using Maximum Likelihood (ML). This estimate is then used to determine the next module.
nextModule with θ cutoffs (cut): Each row of the cutoff matrix holds two module numbers and the threshold between them; the first module is chosen if the value is strictly below the threshold, the second otherwise. At stage 2, θ < 0 → module 2 and θ ≥ 0 → module 3; at stage 3, θ < −1 → module 4, −1 ≤ θ < 1 → module 5 and θ ≥ 1 → module 6 (within the paths allowed by the transition matrix). Two calls show routing for the estimated θ and for a fixed θ of −0.2.
nextModule with score cutoffs (cut.score): Routes based on raw number-correct scores rather than θ estimates. In this case the theta argument must hold the examinee’s summed score over all administered items: here, the score on module 1 (x) plus the score on module 3 (x3), i.e. 4 + 4 = 8, which is below the threshold of 10 between modules 5 and 6, so module 5 is selected. This is useful when IRT scoring is not available or when content-balancing rules are score-based.


Code
it.MST <- rbind(genDichoMatrix(8, model = "2PL"),

title: MST
text:
Simulation Examples
This section runs full MST simulations using randomMST and compares MST performance against CAT using randomCAT. A 100-item bank (five distinct 2PL items recycled 20 times) is used; 90 of its items are assembled into six modules of 15 items each in a 1-2-3 design.
Item bank (it.2PL): Five 2PL items with discrimination values from 0.8 to 1.2 and difficulties spanning −0.8 to 1.1, recycled to fill a 100-item bank. Parameters c = 0 and d = 1 indicate no guessing and no slipping.
Module membership (A1–F1): Six pre-defined sets of 15 item indices each, assembled into module1. A1 is the stage-1 routing module; B1/C1 are the two stage-2 modules; D1/E1/F1 are the three stage-3 modules. Because the bank repeats only five items, the modules have nearly identical difficulty (mean b from −0.11 to 0.21), so “easier” and “harder” refer to routing position rather than to item content.
Simulation 1 — MFI module selection (mst.ex1): A single MST run at true θ = 0 using ML scoring and Maximum Fisher Information (MFI) for module selection. The two Ii() calls confirm the routing decision by comparing total Fisher information in module 2 vs. module 3 at the stage-1 θ estimate (mst.ex1$thetaProv[1], available because allTheta = TRUE) — the module with higher information should be selected. plot(mst.ex1) draws the routing path taken through the MST design.
Simulation 2 — θ cutoff routing (mst.ex2): Routes modules using θ thresholds: at stage 2, θ < 0 → module 2 and θ ≥ 0 → module 3; at stage 3, θ < −0.3 → module 4, −0.3 ≤ θ < 0.3 → module 5 and θ ≥ 0.3 → module 6 (within the paths allowed by the transition matrix). Run at true θ = 1 to verify that the design routes along the upper path (modules 1 → 3 → 6).
Simulation 3 — score cutoff routing (mst.ex3): Routes using raw number-correct score thresholds rather than θ estimates. The scoring method is set to "score" for both routing (test3) and final scoring (final3), so thFinal is the number-correct score rather than a θ estimate — useful when IRT calibration is not available at administration time.
ASB and RMSE across the ability range: A large-scale simulation (1000 replications × 9 ability levels from −2 to +2, all routed through the module1 design with BM provisional scoring and ML final scoring) estimates two accuracy metrics across the full latent trait range:

ASB (Average Signed Bias): mean difference between estimated and true θ — positive values indicate systematic overestimation, negative indicate underestimation.
RMSE (Root Mean Square Error): overall estimation accuracy combining both bias and variance. Lower values indicate a more precise test design.

MST vs. CAT comparison: The final block compares MST (BM scoring, MFI module selection) against CAT (45-item stopping rule, BM scoring, MFI item selection, randomesque = 5 for item exposure control) across 9000 simulated examinees spanning θ from −2 to +2. Both formats administer 45 items. Each simulee’s full response pattern to the 100-item bank is generated once with genPattern and passed to both randomCAT and randomMST through responses, so the two designs are compared on the same simulated examinees. Both thFinal (final ability estimate) and seFinal (standard error of measurement) are stored in RES for comparison of precision between the two adaptive testing formats.


Code
A1 <- c(7, 13, 14, 15, 22, 28, 34, 38, 51, 59, 70, 84, 85, 87, 89)

final <- list(method = "ML")

Accuracy across the ability range
The block below runs 1000 replications at each of 9 true θ levels (from −2 to +2) through the module1 design, then computes ASB and RMSE at every level from the resulting θ estimates. Response patterns are generated once with genPattern and passed to randomMST through responses, so every simulee answers independently generated items.


Code
s <- seq(-2, 2, 0.5)
TH <- rep(s, each = 1000)
DATA <- genPattern(TH, it.2PL, seed = 1)
RES <- matrix(NA, length(TH), 1)
start <- list(theta = 0)
test <- list(method = "BM", moduleSelect = "MFI")
final <- list(method = "ML")

for (i in 1:length(TH)){
  prov <- randomMST(trueTheta = TH[i], responses = DATA[i, ],
                    itemBank = it.2PL, modules = module1,
                    transMatrix = trans, start = start,
                    test = test, final = final)
  RES[i, 1] <- prov$thFinal
}

res.ASB <- res.RMSE <- matrix(NA, length(s), 1)
ASB <- function(t, th) mean(t-th)
RMSE <- function(t, th) sqrt(mean((t-th)^2))

for (i in 1:length(s)){
  ind <- which(TH == s[i])
  res.ASB[i, 1] <- ASB(RES[ind, 1], s[i])
  res.RMSE[i, 1] <- RMSE(RES[ind, 1], s[i])
}

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +

ASB stays close to zero in the middle of the range and drifts slightly outward at the extremes (-0.06 at θ = −2, 0.05 at θ = +2), the typical outward bias of ML final estimates: very low abilities are slightly underestimated and very high abilities slightly overestimated. RMSE is lowest near the middle of the scale (0.31 at θ = -0.5) and rises to 0.5 at θ = −2 and 0.46 at θ = +2, because the bank’s item difficulties (−0.8 to 1.1) concentrate information near the middle of the scale.


MST vs. CAT comparison
This block compares MST (BM scoring, MFI module selection) against CAT (45-item stopping rule, BM scoring, MFI item selection, randomesque = 5 for item exposure control) across 9000 simulated examinees spanning θ from −2 to +2.


Code
s <- seq(-2, 2, 0.5)
TH <- rep(s, each = 1000)
DATA <- genPattern(TH, it.2PL, seed = 1)
set.seed(1)
RES <- matrix(NA, length(TH), 4)

start.mst <- list(theta = 0)
start.cat <- list(theta = 0, randomesque = 5)
test.cat <- list(method = "BM", itemSelect = "MFI", randomesque = 5)
test.mst <- list(method = "BM", moduleSelect = "MFI")
stop <- list(rule = "length", thr = 45)
final <- list(method = "BM")

for (i in 1:length(TH)){
  pr <- randomCAT(trueTheta = TH[i], responses = DATA[i, ],
                  itemBank = it.2PL, start = start.cat,
                  test = test.cat, stop = stop, final = final)
  RES[i,1] <- pr$thFinal
  RES[i,2] <- pr$seFinal
  pr <- randomMST(trueTheta = TH[i], responses = DATA[i, ],
                  itemBank = it.2PL, modules = module1,
                  transMatrix = trans, start = start.mst,
                  test = test.mst, final = final)
  RES[i,3] <- pr$thFinal
  RES[i,4] <- pr$seFinal
}

  theta     = TH,
  cat_theta = RES[, 1],
  cat_se    = RES[, 2],
  mst_theta = RES[, 3],

    mst_ASB  = ASB(df_compare$mst_theta[ind], th),
    mst_RMSE = RMSE(df_compare$mst_theta[ind], th),
    mst_SE   = mean(df_compare$mst_se[ind])
  )
}))

With both formats answering the same simulated response patterns, CAT has a lower RMSE than MST at 9 of 9 θ levels (CAT 0.27–0.38 vs. MST 0.28–0.44) and a lower average SE at 9 of 9 levels. The RMSE gap is small near the middle of the scale and largest at the extremes (0.06 at θ = 2). Both formats show the inward bias typical of BM scoring — positive ASB at low θ and negative ASB at high θ, i.e. estimates pulled toward the prior mean of 0 — and it is somewhat stronger for MST (ASB 0.29 at θ = −2 and -0.26 at θ = +2, vs. 0.22 and -0.19 for CAT). This is the expected pattern: CAT selects the single best item at every step, so it should match or beat MST’s precision — MST instead trades some of that per-item precision for the practical advantages of pre-assembled, reviewable modules (content balancing, easier quality control, and no need for real-time item-level adaptation).

title: MST
text:
Conclusion
This vignette worked through MST from the ground up: routing a single examinee by hand with startModule/nextModule (via both θ and raw-score cutoffs), running full simulated administrations with randomMST under three different routing rules, and evaluating a complete design’s accuracy (ASB, RMSE) across the ability range. The final comparison against catR’s randomCAT quantifies the precision MST gives up relative to fully adaptive CAT in exchange for its practical advantages — fixed, reviewable modules assembled ahead of time rather than item-by-item adaptive selection.

title: CAT Simulation
text:
This document is a practical exercise illustrating a Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) simulation. CAT is grounded in Item Response Theory (IRT) and requires prior estimation of item parameters. Its purpose is to deliver short, tailored questionnaires by selecting items from a pool in real time based on each respondent’s estimated ability. For example, if a participant answers a difficult item correctly, the algorithm skips easier items and instead presents a harder one to narrow down the ability estimate more efficiently. As a result, participants do not need to respond to every item in the pool. This simulation uses an item pool of 200 items with a maximum of 40 items administered per respondent. The catR package handles the simulation, while foreach and doSNOW are used for parallel computation.


Code
library(catR)
library(foreach)
library(doSNOW)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)




This simulation uses the 2PL (two-parameter logistic) model, which assigns two parameters to each item: a discrimination parameter (a), reflecting how well the item distinguishes between ability levels, and a difficulty parameter (b), reflecting how hard the item is. The genDichoMatrix function from catR generates item parameters for dichotomous (binary) items — items scored as either correct (1) or incorrect (0), such as multiple-choice questions.
The 200-item bank is generated with the following priors:

Parameter a follows a normal distribution with mean 2 and SD 0.1, ensuring all discrimination values are positive.
Parameter b follows a normal distribution with mean 0 and SD 4, producing items that span a wide range of difficulty — from very easy (large negative b) to very hard (large positive b).

A high a value means the item sharply differentiates between respondents near its difficulty level; a high b value means only respondents with high ability are likely to answer correctly.
genDichoMatrix also includes c (pseudo-guessing) and d (inattention) parameters. Since their values default to 0 and 1 respectively, they have no practical effect and the model reduces to a standard 2PL formulation.


Code
itemBank<-genDichoMatrix(items=200,model="2PL",aPrior=c("norm",2,.1),bPrior=c("norm",0,4))
head(itemBank)
