Treating the simulated response matrix as real participant data (one row per respondent), the mirt package is used to estimate item parameters and respondent ability scores under the assumption that all items were administered. These full-information scores serve as a benchmark against the CAT estimates produced in the next step.


Code
mirt_model<-mirt::mirt(data=data.frame(data),model=1,itemtype="2PL",technical=list(theta_lim=c(-6,6),NCYCLES=10000))





Each respondent is administered a CAT drawn from the 200-item pool, with a maximum of 40 items. The simulation is configured through four control lists:

start — defines first-item selection. The initial item is chosen to have a difficulty closest to θ = 0 (startSelect = "bOpt"), a neutral starting point before any ability information is available.
test — controls item selection and scoring during the adaptive phase. Ability is estimated using Bayesian Modal (BM) estimation (Birnbaum, 1969). EAP (the default of mirt::fscores) is a common choice; here BM, catR’s default, produced scores that correlate highly with the mirt EAP benchmark (see Plot 1). BM uses catR’s default standard normal prior N(0, 1), which pulls extreme estimates toward 0; this shows up in the conditional bias reported by simulateRespondents at the end of the page. Items are selected by bOpt (the item whose difficulty b is closest to the current ability estimate), and randomesque = 5 adds slight randomisation by drawing the next item at random from the 5 items with b closest to the current estimate. The estimation range is widened from the default [−4, 4] to [−20, 20] so that estimates are not cut off at ±4.
final — specifies the scoring method applied at test termination (BM, same range).
stop — defines termination criteria. The test ends when either 40 items have been administered or the standard error of the provisional ability estimate drops to 0.3 or below — whichever occurs first.



Code
start<-list(theta=0,nrItems=1,startSelect="bOpt")
test<-list(method="BM",itemSelect="bOpt",randomesque=5,range=c(-20,20))
final<-list(method="BM",range=c(-20,20))
stop<-list(rule=c("length","precision"),thr=c(40,0.3))
cl<-makeCluster(parallel::detectCores())
registerDoSNOW(cl)
result<-foreach(participant=1:nrow(data),.combine=rbind,.packages=c("catR")) %dopar% {
  rc_result<-randomCAT(itemBank=itemBank,
                       model=NULL,
                       responses=data[participant,],
                       start=start,
                       test=test,
                       stop=stop,
                       final=final)
  data.frame(questions=length(rc_result$thetaProv),
             est_theta=rc_result$thFinal,
             se=rc_result$seFinal)
  
}
stopCluster(cl)
result<-data.frame(result,mirt_scores=as.numeric(mirt::fscores(mirt_model)))





The results are summarised graphically across six panels:

Plot 1 — CAT vs. mirt scores: Scatter plot of CAT ability estimates against mirt EAP scores. CAT respondents answered at most 40 items, while mirt scores are based on all 200 responses. High agreement between the two validates the adaptive procedure.
Plot 2 — Items administered vs. CAT theta: Respondents with extreme abilities need more items, because the CAT starts at θ = 0 and the first items, with b near 0, carry little information about them. The estimate has to work its way outward, slowed by the N(0, 1) prior, and the pool also has fewer items in the tails (b ~ N(0, 4)).
Plot 3 — Items administered vs. SE: For tests that ended before 40 items the SE sits just below the 0.3 target (between 0.28 and 0.3), because these tests stopped once precision was reached. SE above 0.3 appears only at exactly 40 items: these 283 respondents hit the length cap before reaching the target, which happens for extreme abilities where the pool has few items with matching difficulty.
Plot 4 — CAT theta vs. SE: Standard error stays near 0.3 over most of the scale and increases only at the extremes, where the 40-item cap is reached before enough information is collected. Recall that SE is approximately the inverse square root of the test information (for BM, the information plus the prior’s contribution).
Plot 5 — Distribution of CAT estimated scores.
Plot 6 — Distribution of mirt estimated scores.



Code
p1 <- ggplot(result, aes(x = est_theta, y = mirt_scores)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x     = "CAT Theta",
       y     = "mirt Theta",
       title = paste("Pearson r", round(cor(result$est_theta, result$mirt_scores), 4))
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size=11)

p2 <- ggplot(result, aes(x = questions, y = est_theta)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Questions asked", y = "CAT Theta") +
  theme_bw(base_size=11)

p3 <- ggplot(result, aes(x = questions, y = se)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Questions asked", y = "SE") +
  theme_bw(base_size=11)

p4 <- ggplot(result, aes(x = est_theta, y = se)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "CAT Theta", y = "SE") +
  theme_bw(base_size=11)

p5 <- ggplot(result, aes(x = round(est_theta, 0))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "CAT Theta", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_bw(base_size=11)

p6 <- ggplot(result, aes(x = round(mirt_scores, 0))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "mirt Theta", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_bw(base_size=11)

(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4) / (p5 | p6) +
  plot_annotation(theme = theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white")))












The CAT estimates are roughly uniform between about −6 and 6, as expected because the true abilities were evenly spaced, with pile-ups at the ends of their range (-7.3 to 7.9) where the pool runs out and the N(0, 1) prior compresses the most extreme abilities (true θ runs from −10 to 10). The mirt scores are mound-shaped and on a narrower scale because mirt standardises the latent distribution to N(0, 1) when it calibrates the items. In real applications abilities are usually roughly normal, and item banks are built so that information is highest where most respondents are.
catR also provides simulateRespondents, a convenience function that runs a complete CAT simulation and computes summary diagnostics — bias, RMSE, and mean SE — as a function of true ability.
